		<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand Proposes Sweeping Amendments to Anti-Money Laundering Act: Key Reforms and Implications]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 14 May 2025 06:38:48 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">By Dr. Paul Crosio</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>April 2025</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s Ministry of Justice has unveiled draft amendments to the <strong><em>Anti-Money Laundering Act B.E. 2542 (1999)</em></strong>. This signalled a significant escalation in efforts to combat financial crime, corruption, and illicit foreign ownership structures. The proposed changes, open for public consultation until April 25, 2025, aim to align Thailand with global anti-money laundering (AML) standards while addressing systemic vulnerabilities in corporate transparency.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">&nbsp;<strong>1. Expansion of Predicate Offenses&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A “predicate offense " is the underlying act for a more complex crime, often associated with money laundering or other financial crimes. It generates the proceeds that are subsequently laundered.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The draft introduces a robust definition of predicate offenses to include previously overlooked crimes, ensuring stricter enforcement under AML laws:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; i.&nbsp; Bribery of Domestic and Foreign Officials:&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Offering or promising assets or benefits to Thai or foreign public officials, including those in international organizations, is now classified as a predicate offense. This aligns Thailand with Article 23 of the UN Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) (UNODC, 2003), which mandates criminalizing corruption-linked money laundering.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ii.&nbsp; Nominee Structures:&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Criminalizing arrangements where Thai nationals act as proxies for foreign entities to circumvent the Foreign Business Act (FBA). This includes holding shares, jointly <strong>operating businesses under false pretences, or structuring entities to disguise foreign control</strong>. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has long advocated for such measures under Recommendation 24 (2022), emphasizing transparency in beneficial ownership.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; iii.&nbsp;Enforcement Window:&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A 15-year prescription period for predicate offenses allows authorities to address older violations, reflecting Thailand’s commitment to long-term accountability (Bangkok Biz News, 2024).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>2. Joint Liability for Foreign Investors&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The draft eliminates legal loopholes shielding foreign beneficiaries of nominee schemes. Under the joint accountability framework:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Foreign nationals knowingly using Thai nominees to conduct restricted businesses face equal liability.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This reform responds to Thailand’s Department of Business Development (DBD) 2024 policy, which prioritizes holding all parties accountable regardless of nationality.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Implications: Foreign investors must rigorously audit ownership structures to avoid asset seizure or prosecution.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>3. Mandatory Beneficial Ownership Disclosure&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The draft mandates unprecedented transparency for Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs):&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Definition: UBOs include individuals who directly/indirectly own, control, or dominate entities, including through trusts or asset management arrangements.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Reporting Requirements: Financial institutions and designated professions must disclose UBO details to Thailand’s Anti-Money Laundering Office (AMLO). Noncompliance risks a fine of up to THB 500,000 (USD 13,600) plus daily penalties.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Global Alignment: FATF’s 2023/2024 review commended Thailand’s progress on Recommendation 24, which targets opaque corporate structures.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;4. Targeting High-Risk Sectors&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The amendments specifically address sectors prone to foreign ownership abuse:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Real Estate, Hospitality, and Shell Companies:</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Enhanced asset holdings and partnerships scrutiny.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Cross-Border Corruption: Prosecutors gain tools to trace bribes paid to foreign officials, which is critical for multinational investigations.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Rationale and Regional Context&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s reforms respond to mounting pressure from global bodies and domestic economic risks:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">FATF Compliance: Avoidance of the grey list by closing gaps in AML/CFT frameworks.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Foreign Business Act Enforcement: Dismantling nominee networks that undermine Thailand’s restrictions on foreign-controlled sectors (e.g., agriculture, tourism, media).&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Regional Precedent: It follows Singapore’s and Malaysia’s stricter AML laws, prioritizing UBO transparency and cross-border corruption prosecutions.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;Implications for Businesses and Investors&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">·&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <strong>Due Diligence Overhaul: </strong>Foreign entities must audit shareholding patterns, contractual arrangements, and UBO disclosures.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">·&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Sectoral Risks: Industries historically reliant on nominee structures (e.g., property development) face heightened enforcement.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">·&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Compliance Costs: SMEs and nonprofits may struggle with reporting burdens, necessitating government support.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;Next Steps and Stakeholder Engagement&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The public consultation period allows businesses, legal experts, and foreign investors to propose revisions. Key debates may focus on:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The breadth of arrangements subject to UBO reporting.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Proportionality of penalties for noncompliance.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Final legislation is expected by late 2025, pending parliamentary approval.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Conclusion&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s draft AML amendments represent a paradigm shift in combating financial crime and unauthorized foreign investment. The reforms align with global standards while safeguarding domestic economic interests by criminalizing nominee structures, enforcing joint liability, and mandating UBO transparency. Stakeholders must proactively engage in the consultation process to shape a balanced regulatory framework.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>References&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">1. UN Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC), Article 23 (UNODC, 2003).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">2. FATF Recommendation 24 on Beneficial Ownership (2023).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">3. Department of Business Development (DBD), Policy Statement on Joint Accountability (2024).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">4. Bangkok Biz News, Thailand Targets Nominee Networks (2024).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">5. Draft Anti-Money Laundering Act Amendments, Ministry of Justice (2025).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Enforcing Arbitral Awards in Thailand: A Concise Legal Overview]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 04 Jun 2025 00:57:44 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>By Dr. Paul Crosio</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>May 2025</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s arbitration framework, anchored by its ratification of the 1958 New York Convention and the Arbitration Act B.E. 2545 (2002), provides a structured pathway for enforcing domestic and foreign arbitral awards. While the system aligns with global standards, practitioners must navigate unique procedural and practical challenges. This article outlines key considerations for enforcing awards in Thailand.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Legal Framework&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s arbitration regime is governed by the Arbitration Act B.E. 2545, which is based on the 1985 UNCITRAL Model Law. Notably, Thailand has not adopted the 2006 revisions to the Model Law, opting instead for localized adaptations. The Act empowers tribunals to grant interim measures and mandates courts to enforce awards unless limited grounds for refusal exist (e.g., public policy violations or procedural irregularities under Section 43).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">As Gary Born emphasizes, the efficacy of arbitration frameworks hinges on legislation and on judicial cooperation (International Commercial Arbitration, 3rd ed.). Thai courts generally adopt a pro-enforcement stance, yet local interpretations and procedural nuances require careful navigation.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Enforcement Process&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Court Application: A petition must be filed within three years of the award’s enforceability, accompanied by the original award, arbitration agreement, and Thai translations.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Jurisdiction:&nbsp;<ol><li>Commercial disputes: Court of Justice or IP&amp;IT Court.&nbsp;</li></ol><!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Public contracts: Administrative Court.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Judicial Review: Courts assess compliance with Section 43, focusing narrowly on procedural fairness and public policy.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Execution: Once recognized, awards are enforced akin to domestic judgments under the Civil Procedure Code.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Timeframes:&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Initial proceedings: 6–12 months.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Appeals (e.g., to the Supreme Court): 1–2 additional years.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Asset recovery: Often protracted due to debtor resistance.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;Key Challenges&nbsp;</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Debtor Tactics: Delays via procedural objections or annulment requests (e.g., under Section 40).&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Public Policy: Courts may refuse enforcement for conflicts with Thai law or morals. For instance, in Supreme Court Judgment No. 2050/2566, an award was annulled for binding a non-party.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">State Entities: Sovereign immunity and bureaucratic hurdles under the Administrative Procedure Act B.E. 2539 complicate enforcement against state-owned enterprises.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Asset Tracing: Limited prejudgment freezing mechanisms hinder recovery, particularly in insolvency scenarios.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>&nbsp;Investor-State Disputes</strong>&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s participation in Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) cases, such as Walter Bau v. Thailand and Kingsgate v. Thailand, underscores challenges in enforcing awards against state entities. These cases highlight the need to align domestic laws and international treaty obligations.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Conclusion</strong>&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand remains a reliable jurisdiction for arbitration, bolstered by its adherence to the New York Convention and a judiciary increasingly attuned to international norms. However, award creditors must proactively address challenges:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Secure certified translations early.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Anticipate public policy defences.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Engage local counsel for asset tracking and procedural compliance.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Professor Loukas Mistelis notes that arbitration’s success depends on enforcement efficiency (Concise International Arbitration, 2nd ed.). By leveraging Thailand’s structured framework while mitigating risks, parties can optimize outcomes in this dynamic jurisdiction.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>References:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true,"type":"lower-roman"} -->
<ol style="list-style-type:lower-roman" class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Arbitration Act B.E. 2545; New York Convention;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">UNCITRAL Model Law;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Supreme Court Judgments No. 2050/2566, 3872-3873/2566;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Gary Born, International Commercial Arbitration; Loukas Mistelis, Concise International Arbitration.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Securing BOI Privileges in Thailand]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 09 Jun 2025 02:01:13 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand offers a structured, incentive-driven pathway for foreign investment under the Board of Investment (BOI) regime. Obtaining BOI promotion is frequently essential for operational viability and accessing critical legal and fiscal benefits. However, the application process demands precise legal compliance and strategic navigation.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Understanding the BOI Process</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The BOI operates under the Investment Promotion Act B.E. 2520 (1977). Promotion grants qualifying investors significant advantages, including corporate income tax exemptions (up to 13 years), import duty exemptions on machinery/raw materials, land ownership rights (for promoted activities), and streamlined work permit processes.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Eligibility and specific incentives are strictly contingent upon the project's activity classification and compliance with statutory conditions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>The BOI Application Process</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":9189,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/BOI-Infographic-791x1024.webp" alt="" class="wp-image-9189"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>1.   Determining Eligibility &amp; Activity Classification:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;Projects must align precisely with BOI-promoted activities under specific categories (e.g., Advanced Agriculture, Next-Gen Automotive, Digital Services, R&amp;D). Each category has distinct capital, technology, location, and operational mandates.<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;As legal experts, we analyse your business model against the BOI's detailed criteria to confirm eligibility, identify the optimal activity code, and advise on structuring the project to meet stringent conditions and maximize entitled incentives. Misclassification risks rejection or reduced benefits.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>2.   Preparing and Submitting the E-Application:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;Submission occurs via the BOI's E-Investment Promotion System. Documentation must be comprehensive, accurate, and legally sound. Mandatory documents include:<ul><li>Certified Corporate Documents (Affidavit, Certificate of Incorporation, Shareholder List)</li></ul><ul><li>Detailed Business Plan &amp; Feasibility Study (Market Analysis, Financial Projections)</li></ul><ul><li>Comprehensive Investment Plan (Land/Building, Machinery, Operating Costs)</li></ul><ul><li>Technical Specifications &amp; Machinery List</li></ul><ul><li>Manpower Plan (Local/Foreign Roles &amp; Qualifications)</li></ul><ul><li>Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) or Form E (if mandated by activity/location)</li></ul><ul><li>Land Ownership/Lease Evidence</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;We ensure all documentation meets BOI evidentiary standards, anticipate evaluator questions, verify legal sufficiency (e.g., FBA compliance, share structure), and meticulously review the entire package pre-submission. Omissions or inaccuracies cause significant delays or denial.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>3.   Project Evaluation by BOI Officials:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;The BOI conducts rigorous due diligence, assessing project viability, technology level, economic contribution (employment, skills transfer), environmental impact, and alignment with national strategies (e.g., Thailand 4.0, BCG). Review timelines vary (60- 90+ working days) based on project size and complexity.<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;We manage communication with the BOI, provide supplemental information promptly, clarify legal and technical aspects authoritatively, and strategically position the project's compliance and value proposition throughout the evaluation.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>4.   The BOI Project Presentation:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;Applicants present to a BOI panel (legal, technical, investment officers). This is a critical opportunity to substantiate the application, demonstrate compliance, and justify incentive requests. Expect detailed questioning on project specifics, legal structure, investment rationale, and operational plans.<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;We prepare key personnel, develop persuasive legal and commercial arguments, manage the presentation flow, handle complex technical or regulatory questions with authority, negotiate potential conditions, and ensure all representations align precisely with the submitted documentation and Thai law. Presentation quality directly influences approval terms.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>5.   Receiving the BOI Resolution:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;The BOI issues a formal resolution (approval, rejection, or approval with conditions) within seven business days of the decision. Conditions may impose specific operational, reporting, or investment obligations.<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;We immediately review the resolution for legal soundness, assess the feasibility and implications of any conditions, advise on acceptance strategy, and identify potential points for clarification or negotiation before acceptance.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>6.   Accepting the BOI Resolution:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;Applicants must formally accept the resolution within 30 days via the BOI's Promotion Certificate System (or physically for specific cases). Failure to accept voids the approval.<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;We ensure the timely and correct submission of the Acceptance Form, confirming understanding and capacity to meet all stipulated conditions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>7.   Applying for the Promotion Certificate:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;Within 6 months of acceptance, applicants must submit the final Promotion Certificate application. This requires updated, legally verified documents reflecting the project's finalized structure (e.g., confirmed capital injection, shareholder/director lists, finalized operational plans).<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do: </strong>We meticulously prepare and verify all final documentation, ensuring absolute consistency with the approved resolution and underlying BOI standards. Any discrepancy may jeopardize the issuance of the certificate and reduce the associated privileges.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>8.   Issuance of the Promotion Certificate:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What is Required:</strong>&nbsp;The BOI issues the formal Promotion Certificate within approximately. 10 business days of a complete final submission. This certificate legally enshrines the granted privileges and their specific conditions.<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>What we do:</strong>&nbsp;We verify the accuracy of the certificate against the approved resolution. Crucially, they implement systems to ensure ongoing compliance with all BOI reporting requirements (progress reports, annual audits) and conditions throughout the promotion period to prevent revocation of benefits.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Conclusion:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The BOI pathway offers substantial advantages for qualifying foreign investment in Thailand. However, the process is legally intricate, documentation-intensive, and subject to rigorous scrutiny.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Attempting this process without specialized expertise significantly increases the risk of:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Application Rejection:</strong>&nbsp;Due to ineligibility, documentation errors, or non-compliance.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Substantial Delays:</strong>&nbsp;Caused by requests for clarification, resubmissions, or procedural missteps.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Reduced Incentives:</strong>&nbsp;Failure to optimally structure the application or present it effectively.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Compliance Penalties:</strong>&nbsp;Post-approval failures in reporting or meeting conditions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Engaging experienced Thai legal advisors from the outset is a critical success factor.</strong>&nbsp;They provide the necessary legal precision, strategic navigation, and procedural expertise to efficiently secure BOI promotion, maximize entitled benefits, and ensure long-term compliance, thereby protecting your investment and enabling timely market entry.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->]]></content:encoded>

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thai Supreme Court Shuts Door on Long-Term Lease Loopholes: Foreign Property Investors Face New Reality]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 27 Jun 2025 09:20:15 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s attraction for foreign residents and investors often centres on lifestyle and opportunity. However, navigating property ownership remains a significant hurdle due to strict legal prohibitions on foreign land ownership, except for specific exceptions, such as BOI-promoted projects or designated industrial zones (IEAT). For decades, long-term leases structured with renewal options (often referred to as "30+30+30" leases) have offered a popular, albeit legally contentious, path for foreigners seeking extended control over Thai land and houses. A landmark Supreme Court ruling issued on&nbsp;<strong>March 18, 2025</strong>&nbsp;(Case No. 4655/2566) has now decisively closed this door, sending shockwaves through the real estate sector and forcing a major rethink for foreign property seekers.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>The Established Framework: Condos and the Elusive 30-Year Lease</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Thai law, the primary avenues for foreign property acquisition are clear:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true,"start":1} -->
<ol start="1" class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Condominium Freehold:</strong>&nbsp;Foreigners can own units outright under the Condominium Act, subject to the 49% foreign quota per project.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Leasehold:</strong>&nbsp;Long-term leases, capped at&nbsp;<strong>30 years</strong>&nbsp;by Section 540 of the Civil and Commercial Code (CCC), became the go-to solution for land and houses. Crucially, Section 538 mandates that leases exceeding three years must be registered with the Land Department to be enforceable beyond three years.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Seeking stability beyond the initial 30 years, developers, lawyers, and investors commonly employed structures involving pre-agreed renewal clauses or consecutive lease agreements signed upfront, effectively promising control for 60, 90, or even 99 years. This practice, while widespread, always existed under a legal cloud.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>The&nbsp; Ruling: Supreme Court Rejects "30+30+30"</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Supreme Court's March 18th decision obliterated the legal foundation of these extended lease arrangements. As reported by&nbsp;<strong>The Bangkok Post</strong>&nbsp;and&nbsp;<strong>The Nation Thailand</strong>, the Court ruled unequivocally:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true,"start":1} -->
<ol start="1" class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Strict 30-Year Limit Enforced:</strong>&nbsp;Any lease provision attempting to grant a term exceeding 30 years from the commencement date is&nbsp;<strong>void</strong>&nbsp;beyond the initial 30 years.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Pre-Agreed Renewals are Invalid:</strong>&nbsp;Clauses stipulating automatic renewal for subsequent 30-year terms at the end of the initial lease&nbsp;<strong>are invalid and unenforceable</strong>, regardless of:<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The parties' mutual agreement at the outset.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Any rental payments made for the purported renewal periods.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Registration of the original agreement with the Land Department.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Structuring Attempts Fail:</strong>&nbsp;Schemes using multiple pre-signed lease agreements or pre-agreed extensions designed to circumvent the 30-year ceiling were also deemed invalid. The Court focused on the&nbsp;<em>substance</em>&nbsp;(attempting to secure rights beyond 30 years from the start) over the&nbsp;<em>form</em>.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Public Policy Paramount:</strong>&nbsp;The Court grounded its decision in public policy concerns. It highlighted the inherent uncertainties and potential for unfairness over excessively long durations (60-99 years), including unpredictable changes in property values, conditions, and the obligations of future parties bound by a contract signed decades prior.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Industry Reaction: Validation and Concern</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The ruling, while clarifying long-standing legal ambiguity, has caused significant concern.&nbsp;<strong>The Thai Real Estate Association</strong>&nbsp;acknowledged the impact, stating it necessitates "immediate adjustments in standard practices and clearer communication with foreign clients." International property consultants, such as&nbsp;CBRE Thailand&nbsp;and&nbsp;JLL Thailand, have advised clients to review existing agreements and explore alternative structures urgently.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Legal experts broadly agree that the ruling was predictable based on a strict reading of Section 540 CCC.&nbsp;<strong>Dr. Samrit Srichan, a prominent Thai property law scholar</strong>, commented to&nbsp;<strong>The Bangkok Post</strong>: "The Supreme Court has consistently leaned towards a strict interpretation of the 30-year limit. This ruling finally removes any lingering doubt – pre-agreed renewals designed to act like a single long term are against the law and public policy."</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Implications for Foreign Investors: A Crucial Reassessment</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true,"start":1} -->
<ol start="1" class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Existing "30+30+30" Leases:</strong>&nbsp;The enforceability of the renewal clauses is now highly suspect. While the initial 30-year term remains valid (if properly registered), the promised extensions&nbsp;<strong>cannot be enforced</strong>. Property owners relying on these clauses face significant uncertainty and potential loss of value after year 30.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Future Structuring:</strong>&nbsp;Simply structuring leases with pre-agreed renewals or consecutive terms upfront is no longer a viable option. Lawyers are now emphasizing:<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>True Renewal Negotiations:</strong>&nbsp;Renewals must be genuinely negotiated&nbsp;<em>at the end</em>&nbsp;of the initial 30-year term. There is no legal guarantee that the lessor will agree, or on what terms.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Alternative Security:</strong>&nbsp;Exploring options such as usufructs (which have different rules but also complexities) or corporate structures (subject to Foreign Business Act restrictions) may be considered, but require expert, individualized legal advice.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Reduced Certainty:</strong>&nbsp;The maximum secure term achievable via a lease remains firmly capped at 30 years. Investors must factor this reduced long-term security into their plans and valuations.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Condominium Focus:</strong>&nbsp;The ruling reinforces condominium ownership as the most secure freehold option for foreigners within the legal limits. Scrutiny of condo foreign quotas will likely increase.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Conclusion: Clarity at a Cost</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Thai Supreme Court's ruling provides much-needed legal clarity, bringing an end to years of reliance on a legally precarious structure. However, this clarity comes at a significant cost to foreign investors' long-term security over Thai land and houses. The era of easily marketable "virtual freehold" leases spanning 60-99 years is definitively over.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Prospective foreign buyers must now enter leasehold agreements with eyes wide open: the 30-year limit is absolute, and agreements beyond that are legally hollow. Thorough due diligence, realistic expectations about leasehold tenure, and consultation with experienced, reputable Thai legal counsel specializing in property law are now more critical than ever. This ruling underscores the fundamental principle that foreign land ownership in Thailand remains tightly restricted and attempts to circumvent these restrictions through creative lease structures face an increasingly unforgiving legal landscape.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10273,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/real-estate-infographic-471x1024.png" alt="" class="wp-image-10273"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->

<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true,"start":1} -->
<ol start="1" class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Supreme Court of Thailand:</strong>&nbsp;Decision No. 4655/2566, dated 18 March 2025 (Core Subject of Ruling).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[UNLOCKING GROWTH: HOW THAILAND'S BOI CONCESSIONS EMPOWER SMES IN THE NEW TECH &amp; GREEN ECONOMY]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 14 Jul 2025 05:38:46 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Executive Summary:</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10305,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/boi-incentives-sme-infographic-735x1024.png" alt="" class="wp-image-10305"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's Board of Investment (BOI), under its strategic shift towards a "New Economy," has significantly relaxed and targeted its concession packages, creating unprecedented opportunities for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in high-potential sectors like Agriculture Technology (Agritech), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Software Development, Battery Technology, Renewable Energy, and Green Technologies.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For SMEs (defined here according to the BOI as having fewer than 200 employees and annual revenue not exceeding THB 500 million), securing BOI approval is no longer a distant dream reserved for industrial giants. This article examines the specific advantages of BOI status for SMEs, analyzes recent policy relaxations, outlines the application process tailored for smaller entities, and argues that while qualified legal assistance significantly streamlines the journey, determined SMEs can navigate it successfully.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Introduction: BOI’s Evolution and the SME Imperative</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For decades, Thailand's Board of Investment (BOI), established under the Investment Promotion Act B.E. 2520 (1977) and its subsequent amendments, has been the cornerstone of the kingdom's industrial development strategy. Traditionally, its incentives – including significant tax holidays, import duty exemptions, and relaxed foreign ownership rules – were often perceived as primarily targeting large-scale multinational corporations and major domestic conglomerates undertaking substantial capital investments.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">However, recognizing the critical role of innovation, technology adoption, and sustainability in maintaining competitiveness, the BOI has undergone a strategic transformation. The focus has decisively shifted towards promoting a "New Economy," characterized by digitalization, value-added services, advanced manufacturing, and environmental responsibility. This shift is encapsulated in the BOI's current 5-year strategy (2023-2027), heavily emphasizing BCG (Bio-Circular-Green) and Smart Industry principles.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Crucially, a key pillar of this new strategy is&nbsp;<strong>inclusivity for SMEs</strong>. The BOI understands that true technological advancement and sustainable transformation require a vibrant ecosystem where agile, innovative, smaller players thrive. Recent announcements and policy adjustments explicitly aim to lower barriers and tailor benefits to make BOI promotion genuinely accessible and advantageous for qualified SMEs operating in targeted, future-oriented sectors.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Defining the Target SME</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For this article, we define an SME as a business entity in Thailand with:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Employees:</strong>&nbsp;Fewer than 50 full-time staff.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Annual Revenue:</strong>&nbsp;Between THB 20 million and THB 60 million.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Sector Focus:</strong>&nbsp;Operating primarily in Agritech, AI, Software, Battery Tech, Renewable Energy, or other defined Green Technologies.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">It's important to note that Thailand has various official SME definitions (e.g., based on fixed assets or differing employee/revenue brackets across manufacturing/services). However, the above definition aligns with common international SME thresholds and is highly relevant to the BOI's target groups for the sectors discussed. The BOI itself often uses project investment value as a criterion rather than overall company size, which inherently benefits smaller projects typical of SMEs.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Recent BOI Relaxations: Opening Doors for SMEs</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Over the past 2-3 years, there has been a flurry of BOI announcements specifically designed to attract and support SMEs in the target sectors. The BOI continuously updates its list of promoted activities. Recent updates have explicitly included and defined sub-activities highly relevant to SMEs:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Agritech:&nbsp;Precision farming technology, smart irrigation systems, agricultural drones, biotech for crop/livestock improvement, farm management software, post-harvest tech, controlled environment agriculture (CEA) systems. The BOI recognizes that modernizing&nbsp;Thailand's crucial agricultural sector requires innovation at the SME level.<ul><li>AI &amp; Software:&nbsp;Development of AI algorithms, machine learning platforms, natural language processing (NLP) tools, computer vision applications, specialized enterprise software (ERP, CRM, SCM), SaaS platforms, cybersecurity solutions, embedded software for IoT. Emphasis is placed on&nbsp;<em>development</em>, not just application.</li></ul><ul><li>Battery Technology:&nbsp;Production of battery cells and packs (especially for EVs and energy storage - ESS), battery management systems (BMS), battery recycling technology. While large-scale manufacturing exists, opportunities for niche components, BMS software, and recycling tech are ideal for SMEs.</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Renewable Energy &amp; Green Tech:&nbsp;Engineering services for renewable energy projects (solar, wind, biomass, biogas, hydrogen), manufacturing of specific renewable energy components (beyond massive solar panel factories), energy storage systems (ESS), energy efficiency services and technology, water management technology, waste-to-energy tech, air pollution control tech, environmental monitoring systems. The focus here is</strong>&nbsp;often on specialized services and niche manufacturing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">5.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<strong>Enhanced Incentive Packages (Announcement No. 8/2565, Dec 2022):</strong>&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The BOI revamped its incentive structure, introducing tiers (A1 to B+) based on technological sophistication and value addition. Crucially for SMEs:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Longer CIT Holidays:&nbsp;Top-tier activities (A1, such as advanced battery technology and next-gen software) now offer up to&nbsp;13 years&nbsp;of Corporate Income Tax (CIT) exemption. Even Tier A activities (e.g., significant software development, high-efficiency renewable energy tech) offer 8-10 years. This represents a&nbsp;significant departure from previous norms, offering a substantial runway for SME profitability and reinvestment.<ul><li><strong>Reduced Minimum Investment Requirements:</strong>&nbsp;While still project-based, the BOI has shown flexibility for high-tech and service-oriented activities where significant capital expenditure (CapEx) isn't the primary driver. Investment in intellectual property, software development, and specialized training can often be counted effectively. Media reports&nbsp;&nbsp;highlighted the BOI's intent to attract "knowledge-based" investments with lower physical investment thresholds.</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Focus on Merit over Size:</strong>&nbsp;The new tier system emphasizes the&nbsp;<em>nature</em>&nbsp;of the activity and its contribution to Thailand's goals (tech transfer, R&amp;D, environmental benefits) more than sheer project size.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">6.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<strong>Streamlined Application Process &amp; Dedicated Support:</strong>&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The BOI has publicly committed to improving its service for SMEs:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">One Start One Stop Investment Center (OSOS):&nbsp;Provides centralized assistance, including pre-application consultation, which is invaluable for SMEs navigating the process for the first time.<ul><li>Online Systems:&nbsp;Enhanced online application submission and tracking (via the BOI SMART system) improve accessibility and transparency.</li></ul><ul><li>SME Unit:&nbsp;While informal, the BOI has officers experienced in handling SME applications and understanding their specific contexts and challenges.&nbsp;</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Relaxation of Conditions:&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In specific high-priority sectors, requirements related to local content or export ratios have been eased, recognizing the global nature of tech and green markets, as well as the need for SMEs to scale effectively.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">7.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;BOI Benefits:</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For an SME operating within the THB 20-60 million revenue bracket, the benefits of BOI promotion are transformative:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">a.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Significant Tax Savings: The Core Advantage</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Corporate Income Tax (CIT) Exemption:&nbsp;The most compelling benefit. An 8–13-year CIT holiday means 100% of profits during this period are shielded from Thailand's standard 20% CIT. For an SME averaging THB 40 million in annual taxable profit, this represents savings of&nbsp;THB 8 million per year, or&nbsp;THB 64-104 million&nbsp;over the exemption period. This capital is vital for R&amp;D, scaling operations, hiring talent, and market expansion.<ul><li>Import Duty Exemption:&nbsp;Duty-free importation of machinery essential for the promoted activity (e.g., specialized lab equipment for agritech, servers for AI development, precision tools for battery component manufacturing). This drastically reduces setup costs and improves cash flow.</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Raw Material/Component Import Duty Reduction/Exemption:&nbsp;For manufacturing activities (e.g., specific battery components, renewable energy parts), duties on imported raw materials not available locally can be reduced or exempted for up to 2 years, lowering production costs.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">b.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Enhanced Cash Flow, Profitability, and Investor Appeal:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Improved Cash&nbsp;Flow &amp; Profitability:&nbsp;CIT savings directly boost net profit margins, making the business fundamentally more viable and resilient, especially in the critical early growth phase.</strong><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Attractiveness to Investors:&nbsp;BOI status signals credibility, government endorsement, and strong future profitability (due to tax breaks). This makes the SME significantly more attractive to venture capital, angel investors, and strategic partners seeking</strong><strong>&nbsp;</strong>exposure to Thailand's priority sectors.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">c.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Non-Tax Advantages:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Land Ownership Rights:&nbsp;Perhaps the most crucial non-tax benefit for foreign-invested SMEs. Typically, foreigners face severe restrictions on land ownership under the Land Code. BOI-promoted companies&nbsp;<em>can</em>&nbsp;own land for carrying out the promoted activity, providing long-term security and asset value.&nbsp;<ul><li>Foreign Expertise &amp; Work Permits:&nbsp;BOI companies benefit from streamlined processes for obtaining work permits and visas for essential foreign specialists, managers, and technicians. Quotas are more flexible, and approval times are generally faster. Accessing global talent is vital for tech and green SMEs.</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Foreign Ownership Relaxation:&nbsp;In sectors normally restricted by the Foreign Business Act (FBA), BOI promotion can allow up to 100% foreign ownership, removing a significant barrier for international entrepreneurs or investors wanting to establish or fund an innovative Thai SME.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">d.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Competitive Edge and Market Positioning:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Government&nbsp;Endorsement:&nbsp;BOI status is a powerful marketing tool, enhancing credibility with clients, suppliers, and potential partners both domestically and internationally.<ul><li>Access to Support Networks:&nbsp;BOI-promoted companies often gain easier access to government initiatives, R&amp;D matching grants (through other agencies), and networking opportunities within promoted clusters.</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Focus on Core Business:&nbsp;Streamlined import/export procedures and customs facilitation (via BOI Zone privileges) reduce administrative burdens.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">8.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Navigating the BOI Application Process: An SME Roadmap</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While the BOI process is structured, it is navigable for SMEs. Here’s a breakdown of requirements, procedures, and timelines:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">a.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Phase 1: Pre-Application (1-4 Weeks)</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Research &amp; Self-Assessment:&nbsp;<ul><li>Determine if your&nbsp;specific activity&nbsp;is eligible under the current BOI list (Announcements on promoted activities). Scrutinize the definitions and requirements for your target sector (e.g., Agritech, AI Software, Battery Tech).</li></ul><ul><li>Assess if your project meets the technology/value-add tier (A1, A, B+, B) criteria. The BOI website (<a href="http://www.boi.go.th/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">www.boi.go.th</a>) is the primary source. Consider attending a BOI seminar or using OSOS pre-consultation (highly recommended for SMEs).</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Gather Core Company Documents:<ul><li>Company Affidavit (Certified Copy)</li></ul><ul><li>Company Registration Certificate (Certified Copy)</li></ul><ul><li>List of Shareholders &amp; Directors (Certified Copy)</li></ul><ul><li>Company Objectives (must align with promoted activity)</li></ul><ul><li>VAT Registration Certificate (Por Por. 20)</li></ul><ul><li>Latest Financial Statements (Audited preferred, but unaudited may suffice for very new SMEs - consult BOI)</li></ul><ul><li>Business Plan (See below)</li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Develop a Robust Business Plan:&nbsp;This is&nbsp;<em>critical</em>&nbsp;for SMEs. It must clearly demonstrate:</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Project Details: Specific promoted activity, technology used, processes.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Market Analysis &amp; Strategy: Target customers, competition, marketing plan.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Investment Plan: Breakdown of costs (machinery, buildings, IP, training), funding sources.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Operational Plan: Location, staffing (Thai/foreign), production/service capacity.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Technology &amp; Know-How: Explain the sophistication, source of technology (in-house R&amp;D, licensing), and plans for technology transfer/training Thais.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Economic &amp; Social Benefits: Job creation (types of jobs), skills development, environmental benefits (especially for Green Tech), contribution to local suppliers/community.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Financial Projections: 5-year P&amp;L, Cash Flow, Balance Sheet. Must demonstrate viability&nbsp;<em>with</em>&nbsp;and&nbsp;<em>without</em>&nbsp;BOI incentives.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">b.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Phase 2: Application Submission &amp; Review (3-6 Months)</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Prepare &amp; Submit Application:&nbsp;Compile all documents. Submit electronically via the BOI SMART system. Key documents include:<ul><li>BOI Application Form (completed online)</li></ul><ul><li>Detailed Project Proposal (often an expanded Business Plan)</li></ul><ul><li>Company Documents (as above)</li></ul><ul><li>Map of Project Location</li></ul><ul><li>Machinery List (with specifications and values) - if applicable</li></ul><ul><li>Technical Documents: Brochures, specifications of key technologies and processes.</li></ul><ul><li>Licensing Agreements (if technology is licensed)<ul><li>Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) or Initial Environmental Examination (IEE) Screening Form -&nbsp;<em>if required for the activity/location/size</em>. SMEs often fall below EIA thresholds, but IEE screening is standard.&nbsp;</li></ul></li></ul><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>BOI Review Process:</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Completeness Check:</strong>&nbsp;BOI officers check if the application is complete.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Technical and Financial Evaluation:&nbsp;</strong>Specialist committees review the project's technical feasibility, financial viability, technological level, and economic and social benefits against BOI criteria. They may request clarification or additional information.&nbsp;<em>This is where a well-prepared application is vital.</em></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Environmental Review:</strong>&nbsp;Confirmation of EIA/IEE requirements or compliance.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>BOI Sub-Committee Meeting:</strong>&nbsp;The project is presented to a relevant subcommittee for preliminary approval.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>BOI Board Meeting:</strong>&nbsp;Final approval is granted by the full BOI Board, chaired by the Prime Minister. Meetings are typically monthly.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">c.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Phase 3: Post-Approval &amp; Utilization (Ongoing)</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Receiving the Promotion Certificate:</strong>&nbsp;Upon approval, the SME receives the official BOI Promotion Certificate, which outlines the conditions and benefits.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Fulfilling Pre-Operational Conditions:</strong>&nbsp;This may include registering machinery imports, finalize land purchase or lease, and officially incorporating the promoted activity into company objectives.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Applying for Visa/Work Permits:</strong>&nbsp;Submit applications for foreign staff via the BOI's One-Stop Service Center (OSSC).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Claiming Incentives:</strong>&nbsp;File requests for import duty exemptions&nbsp;<em>before</em>&nbsp;importing machinery/raw materials. Maintain meticulous records for CIT exemption claims during operation.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Compliance Reporting:</strong>&nbsp;Submit semi-annual and annual progress reports to the BOI, demonstrating compliance with investment schedules, employment targets, and other conditions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">9.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Realistic Timeline for SMEs:</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Preparation:</strong>&nbsp;1-2 Months (Can be done concurrently with business setup)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>BOI Review &amp; Approval:</strong>&nbsp;3-6 Months (Highly dependent on project complexity, completeness of application, responsiveness to BOI queries, and BOI meeting schedules).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Post-Approval Setup (Pre-Operation):</strong>&nbsp;1-3 Months (Land, permits, importing key machinery).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Total (From Application Submission to Operation with BOI status):</strong>&nbsp;<strong>5-10 Months.</strong>&nbsp;Proactive preparation and a strong application have a significant impact on the timeline.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">10.&nbsp;Challenges and Considerations for SMEs</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">a.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Competition:&nbsp;As BOI promotion becomes more attractive in these sectors, competition for approval increases. A truly innovative and well-prepared application is key.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">b.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Demonstrating Technology/Sophistication:&nbsp;SMEs must convincingly articulate the advanced nature of their activity compared to standard offerings in the market. Patents, unique algorithms, specialized expertise, or partnerships with research institutions bolster this.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">c.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Justifying Investment:&nbsp;While thresholds are more flexible, SMEs still need a credible investment plan. Focusing on IP value, specialized software development costs, and high-skilled labor can be effective strategies beyond just machinery.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">d.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Compliance Burden:&nbsp;Maintaining BOI status requires rigorous record-keeping and reporting. SMEs need internal processes or affordable accounting support to manage this efficiently.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">e.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Focus Beyond Tax Holidays:&nbsp;While the CIT exemption is essential, SMEs must plan for long-term sustainability&nbsp;<em>after</em>&nbsp;the tax holiday ends. The non-tax benefits (land ownership, talent access) provide enduring value.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">11.&nbsp;Conclusion: An Opportunity for SMEs</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's BOI has unequivocally opened its doors to innovative SMEs driving the future in Agritech, AI, Software, Battery Technology, Renewable Energy, and Green Tech. The recent relaxations – including extended tax holidays, refined activity lists, a focus on merit and technology, and streamlined processes – are a direct invitation. For an SME meeting the criteria, the advantages are transformative: substantial tax savings, unlocking capital for growth, the ability to own land and attract global talent, and enhanced credibility in a competitive market.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Thai government is betting on SMEs to fuel its New Economy vision.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand's Unprecedented Crackdown on Illegal Nominee Structures: Compliance Options]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 21 Jul 2025 06:44:43 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thai authorities are executing their most aggressive campaign to date against illegal nominee structures used to bypass the Foreign Business Act (FBA). This multi-agency enforcement effort, widely reported by outlets such as the&nbsp;Bangkok Post, leverages powerful new data integration tools and legal reforms, fundamentally altering the risk landscape for non-compliant foreign investment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Enforcement Arsenal: Technology and Targeted Action</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The cornerstone of the crackdown is the&nbsp;<strong>real-time data integration</strong>&nbsp;between the Department of Business Development (DBD) and the Revenue Department. This system cross-references corporate filings (shareholder lists, directors, and capital) with tax records, exposing financial inconsistencies that signal the use of nominees. Key red flags include Thai shareholders lacking proof of capital sources, absence of proportionate dividend income, or disguised management fees paid to foreigners.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Enforcement is highly targeted. Over&nbsp;46,918 entities&nbsp;in high-risk sectors – notably real estate (Phuket, Bangkok, and other hotspots), tourism, e-commerce/logistics, agriculture, and construction – are expected to face inspections in 2025. Authorities now conduct&nbsp;unannounced site visits&nbsp;and&nbsp;interview Thai shareholders&nbsp;to verify their genuine understanding of the business and financial involvement. Passivity or ignorance is a critical red flag, reinforcing the judiciary's "substance over form" doctrine, as established in precedents such as Supreme Court Decision No.&nbsp;2975/2547.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Penalties are escalating severely.&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Proposed amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA) aim to classify serious FBA violations as&nbsp;<strong>predicate offenses for money laundering</strong>. This empowers the Anti-Money Laundering Office (AMLO) to&nbsp;<strong>freeze or seize assets</strong>&nbsp;(including land, buildings, and accounts) acquired through illegal nominees. This drastic step compounds existing FBA penalties:&nbsp;<strong>criminal charges</strong>&nbsp;(up to 3 years imprisonment, fines up to 1 million THB per violation under Sections 36/37), company dissolution, deportation, and blacklisting.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Table 1: Key Risk Factors Triggering Investigations</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><em>Category</em></td><td><em>Specific Red Flags</em></td></tr><tr><td><em>Shareholding Patterns</em></td><td>Foreigners hold 49.99%; Thai shareholders hold minimal stakes (e.g., 1-2% each); the same Thai shareholders own multiple companies.</td></tr><tr><td><em>Financial Inconsistencies</em></td><td>Thai shareholders lack proof of capital source; no declared dividend income in tax records commensurate with shareholding.</td></tr><tr><td><em>Operational Control</em></td><td>Thai shareholders/directors are passive; foreigners control bank accounts, contracts, and key decisions.</td></tr><tr><td><em>Industry Focus</em></td><td>Real estate, tourism/hospitality, e-commerce/logistics, agriculture, construction.</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Regulatory Shifts &amp; Legal Foundations</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This crackdown coincides with significant regulatory changes. While recent FBA amendments aim to liberalize&nbsp;some&nbsp;sectors, the government operates on a&nbsp;"clean-up before liberalization"&nbsp;principle. Eliminating illegal shadow structures is a prerequisite for any future, more open investment regime, ensuring transparency within revised legal frameworks.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's bid for OECD membership intensifies pressure. Its poor ranking on the OECD FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index (FDIRRI) necessitates demonstrably&nbsp;effective enforcement&nbsp;against circumvention, like nominees, to prove a transparent market. Thai courts consistently uphold the illegality of structures that mask foreign control, focusing on&nbsp;actual control&nbsp;and&nbsp;funding source, regardless of paperwork compliance – a principle solidified in rulings like the 2024 Phuket nominee case, which resulted in criminal convictions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Digital Transformation as an Enforcement Tool</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The mandatory&nbsp;DBD Biz Regist platform&nbsp;is central to compliance enforcement. It creates a&nbsp;centralized digital footprint&nbsp;for every company, recording structures, shareholders, directors, and capital. This database enables seamless cross-verification with Revenue Department tax filings. Authorities use algorithms to flag high-risk patterns (e.g., multiple companies using the same passive Thai shareholders) for immediate investigation. This digital shift also supports Thailand's World Bank B-READY assessment goals while making circumvention harder.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Compliance Pathways: Legitimate Strategies Only</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The heightened risks make abandoning existing nominee models&nbsp;immediate and imperative. The potential consequences – criminal prosecution, asset seizure, dissolution, deportation – are catastrophic. Foreign investors must proactively adopt legitimate structures:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Board of Investment (BOI) Promotion:&nbsp;Offers the most significant benefits, including&nbsp;100% foreign ownership, tax incentives, work permit facilitation, and land ownership rights for eligible projects in promoted sectors (e.g., tech, advanced manufacturing). Requires demonstrating substantial investment, technology transfer, and job creation.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Foreign Business License (FBL):&nbsp;Essential for activities under FBA Lists 2 (national security/arts/resources) and 3 (services). Allows foreign ownership above standard thresholds (up to 60% for List 2, above 49.99% for List 3). Applications require proof of&nbsp;significant capital (minimum 3 million THB, often significantly higher), technology transfer, job creation for Thais, and economic benefits. Expect rigorous scrutiny and lengthy approval.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Treaty Protections:&nbsp;The US-Thai Amity Treaty allows qualifying US investors to hold majority or 100% ownership in many (but not all) FBA-restricted sectors without an FBL. Eligibility and sector coverage require careful legal verification.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Genuine Thai Partnerships:&nbsp;If Thai equity is mandated, partner only with&nbsp;active, credible Thai investors&nbsp;contributing real capital, expertise, or assets. Ensure&nbsp;profit-sharing aligns transparently with genuine ownership&nbsp;and conduct thorough due diligence. Formalize all agreements meticulously.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Industrial Estate Authority of Thailand (IEAT):&nbsp;Operating within promoted IEAT zones can offer specific FBA exemptions and other incentives.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Real Estate-Specific Compliance</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Legal alternatives are essential:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">·             Leases: Up to 30 years.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">·&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Usufructs/Superficies:&nbsp;Rights to use/derive profit from land or own buildings on leased land.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">·&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Condominium Freehold:&nbsp;Purchase within the foreign quota (typically 49% of a project's unit area).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Crucially, using a Thai nominee company to hold land is now considered exceptionally high-risk and strongly discouraged. Utilizing DBD Biz Regist&nbsp;with complete accuracy and transparency is a critical first line of defense, providing verifiable proof of legitimate structures.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Table 2: Thailand's Foreign Business Act Framework &amp; Compliance Pathways</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><em>FBA List/Exemption</em></td><td><em>Description</em></td><td><em>Foreign Limit</em></td><td><em>Key Approval</em></td></tr><tr><td><em>List 1</em></td><td>Prohibited (e.g., media, rice farming, land trading)</td><td>0%</td><td>Prohibited</td></tr><tr><td><em>List 2</em></td><td>Security/Arts/Resources (e.g., transport, mining)</td><td>Max 60% (Min Thai 40%)</td><td>FBL +&nbsp;Cabinet Approval</td></tr><tr><td><em>List 3</em></td><td>Services "Thai-not-ready" (e.g., legal, retail)</td><td>Max 49.99% (without license)</td><td>FBL +&nbsp;Foreign Business Committee</td></tr><tr><td><em>Exemptions</em></td><td>BOI, IEAT, Treaties (e.g., US Amity)</td><td>Up to 100%</td><td>BOI Certificate / IEAT Permit / Treaty Benefit</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Legitimacy is Non-Negotiable</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's integrated data systems, severe penalties, and judicial backing make illegal nominee structures unsustainable. The dual strategy of&nbsp;rigorous enforcement&nbsp;and&nbsp;digital transparency&nbsp;aims to channel foreign investment into legitimate pathways, such as BOI promotion and FBLs. While compliance complexity has increased, meticulous adherence to the FBA, leveraging legal exemptions, and maintaining complete transparency are now fundamental for sustainable operation in Thailand. Businesses relying on nominees face urgent operational and legal jeopardy; comprehensive restructuring is essential for survival. Thailand's future as an investment destination depends on striking a balance between openness and robust, technology-driven enforcement of its foreign ownership laws.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10322,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/nominee-infographic-730x1024.webp" alt="" class="wp-image-10322"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->
