					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Comprehensive Guide to Registering a Company to Import Wine and Spirits into Thailand: Laws, Requirements, and Sales Permissions]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Tue, 22 Jul 2025 08:23:50 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s alcoholic beverage market offers significant business potential, but entering it requires careful compliance with a strict regulatory framework. The key authorities involved are the&nbsp;<strong>Excise Department</strong>,&nbsp;<strong>Customs Department</strong>, and the&nbsp;<strong>Revenue Department</strong>&nbsp;— each playing a distinct role in the approval, taxation, and import process. This guide outlines the essential steps for company registration, obtaining import licenses, and understanding the regulatory differences between wholesale and retail distribution.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1.&nbsp;&nbsp;Legal Framework</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Alcoholic Beverage Control Act B.E. 2551 (2008)<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Regulates production, import, sale, and advertising.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Excise Tax Act B.E. 2560 (2017)<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Governs taxation and licensing for excisable goods.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Customs Act B.E. 2560 (2017)<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Controls import/export procedures.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Foreign Business Act B.E. 2542 (1999)<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Restricts foreign-majority companies from retail without special licenses.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2.&nbsp;&nbsp;Company Registration Requirements</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Company Type:</strong><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Register a&nbsp;private limited company&nbsp;with the Department of Business Development (DBD).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Foreign shareholders &gt;49% require&nbsp;a Foreign Business License (FBL)&nbsp;for import/wholesale (List 3 of FBA).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Minimum Capital:</strong><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">No fixed minimum, but sufficient for operations (<strong>typically&nbsp;฿2–5 million</strong>).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Registered Address:</strong><!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A physical Thai address for official correspondence and for excise license purposes.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3.&nbsp;&nbsp;Location Requirements</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The business must be located in an area where alcohol sales are permitted, regardless of the type of license requested. Even an import license will not be granted if the premises are situated in a zone designated as alcohol-free. These restricted areas are typically near temples, schools, dormitories, or national parks.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Each local Excise Department office can provide detailed zoning maps upon request.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4.&nbsp;&nbsp;Excise Department / Licensing&nbsp;:</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Excise Department - Company Documents :</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Certificate of Incorporation.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Company Tax ID (from the Revenue Department).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">VAT Registration (if revenue &gt;฿1.8 million/year).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Full lease agreement, including all the attachments – floor plan, chanot, tabian baan, ID cards of landlord(s) if physical persons or DBD and ID card of legal representative of the Company if juristic person.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Alcoholic bevarages Import License:</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Form Por. 1 (Application for Alcoholic Beverage Importer License).  The license allows the Company to import alcoholic beverages – This process is normally documentary; in some specific cases Excise may request a set of pictures of the venue. Rarely is a physical inspection is conducted.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Alcoholic beverages sales licenses</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Normally two kind of licenses are obtained: </p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">1) sales type 1, wholesale – can sell minimum quantity 10 liters, no subject to sales time restrictions; </p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">2) sales type 2, retail – can sell by bottle with a maximum of 10 liters, only during allowed times.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Additional licenses are legally required for venues such as restaurants, clubs, or bars that operate past midnight or serve alcohol by the glass. These include restaurant, entertainment, or nightclub licenses, depending on the type of activity. In such cases, a complete set of venue photographs is mandatory for the license application.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Product-Specific Approvals:&nbsp;</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":4} -->
<h4 class="wp-block-heading">Label Approval:&nbsp;</h4>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Labels must be submitted to the Thai FDA (the labels must include Thai language, alcohol content, health warnings).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":4} -->
<h4 class="wp-block-heading">Retail Price Calculation</h4>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Enter the retail price breakdown into the system — this is used to calculate the 5% retail tax. Your operator will input all relevant cost data for your product, including FOB cost, freight, customs clearance, taxes, local delivery, marketing, management, company overheads, and commercial margin. Once this information is entered, you’ll define the final retail price, and the system will calculate your profit per bottle. Please note: the retail price must match your official company pricelist and may be verified during post-market inspections by the Excise Department.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">5.&nbsp;&nbsp;Import Process &amp; Taxes</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Customs :&nbsp;Clearance: Submit import declaration (Form 99/1) with:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Commercial invoice</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Bill of lading</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Certificate of Origin (for tariff reductions)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Excise Department permit</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><a href="https://www.siamdevelopment.com/regulatory-services-in-thailand-company-registration/company-registration-thailand/import-alcohol-in-thailand/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Tax Calculation:</a></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Customs Duty: 0% for all Countries</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Excise Tax:&nbsp;1000 THB per liter of alcohol in one liter of product. Therefore, the formula is: 1,000 THB X content in liters X percentage of alcohol. Example for a 0.75 liters bottle with 14% alcohol: {14 x 0.75 x 1,000)/100 = 105 THB.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Additional (local tax): a total of 17,5% of the amount of excise tax. In our case, 105 x 17.5% = 18.375 THB. Total due to excise: 105 + 18.375 = 123.375 THB</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>5% retail tax: base on your declared retail price.</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">VAT:&nbsp;7% (on sum of CIF + duty + excise + retail tax).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">6.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additional requirements and definitions</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The importer/distributor must keep records of sales and report monthly to the Excise Department</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Ownership Restrictions:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Foreign-majority companies require&nbsp;<strong>FBL (List 1)</strong>&nbsp;– rarely granted for retail.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Thai nationals or 51% Thai-owned entities preferred.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Operating Hours:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Sales prohibited&nbsp;2:00–5:00 PM and 12:00 (midnight)–11:00 AM daily (see recent updates on location specific exemptions such as entertainment venues and hotels).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">7.&nbsp;&nbsp;Wholesale Sales Process: Step-by-Step Flowchart</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10333,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/importing-alcohol-reduced-421x1024.webp" alt="" class="wp-image-10333"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">8.&nbsp;&nbsp;Practical Tips</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Consult Experts:</strong>&nbsp;Engage a Thai law firm for FBL/licensing support.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Local Partnerships:</strong>&nbsp;Collaborate with Thai entities for retail market access.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Digital Compliance:</strong>&nbsp;Use Excise Department’s&nbsp;<strong>e-Excise System</strong>&nbsp;for filings.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">9.&nbsp;&nbsp;Conclusion</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Importing wine and spirits into Thailand demands meticulous planning across company registration, licensing, tax, and sales compliance. While wholesale is feasible for foreign investors, retail sales remain heavily restricted. Success hinges on understanding Thailand’s excise laws and partnering with local experts to navigate bureaucratic hurdles. Things in Thailand changes quickly: always verify requirements with the Excise Department, as regulations frequently evolve.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Australia’s Bunnings Ruling Sounds Alarm for Facial Recognition Use in Thailand]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 30 Jul 2025 04:36:30 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:image {"id":10359,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/facial-pdpa-infographic-629x1024.png" alt="" class="wp-image-10359"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">HOW AN AUSTRALIAN DATA PRIVACY CASE SIGNALS STRICT LIMITS ON FACIAL RECOGNITION TECHNOLOGY USE IN THAILAND.</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A landmark ruling against Australia’s hardware store “Bunnings” for the unlawful use of facial recognition technology (FRT) serves as a wake-up call for Thai businesses.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The November 2024 decision by Australia’s Privacy Commissioner – finding mass biometric collection without consent, transparency, or proportionality illegal – directly parallels Thailand’s&nbsp;Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) requirements. With Thai regulators increasingly scrutinizing FRT deployments (like recent controversies at 7-Eleven Thailand and MBK Center), companies should urgently align practices with PDPA mandates or face severe penalties.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Bunnings Precedent &amp; Its Thai Relevance</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Australia’s OAIC ruled Bunnings violated privacy laws by scanning faces across 62 stores (2019–2021). Key findings included:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Illegal Collection:</strong> Capturing biometrics without consent breached "sensitive information" protections.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Inadequate Transparency:</strong> Small signage and vague policies failed to notify customers meaningfully.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Disproportionality:</strong> Mass surveillance of all customers was unjustified for theft prevention.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>The "Milliseconds" Myth:</strong> Data held for 4.17 MS (Bunning’s quoted processing time to determine facial parameters) still constituted illegal "collection."</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Thai Parallel:</strong>&nbsp;This mirrors PDPA’s core tenets. Biometric data is explicitly classified as&nbsp;<strong>"</strong><strong>Sensitive Personal Data" Under Section 26</strong>, demanding&nbsp;<em>explicit consent</em>. Recent Thai media exposés similar FRT misuse:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>7-Eleven Thailand:</strong> Faced public outcry in 2023 after deploying FRT without clear signage or consent mechanisms, violating PDPA’s transparency requirements (Bangkok Post, 15 March 2023).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Bangkok Mall Pilot:</strong> A major shopping center halted FRT trials in 2024 following PDPA Office warnings about insufficient customer notice (The Nation, 2 May 2024).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">PDPA vs. Bunnings: Legal Alignment</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s PDPA (fully enforced since 2022) and Australia’s Privacy Act share stringent FRT restrictions:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><thead><tr><td><strong>Issue</strong></td><td><strong>Australia (Bunnings Ruling)</strong></td><td><strong>Thailand (PDPA)</strong></td><td><strong>Thai Media Context</strong></td></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Biometric Data Classification</td><td>"Sensitive Information"</td><td><strong>Section 26:</strong>&nbsp;"Sensitive Personal Data" requires&nbsp;<strong>explicit consent</strong></td><td>The PDPA Office repeatedly emphasizes the sensitivity of biometrics in its guidelines (2023).</td></tr><tr><td>Consent Requirements</td><td>Mandatory, "impracticality" rejected</td><td><strong>Section 19:</strong>&nbsp;Explicit, informed, freely given consent required. No exceptions for convenience.</td><td>The 7-Eleven case shows that implied consent (via entry) is&nbsp;<strong>insufficient</strong>&nbsp;under PDPA.</td></tr><tr><td>Transparency Obligations</td><td>APP 5.1: Notice must be clear, accessible</td><td><strong>Section 23:</strong>&nbsp;Must inform subjects of purpose, retention, and rights&nbsp;<strong>before collection</strong>.</td><td>MBK Center pilot criticized for "discreet signage," failing PDPA’s prominence standard (Prachatai, 30 April 2024).</td></tr><tr><td>Proportionality &amp; Necessity</td><td>Mass surveillance deemed disproportionate</td><td><strong>Section 24(3)</strong>:&nbsp;Collection must be "necessary" and "least intrusive" means.</td><td>Thai retailers have been warned that FRT must be a last resort, after enhanced CCTV or guards (PDPA Office Guidance, 2023).</td></tr><tr><td>"Collection" Definition</td><td>Milliseconds-long processing is still illegal</td><td><strong>Section 19:</strong>&nbsp;"Collection" includes&nbsp;<strong>any</strong>&nbsp;capture/processing, regardless of duration.</td><td>Thai tech firms warned that transient data processing still triggers PDPA compliance (Digital Economy Council, 2024).</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">PDPA Compliance Guidelines for Thai Businesses</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Explicit Consent is Mandatory:</strong><br>Security claims DO NOT override consent. PDPA <strong>Section 26</strong> demands <strong>opt-in consent</strong> for biometrics. Bunnings’ "impractical consent" defense failed; Thai businesses (such as 7-Eleven) cannot rely solely on signage.<br><strong>Best Practice:</strong> Deploy <strong>consent kiosks</strong> at entrances with multilingual opt-in options. Document consent records.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Conduct a PDPA-Compliant PIA:</strong><br>Australia mandated PIAs for FRT. PDPA <strong>Section 39</strong> requires <strong>Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)</strong> for high-risk processing (like FRT). Document:<ol><li>Why FRT is essential and why less invasive options (e.g., traditional CCTV + guards) fail.</li></ol><!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Measures to prevent functionality creep and bias.<br>(See PDPA Office’s "DPIA Guideline," June 2023").</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Prioritize Proactive Transparency:</strong><br>Bunnings’ "layered" notices were deemed inadequate. PDPA <strong>Section 23</strong> requires a <strong>prominent, pre-collection notice</strong>.<br><strong>Best Practice:</strong> Use <strong>eye-level signage</strong> with icons + QR codes linking to concise privacy notices (Thai/English). Avoid "legalese."</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Reject the "Milliseconds" Loophole:</strong><br>Thai businesses cannot claim that fleeting data retention is exempt from the PDPA. <strong>Any</strong> facial capture constitutes "collection" under <strong>Section 19</strong> – as confirmed by the "DPIA Guideline," June 2023 guidance.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Narrowly Interpret "Vital Interest" Exceptions:</strong><br>While <strong>Section 26(4)</strong> allows processing sensitive data for "life safety" without consent, regulators (like Australia’s) interpret this <strong>strictly</strong>. FRT must be the <em>only </em>viable solution to an imminent, documented threat – not general theft deterrence.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Path Forward: FRT Under Thai Scrutiny</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">With FRT adoption rising in Thai retail, malls, and airports, regulators are escalating oversight:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Suvarnabhumi Airport FRT:</strong> Already under PDPA Office review for balancing security with traveler consent (Bangkok Post, 28 Nov 2024).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>PDPA Enforcement:</strong> Fines up to <strong>THB 5 </strong><strong>Million</strong> (+ criminal penalties) under <strong>Section 8</strong><strong>4</strong> for violations.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Proactive Steps for Thai Businesses:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Audit &amp; Destroy:</strong> Review of all FRT deployments. Destroy non-compliant historical biometric data.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Adopt Privacy-Enhancing Tech:</strong> Explore anonymized analytics or on-device processing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Update Policies:</strong> Explicitly detail FRT use in PDPA-mandated privacy notices (<strong>Section 23</strong>).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion: Prioritize Privacy or Face Penalties</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Bunnings ruling underscores a global reality:&nbsp;<strong>convenience and security claims cannot override fundamental privacy rights.</strong>&nbsp;Thailand’s PDPA enforces identical principles – requiring explicit consent, necessity, and radical transparency for FRT. Thai businesses risk significant fines and reputational damage (as seen in the 7-Eleven backlash) if they ignore these lessons. As PDPA enforcement matures, proactive compliance is no longer optional – it’s essential for maintaining ethical and legal operations in Thailand.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s TouristDigiPay: An Overview of the New E-Wallet Scheme for Visiting Thailand]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Tue, 19 Aug 2025 06:57:21 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s tourism sector is advancing into the digital era with the launch of&nbsp;<strong>TouristDigiPay</strong>, a regulatory sandbox initiative that allows foreign tourists to top up e-money wallets with various assets, including cryptocurrencies, other digital or tokenized assets, and traditional assets such as cash or possibly via telegraphic transfers (TT), converting them into Thai Baht for seamless electronic payments utilizing Thailand’s widespread QR payment scheme.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Announced on 18 August, 2025, by the <strong>Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Thailand</strong>, in collaboration with the Ministry of Finance, the Anti-Money Laundering Office (AMLO), and the Ministry of Tourism and Sports, this 18-month pilot project is subject to stringent Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundrering Office (AMLO) regulations to ensure compliance with existing financial requirements by the BoT. The program attracts a broad range of tourists, including digital nomads, potentially holders of the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV), and all visitors seeking convenient payment options, with potential for broader rollout to other visitor categories in the future, enhancing access to Thailand’s QR payment and providing infrastructure for all tourists, who were previously excluded from such convenience.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">What is TouristDigiPay?<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">TouristDigiPay is an innovative initiative designed to provide foreign tourists with an e-wallet for visiting Thailand, enabling them to top up e-money wallets with various assets, such as cash, cryptocurrencies (e.g., Bitcoin, Ethereum), which are then converted into Thai Baht for electronic payments using the QR code-based transactions that are widely accepted across Thailand. The program operates under a&nbsp;<strong>regulatory sandbox</strong>&nbsp;overseen by the SEC Thailand and the Bank of Thailand (BoT), ensuring strict compliance with financial regulations. It does not permit direct payments with assets or cash; instead, funds are converted into Baht and held in e-money wallets for spending at merchants nationwide, from large retailers to small vendors.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">With a trial period of 18 months starting in Q4 2025, TouristDigiPay aims to enhance Thailand’s competitiveness as a global tourism and digital finance hub by catering to all tourists, including those using traditional payment methods like cash or TT, digital nomads, and DTV visa holders, with the potential to expand to other visitor categories.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">How TouristDigiPay Works<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">TouristDigiPay enables foreign tourists to deposit funds from various sources, whether traditional finance or crypto, into accounts managed by&nbsp;<strong>SEC-licensed asset operators</strong>&nbsp;(for digital or tokenized assets) or&nbsp;<strong>BOT-regulated financial institutions</strong>&nbsp;(for traditional instruments like cash or TT). It is not certain if the same provider could take both traditional and crypto at this point.&nbsp; These assets are converted into Thai Baht at market rates and credited to a&nbsp;<strong>BOT-regulated e-money wallet</strong>&nbsp;for use in electronic payments. The process includes:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true,"start":1} -->
<ol start="1" class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Fund Deposit</strong>: Tourists can deposit cryptocurrencies, tokenized assets, cash, or funds via TT. Digital assets are transferred to the operator’s platform and verified. Cash deposits may be made through partnered banks or authorized agents (e.g., 7-Eleven counters), while TTs are processed via bank accounts, subject to standard banking verification.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Conversion to Baht</strong>: Assets or funds are converted into Thai Baht through licensed operators or banks, with funds credited to a linked e-money wallet.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Payment Usage</strong>: Tourists use the e-money wallet for payments via QR code scans or other electronic methods at merchants across Thailand, facilitated by payment gateways like PromptPay. Direct payments with assets or cash are prohibited; only Baht from the e-money wallet is accepted.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Spending Limits</strong>: Monthly caps are set at <strong>50,000 THB</strong> (≈$1,429) for transactions at small retail merchants and <strong>500,000 THB</strong> (≈$14,286) for transactions at merchants with card terminals (e.g., hotels, restaurants). These limits apply at the <strong>vendor level</strong>, meaning they restrict the amount a tourist can spend per month at each type of merchant, not the total spending across all vendors. </li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For example, a tourist could spend up to 50,000 THB at one small merchant and another 50,000 THB at a different small merchant, and up to 500,000 THB at a hotel, within the respective vendor categories.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This process ensures accessibility for all tourists, by integrating with Thailand’s widely adopted QR payment system that is available everywhere from high end retailers to street-stalls, making it convenient for both tech-savvy and traditional travelers.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Expected Providers for TouristDigiPay<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While the SEC and BOT have not yet released a definitive list of providers, TouristDigiPay requires participation from&nbsp;<strong>SEC-licensed asset operators</strong>&nbsp;for digital assets and&nbsp;<strong>BOT-regulated banks or e-money providers</strong>&nbsp;for both digital and traditional financial instruments like cash or TT. PromptPay, as a payment gateway, facilitates the QR transactions but is not an end-user provider; instead, traditional banks and e-money platforms are expected to serve as the primary interfaces for tourists. Based on our knowledge of Thailand’s financial ecosystem, several providers are expected to participate:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Digital Asset Operators<strong></strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Gulf Binance</strong>: The local entity for Binance, one of the leading global exchanges, Binance is a leading SEC-licensed cryptocurrency platform and a likely candidate due to its robust infrastructure and support for Thailand’s crypto initiatives, as noted by its CEO, Nirun Fuwattananukul.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Bitkub</strong>: Thailand’s largest crypto exchange, Bitkub is SEC-licensed and well-positioned to handle digital asset-to-Baht conversions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Satang</strong>: An SEC-regulated exchange, Satang could support tourists’ digital asset deposits.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Upbit Thailand</strong>: With its focus on secure transactions, this regulated platform is another potential participant, and like the others listed above already provides a crypto “off-ramp” to KYC verified users.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Traditional Banks<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>SCB (Siam Commercial Bank)</strong>: SCBX, through its fintech arm SCB 10X, is a key player in Thailand’s digital finance landscape. SCB 10X’s <strong>Rubie Wallet</strong>, tested during the Ethereum Foundation’s Devcon 2024 in Bangkok (November 5–25, 2024), converts USD-pegged stablecoins to THBX (Thai Baht stablecoin) for QR payments via PromptPay. Developed under a BOT and SEC sandbox with partners like InnovestX, Fireblocks, Elliptic, Circle, and Base, SCBX is highly likely to participate in TouristDigiPay, potentially extending Rubie Wallet to support digital assets, cash, or TT for all tourists. SCBX’s banking infrastructure also supports cash deposits and TT processing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Kasikornbank (KBank)</strong>: KBank’s <strong>TAGTHAi Easy Pay</strong> e-wallet supports QR payments via the Prepaid PAY&amp;TOUR card for international tourists, currently handling traditional currency top-ups. KBank is well-positioned to integrate with TouristDigiPay to accept cash, TT, or digital assets, leveraging its PromptPay-enabled infrastructure.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Krungthai Bank</strong>: With a virtual banking license and partnerships with AIS and PTT Group, Krungthai could offer e-wallet services, supporting cash, TT, or asset-based top-ups through its PromptPay integration.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Bangkok Bank</strong>: A major bank with strong mobile banking and PromptPay integration, Bangkok Bank could participate, handling cash or TT top-ups alongside digital assets.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Other Commercial Banks</strong>: Banks like TMBThanachart, UOB Thailand, or Krungsri, with PromptPay and mobile banking capabilities, may join if partnered with SEC-licensed operators or equipped to handle cash/TT deposits.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">E-Money Providers<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>TrueMoney</strong>: A BOT-regulated e-money provider, TrueMoney is widely used for QR payments via PromptPay and is a strong contender for integration with TouristDigiPay, potentially handling cash deposits at retail points like 7-Eleven.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>ShopeePay</strong>: Operated by SeaMoney, ShopeePay is a BOT-regulated platform with broad merchant acceptance and PromptPay integration.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Rabbit LINE Pay</strong>: This e-money platform, popular for QR payments via PromptPay, may also participate.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Role of PromptPay and Inclusivity for All Tourists<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">PromptPay serves as a payment gateway facilitating QR transactions. Traditional banks like SCBX, KBank, and others, along with e-money platforms, will act as the primary providers, offering e-wallets that support digital assets, cash (via branches, ATMs, or agents like 7-Eleven), and TT (via international bank transfers).&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This ensures the e-wallet is accessible to all tourists aligning with Thailand’s goal of enhancing payment convenience. The BOT’s planned “Tourist Wallet” is expected to streamline these top-up options, integrating both modern and traditional methods.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Pre-consultation with operators began in August 2025, and the SEC and BOT are expected to announce confirmed providers closer to the Q4 2025 launch.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Documentary Requirements for TouristDigiPay<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Participation in TouristDigiPay requires compliance with stringent&nbsp;<strong>Know Your Customer (KYC)</strong>&nbsp;and&nbsp;<strong>Customer Due Diligence (CDD)</strong>&nbsp;requirements, as mandated by AMLO and aligned with global anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorism financing (CFT) standards. Below are the key documentary requirements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">For Foreign Tourists<strong></strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Identity Verification Documents</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Valid Passport</strong>: A government-issued passport is required to verify the tourist’s identity and confirm their status as a non-resident visitor.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Proof of Temporary Residence</strong>: Documents such as a visa (including the DTV) or entry stamp may be required to verify the tourist’s temporary stay, as the program is initially exclusive to foreign tourists, as well as a hotel booking or potentially other verification of address.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Asset or Fund Source Information</strong>: For digital or tokenized assets, tourists must disclose the source wallet address, verified using blockchain forensic tools. For cash or TT, proof of funds (e.g., bank statements, TT receipts, or cash deposit confirmations) may be required.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Account Setup with Regulated Providers</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Tourists must register with an SEC-licensed asset operator (for digital/tokenized assets) and/or a BOT-regulated bank or e-money provider (for cash/TT), submitting personal details and identity documents during onboarding.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The e-money account must be linked to the same name as the asset or funding account to ensure traceability.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Declaration of Asset or Fund Source</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Tourists must provide information on the origin of their deposited assets or funds, such as transaction histories, proof of acquisition (e.g., exchange records, token issuance documents, bank statements, or TT receipts), to comply with AMLO’s AML/CFT guidelines.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Spending Limits Acknowledgment</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Tourists must acknowledge monthly spending caps (50,000 THB for small merchants, 500,000 THB for larger merchants) at the vendor level during account setup, though no separate document is required.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">For Asset Operators, Banks, and E-Money Providers<strong></strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Licensing and Partnership Documentation</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Operators must hold a valid SEC license for digital/tokenized assets or a BOT license for banking/e-money services and provide proof of good standing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A partnership agreement between asset operators, banks, or e-money providers is required, detailing integration for asset-to-Baht conversions or cash/TT processing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>AML/CFT Compliance Framework</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Operators and banks must submit an AML/CFT policy, including KYC/CDD procedures, transaction monitoring, and blockchain forensic tools (for digital assets) or equivalent verification methods (for cash/TT).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Transactions exceeding <strong>450,000 THB</strong> require a detailed report to the SEC or BOT, including the purpose and supporting documentation.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Exit Strategy Plan</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Operators and banks must provide a plan for winding down services at the end of the 18-month sandbox, ensuring consumer funds are protected.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Application for Sandbox Participation</strong>:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Businesses must submit an application to the SEC or BOT, including operational plans, risk management protocols, and proof of compliance with capital requirements, with reviews completed within 60 days.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Regulatory Framework and Safeguards<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">TouristDigiPay operates within a tightly controlled regulatory sandbox to balance innovation with consumer protection. Key safeguards include:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Prohibition on Direct Payments</strong>: Assets or cash cannot be used directly; only converted Baht in e-money wallets is accepted.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Spending Limits</strong>: Vendor-level caps of 50,000 THB for small merchants and 500,000 THB for larger merchants prevent misuse.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>No Cash Withdrawals</strong>: Cash withdrawals from e-money accounts are prohibited until account closure to reduce AML risks.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Transaction Restrictions</strong>: High-risk businesses, as identified by AMLO, are excluded from accepting payments.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Verification</strong>: Operators and banks must use blockchain forensics for digital assets or equivalent methods for cash/TT, with mandatory reporting to AMLO and the SEC/BOT.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The SEC has introduced exemptions, such as waiving suitability/knowledge tests for tourists and modifying advertising rules.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Challenges and Opportunities<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">TouristDigiPay presents significant opportunities but also faces challenges:</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Usability Hurdles</strong>: The KYC process and QR payments may deter less tech-savvy tourists. Multilingual support and simplified onboarding could help.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Privacy Concerns</strong>: Stringent KYC/AML requirements may raise privacy issues, as noted in online discussions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Market Potential</strong>: By supporting digital assets, cash, and TT for QR payments via PromptPay, the program attracts all tourists, including digital nomads, DTV visa holders, and traditional travelers, with potential for broader rollout, boosting tourism revenue.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For businesses, participating in the sandbox offers a first-mover advantage, allowing operators and banks to tap into a growing market.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion<strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s TouristDigiPay initiative is a groundbreaking step toward integrating digital assets, cash, and telegraphic transfers into the tourism economy, offering all foreign tourists, including digital nomads, DTV visa holders, and traditional travelers, a secure and regulated e-wallet for visiting Thailand. By topping up with various assets or funds for QR-based payments in Thai Baht via PromptPay, the program enhances accessibility to Thailand’s payment infrastructure. Compliance with&nbsp;<strong>KYC/CDD requirements</strong>, including passport verification, proof of temporary residence, and asset or fund source documentation, is non-negotiable due to stringent AMLO regulations. Traditional banks like SCBX, with Rubie Wallet experience, and others like KBank are poised to play a key role, alongside digital asset operators like Gulf Binance, the local entity for Binance. By understanding these requirements and leveraging the scheme’s opportunities, stakeholders can position themselves at the forefront of Thailand’s digital finance revolution.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">It will be interesting to see how the no-cash withdrawals stipulation will work as when tourists leave, they will be expecting to be able to redeem unused funds.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For guidance on navigating the TouristDigiPay sandbox or ensuring compliance with SEC Thailand regulations,&nbsp;<strong>contact SILQ’s expert team</strong>&nbsp;today.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:image {"id":10419,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/visa-thailand-1024x683.webp" alt="" class="wp-image-10419"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s appeal as a destination for students, digital nomads, retirees, and expatriates is undeniable, but navigating its immigration system has become increasingly complex.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A 2025 crackdown on visa misuse, particularly Non-Immigrant ED (student) and Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) fraud, combined with stricter banking policies led by Bangkok Bank, has put foreign nationals under intense scrutiny. Relying on dubious visa agents offering “easy visas” can lead to visa cancellations, fines, or bans. To stay compliant, expats must report status changes, meet banking requirements, and avoid falsifying their applications.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Student and DTV Visa Crackdown: No Tolerance for Misuse</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">On 23 August 2025, the&nbsp;<em>Bangkok Post</em>&nbsp;reported that the Immigration Bureau revoked nearly 10,000 student visas for foreign nationals who failed to meet educational requirements. Pol Maj Gen Panthana Nuchanart, deputy commissioner, revealed that thousands entered Thailand on Non-Immigrant ED visas but did not attend classes, often using sham documents from language schools to secure extensions. “If someone enters Thailand on a student visa but doesn’t actually study, it’s standard procedure to revoke that visa,” he said. The Bureau now collaborates with the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation (MHESI) to verify enrolment through a centralized database.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Destination Thailand Visa (DTV), launched in 2024 for remote workers and cultural enthusiasts, is also under scrutiny. Some DTV holders have misrepresented activities, such as claiming participation in Muay Thai or cooking courses without attending, or failing to prove remote work, leading to visa cancellations. For instance, some Asian nationals were found working in unrelated industries while holding student or DTV visas issued by suspect institutions. This follows 2023 allegations by Chuvit Kamolvisit, who claimed immigration officers in Khon Kaen and Chiang Mai accepted bribes from 100,000 to 300,000 baht to approve non-immigrant visas with falsified documents. The National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) is investigating 107 officers, with findings pending.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>The Risks of “Easy Visas” and Priority Fees</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Some visa agents in Thailand offer ways to simplify visa applications by paying “priority fees” to bypass certain requirements, such as proof of income or enrolment. These practices are rumoured to occur more in border provinces or popular tourist destinations.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Foreigners need to be careful that their agent is doing everything legally.&nbsp; As most of the government officers speak mostly Thai, it is much easier for a foreigner to engage a local agent who can assist in interpretation. For example, if a foreigner hired an agent for a student or DTV visa extension, they might remain unaware that the agent had submitted phony documents or paid an unofficial fee, sometimes in a different province. This lack of transparency and limited communications leaves applicants vulnerable to issues, as immigration officials may demand missing documents or probe irregularities during subsequent applications.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Doubtful practices can lead to visa denials, fines, or bans, jeopardizing long-term residency goals like the Thailand Elite Privilege, Permanent Residence, or Long-Term Resident (LTR) visas.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Banking Restrictions: Thai Banks’ Stricter Oversight</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thai Banks overall, led initially by Bangkok Bank are currently implementing a crackdown on foreign account holders. Since July 2025 all major banks, such as Kasikorn Bank, Siam Commercial Bank (SCB), and Krungthai Bank have followed suit. Opening a bank account as a foreigner now requires a valid non-immigrant visa (e.g., ED or DTV), proof of Thai residence, and sometimes a work permit. DTV holders and tourists face rejections, though some branches may be more lenient. Existing account holders are also facing reviews, with some reporting frozen accounts or restricted access. For example, a DTV holder on an X forum noted that Bangkok Bank froze their account for insufficient proof of remote work, requiring in-person verification.&nbsp; Another person overseas was complaining they couldn’t return before an arbitrary reporting deadline, and their account was shut down.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Banks are also enforcing stricter visa “savings” rules to align with immigration requirements. DTV holders must show 500,000 baht in a Thai account, while retirees on Non-Immigrant O (Thai Spouse) / O-A, O-X (Retirement) visas need 400,000 / 800,000 baht for three months before and after renewals, respectively.&nbsp; If the account holder has not had the money in the account for that length of time the bank will either refuse to issue the certificate for immigration or request that the account holder pledge to keep the money in the account for an additional four months.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Report Status Changes: Avoiding Cancellation</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Foreign nationals must notify the Immigration Bureau of changes in visa status or activities to avoid cancellation. Student visa holders must maintain full-time enrolment in accredited programs with verifiable attendance. DTV holders must provide ongoing proof of remote work or cultural activities, as misrepresentation (e.g., working locally) risks revocation and fines.&nbsp; Any change in status must be reported within seven days.&nbsp; Failure to update status can lead to fines, detention, or visa cancellation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Misrepresentation: Severe Consequences</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Misrepresenting visa status—skipping classes, studying insufficient hours, or failing to fulfil DTV requirements—carries serious penalties.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Immigration Bureau has exposed cases of sham documents from language schools or cultural programs used to grant or extend student or DTV visas. For example, some DTV holders falsely claimed Muay Thai enrolment while working at unauthorized jobs. Consequences include visa cancellation, fines for the visa holder and employer of up to 100,000 baht, detention in the Immigration Detention Center, and re-entry bans of 1–5 years. Overstaying a visa by more than 200 days can lead to deportation. Immigration officials have also warned that fraudulent applications may jeopardize future entry.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Take Action: Secure Your Stay</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s tightened rules require proactive compliance from student and DTV visa holders. To stay lawful:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Attend required classes or fulfil DTV commitments</strong> to maintain visa validity.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Notify immigration immediately</strong> of status or activity changes.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Maintain funds in bank accounts</strong> for immigration-required durations.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Provide accurate documentation</strong> to banks and immigration.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Use reputable experts</strong> to avoid risky agents offering facilitation fees.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Summary: Implications for Thailand’s Future</strong><strong></strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s visa and banking crackdown aims to protect its immigration system and economic integrity, but its impact is broader than that.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">By targeting student and DTV visa fraud, the measures may deter scammers operating in call centers, “financial advisors” peddling fraudulent / semi-legal investment packages or timeshares, and foreigners working in prohibited roles, such as unlicensed tour guides or real estate agents. Stricter oversight could reduce illegal activities linked to visa misuse, enhancing Thailand’s reputation as a secure destination.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">However, the tightened rules risk deterring legitimate tourists, students, and digital nomads, potentially impacting tourism revenue and the education sector. Balancing enforcement with accessibility will be crucial to maintain Thailand’s appeal while curbing illicit operations. For now, compliance remains the safest path for foreigners seeking to enjoy the Land of Smiles.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Unsure about your visa status? Contact SILQ for a free 5-minute consultation</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Let us help you review your student or DTV visa compliance. Open to members of AustCham, BCCT and TICC or their friends, this consultation can identify risks before they lead to penalties. Visit our website or call our Bangkok office today. For official guidance, check the Thai Immigration Bureau’s website. For banking issues, contact your bank’s contact center.</p>

		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s Amended Organic Act on Anti-Corruption: Enhanced Whistleblower Protection and Corporate Compliance Requirements]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Thu, 28 Aug 2025 06:38:59 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">On June 5, 2025, the&nbsp;amended Organic Act on Anti-Corruption (No.2) B.E. 2568 (2025) was enacted. This legislation, which took immediate effect, substantially enhances the legal protections afforded to individuals who report acts of corruption. For all companies operating within the Kingdom of Thailand, understanding these changes is essential for maintaining robust legal compliance and corporate governance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Background and Rationale for the Legislative Reform</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Corruption remains a pervasive challenge with profound social and economic implications for Thailand. As noted in reports from international observers such as Transparency International, the perception of corruption remains a significant hurdle to social and commercial development. A primary obstacle to combating this issue has been the legitimate fear among potential whistleblowers of facing severe retaliation. Such retaliation has historically included wrongful termination, demotion, harassment, or even civil and criminal lawsuits, such as those for defamation, initiated by the individuals who are the&nbsp;subjects of their reports. The recent amendment, as reported in the Bangkok Post recently, is a direct response to this barrier. Its fundamental purpose is to foster a more transparent environment by legally ensuring that individuals who report corruption in good faith are shielded from reprisal, thereby encouraging more disclosures and supporting the nation's broader anti-corruption objectives.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Key Provisions of the Amended Act</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The cornerstone of this amendment is the introduction of Article 132 of the Organic Act on Anti-Corruption (No.2) B.E. 2568 (2025), which establishes a comprehensive framework for whistleblower protection.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The article grants the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) the authority to provide formal immunity to bona fide whistleblowers. Upon a resolution from the NACC, an individual who, in good faith and without personal malice and in the public interest, provides information to a competent authority is explicitly exempt from criminal, civil, and disciplinary liability. It is important to note that while immunity from criminal and civil liability extends to all citizens, both in the public and private sectors, the exemption from disciplinary liability pertains specifically to public officials.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Furthermore, the amendment introduces a powerful mechanism to deter retaliatory lawsuits. Pursuant to Article 132/1 of the Organic Act on Anti-Corruption (No.2) B.E. 2568 (2025), In instances where a legal action is pursued against a whistleblower, the NACC is empowered to issue an official opinion to the relevant investigatory or judicial bodies, such as the police, public prosecutors, or courts, stating that the individual is not guilty. This opinion must be given due consideration during any subsequent investigation or legal proceeding, creating a substantial procedural hurdle for those seeking to use the justice system for retaliation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The NACC's role has also been reinforced with broader protective mandates. The Commission may now request that any government agency, including the police and courts, provide necessary protection to a whistleblower. It is also authorized to offer comprehensive legal assistance, which includes assigning legal counsel and covering associated litigation costs. For whistleblowers within public organizations, the NACC can issue orders mandating the remediation of any disadvantages suffered, such as reinstatement after a wrongful dismissal, as provided under Article 132/2 of the Organic Act on Anti-Corruption (No.2) B.E. 2568 (2025).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Implications for all Companies in Thailand and Necessary Compliance Measures</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For the private sector, this legislative shift creates a new operational reality. Employees, contractors, and other business partners now operate within a far safer environment for reporting corporate misconduct, such as bribery or embezzlement, directly to external authorities like the NACC. This significantly increases the likelihood that internal malfeasance will be exposed and investigated by external bodies, potentially leading to severe legal and reputational consequences for the involved companies.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While the Organic Act on Anti-Corruption itself does not directly impose obligations on private companies to mirror the NACC’s protective measures for internal reports, the practical effect of the law makes a compelling case for corporate action. A proactive and strategic approach to internal compliance is now the most effective risk mitigation strategy.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Companies are strongly advised to review and strengthen their internal whistleblowing policies and procedures. The objective is to create a trusted, internal first-resort mechanism that employees&nbsp;prefer over immediate external reporting. This involves ensuring the absolute independence and confidentiality of internal reporting channels, such as through dedicated hotlines managed by third-party providers or a specialized internal audit committee. Furthermore, internal regulations must be unequivocally updated to explicitly prohibit any form of retaliation against whistleblowers, and this policy must be rigorously enforced to build trust. The processes for investigating reports must also be conducted with demonstrable fairness and transparency.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A thorough re-examination of the company’s entire compliance structure is also prudent. This includes verifying that all internal policies, codes of conduct, and procedures for preventing bribery and corruption are not only in place but also fully aligned with&nbsp;current legal requirements and international best practices. Finally, comprehensive awareness and education programs for all employees are crucial. Training should communicate the contents of this new amendment, the company’s unwavering commitment to ethical practices, and the details of its internal reporting mechanisms.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Conclusion</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The amended Organic Act on Anti-Corruption represents a necessary change to Thailand’s legal framework, significantly altering the compliance environment for businesses. Rather than seeing these changes solely as an escalation of risk, forward-thinking companies will recognize them as an opportunity. By embracing this new standard of transparency and proactively fortifying their internal governance and whistleblower protocols, companies can not only ensure compliance but also enhance their operational integrity, foster a culture of ethics, and solidify their reputation as responsible corporate citizens in the Thai market.<br>Leading our corporate governance practice is Dr. Paul Crosio, a seasoned management expert with extensive experience in advising multinational and local companies on compliance, anti-corruption, and corporate governance frameworks. Paul has a deep understanding of Thailand’s legal and regulatory environment, coupled with international best practices, enabling him to advise on effective compliance programs that mitigate risks and align with global standards. His expertise includes working with a variety of different multinational corporations as Corporate Counsel or Chief Financial Officer as well as being appointed as Board Member and Executive Chairman for a number of listed corporations.<br>SILQ offers end-to-end support, from reviewing and strengthening internal whistleblowing systems to conducting compliance audits and providing strategic counsel on governance matters. With Paul Crosio’s leadership and our team’s commitment to excellence, SILQ is your trusted partner in compliance, safeguarding your business, and reinforcing your reputation as a responsible corporate citizen in Thailand.<br>For expert guidance on aligning your business with Thailand’s anti-corruption laws and enhancing your corporate governance framework, contact SILQ today using the form below or via email at <a href="mailto:info@silqlaw.com">info@silqlaw.com</a>.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand Strengthens Consumer Protections with New Residential Leasing Regulations]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 05 Sep 2025 07:15:10 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Several mandatory provisions have been introduced into short-term leases to address longstanding tenant grievances. Thailand’s Office of the Consumer Protection Board (OCPB) has enacted stricter regulations for the residential leasing sector.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The new rules, which come into effect on September 4, 2025, aim to curb unfair contract terms and practices that have been the subject of widespread consumer complaints.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Notification of the Contract Committee Re: The Stipulation of Residential Property Leasing as a Contract-Controlled Business B.E. 2568 (2025), published in the Royal Thai Government Gazette on June 6, 2025. This notification repeals and replaces the previous 2019 framework, introducing several critical changes to tenant rights and landlord obligations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This regulatory change has been anticipated by industry observers. Media outlets, including&nbsp;<em>Bangkok Post</em>&nbsp;and&nbsp;<em>Prachachat</em>, have reported on the growing number of complaints related to unjustified security deposit deductions and inflated utility charges, placing pressure on authorities to intervene.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Key Provisions of the 2025 Notification</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The notification distinguishes between two contract types: short-term leases (lasting up to three years) and long-term leases (lasting more than three years, up to 30 years or for the duration of the tenant's life). While the use of official standard contracts is not mandatory, any lease agreement used must not contravene the stipulated requirements and prohibitions of the notification.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A primary change is the&nbsp;<strong>expansion of its scope</strong>. The rules now&nbsp;<strong>apply to any lessor leasing three or more residential units</strong>, a reduction from the five-unit threshold under the 2019 law.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This change brings a larger number of property owners and small-scale landlords under the OCPB’s purview. The regulation expressly includes leases conducted through digital platforms, ensuring online rental agreements are subject to the same consumer protections.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mandatory Contractual Terms</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Lease agreements must be written in clear Thai text of a specified minimum size. Several terms are now compulsory, including detailed party information, a description of the property, and all associated fees.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Key mandatory provisions include:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Invoices and Transparency:</strong> Landlords must provide written invoices for rent and utilities at least three days before payment is due. Tenants have an explicit right to request supporting documentation for utility and service charges.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Move-in Inspection:</strong> A jointly signed condition report, which may include photographs, must be completed and attached to the lease agreement.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Deposit Return:</strong> Security deposits must be returned immediately upon lease termination. If an inspection is necessary, refunds must be processed within seven days if no damage is found, or within 14 days after deducting verified repair costs.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Early Termination:</strong> Tenants in fixed-term leases gain the right to terminate after occupying the property for at least half of the lease term, provided they give 30 days' notice and settle all outstanding payments.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Landlord Termination:</strong> Landlords must provide a minimum of 30 days' written notice before termination, except in cases of urgent misconduct, which requires seven days' notice.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">If these terms are omitted from a contract, they are deemed to be implied by law.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Prohibited Contract Clauses</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The notification explicitly bans several unfair practices by declaring certain clauses unenforceable.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Prohibited terms include those that:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Allow security deposits or advance rent exceeding three months' rent for short-term or monthly long-term leases, or one year’s rent for annually paid long-term leases.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Permit landlords to unilaterally increase rent or service charges before the lease term expires.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Authorize the confiscation of deposits or advance rent without justification or fault of the tenant.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Set utility charges at rates higher than those prescribed by the relevant state authorities.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Allow landlords to lock out tenants, confiscate belongings, or conduct non-emergency inspections without prior notice.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Impose liability on tenants for damages resulting from normal wear and tear.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Compliance and Penalties</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Non-compliance with these regulations constitutes a violation of Thailand’s Consumer Protection Act B.E. 2522 (1979). Businesses or landlords found using non-compliant contracts may face criminal penalties, including imprisonment for up to one year, a fine of up to THB 200,000, or both.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">We advise landlords and property management companies to thoroughly review and revise their standard lease agreements well before the September 4, 2025, effective date to ensure alignment with the new legal requirements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Landlords should also consider modifying their agreements with leasing agents to allow for clawback of commissions should a lease terminate early.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Sources:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Royal Thai Government Gazette. (2025, June 6). Notification of the Contract Committee Re: The Stipulation of Residential Property Leasing as a Contract-Controlled Business B.E. 2568 (2025).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Thailand's Office of the Consumer Protection Board (OCPB). Official communications and press statements.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Consumer Protection Act, B.E. 2522 (1979).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><em>Bangkok Post</em>. (2025). Reports on residential leasing complaints and regulatory developments.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><em>Prachachat</em>. (2025). Coverage of the OCPB's policy announcements.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->
