					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand's Digital Assets Blueprint: Balancing Fintech Innovation with Firm Control]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 08 Sep 2025 10:04:33 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand is rapidly developing one of Asia's most structured frameworks for digital assets, shifting from outright prohibition to a nuanced model of&nbsp;<strong>"regulated innovation."</strong>&nbsp;For legal and fintech professionals, the recent developments offer a masterclass in how a jurisdiction can cautiously open doors without compromising financial integrity.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Here’s a breakdown of the key regulatory shifts:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"> <strong>1. The Payment Prohibition &amp; Strategic Pilots</strong> </h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Bank of Thailand (BOT) maintains its firm stance: <strong>cryptocurrencies are not legal tender.</strong> However, this isn't a rejection of digital currency technology itself. The BOT is actively piloting its own solutions, including a Retail CBDC and the cross-border <strong>"mBridge" project</strong>, signalling a clear preference for state-sanctioned digital money over volatile private assets.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The mBridge project is a collaborative initiative focused on developing a wholesale Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) for international remittances, with contributions from the Bank of Thailand and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>2. The SEC's Sandbox and Carve-Out Strategy</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""> The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is demonstrating pragmatism through its regulatory sandboxes. The upcoming 2025 tourism program, allowing visitors to convert digital assets into Baht via licensed operators, is a prime example. </p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The six eligible digital asset-related services under the original “sandbox” criteria are: (1) Digital Asset Exchange, (2) Digital Asset Broker, (3) Digital Asset Dealer, (4) Digital Asset Fund Manager, (5) Digital Asset Advisor, and (6) Digital Asset Custodial Wallet Provider. The Sandbox participants must incorporate their innovations into the development of digital asset services in the Thai capital market, or must participate in a sandbox of the money market regulatory agency</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>3. Tightening Controls &amp; Acknowledging Stablecoins</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""> Draft regulations aim to extend payment prohibitions to custodial wallet providers. In a significant move, the SEC added USD Coin (USDC) and Tether (USDT) to its list of approved cryptocurrencies on March 16, 2025. This regulatory change allows digital asset exchanges to use these stablecoins as base trading pairs and enables ICO portals to accept them from investors and issuers. The move expands Thailand's digital asset market, enhances flexibility for businesses, and provides more payment options within the country's digital asset ecosystem, which aims to foster innovation in the sector. This is a critical step in gradually broadening the acceptable use of digital assets within a controlled environment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>4. Elevating ICOs &amp; Integrating Cybercrime Law</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""> Fundraising is a major supervisory priority. New SEC requirements for ICOs (effective August 2025) focus on governance, token holder rights, and stricter advertising, bringing investor protections closer in line with those of traditional capital markets. Crucially, amendments to the <strong>Cybercrime Law (2023)</strong> create liability for mule accounts and impose joint responsibility on operators failing security obligations. This directly integrates digital asset regulation with broader frameworks for financial crime prevention.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>5. Tax Incentives to Drive On-Exchange Activity</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""> Perhaps the clearest signal to encourage regulated activity is in the tax code. Since January 2025, individuals have enjoyed a <strong>five-year capital gains tax exemption</strong> for trades on licensed exchanges, while issuers of investment tokens remain exempt from corporate income tax and VAT.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>The Bottom Line:</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""> Thailand is executing a dual strategy: <strong>promote growth within a licensed, supervised ecosystem</strong> while maintaining <strong>strict controls against unlicensed activity.</strong> This creates significant opportunities for compliant operators but demands rigorous legal compliance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[New Strict Alcohol Sales Laws in Thailand Effective November 2025]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 10 Sep 2025 15:16:14 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The new Alcoholic Beverage Control Act (No. 2) B.E. 2568 (2025) has been published in the Royal Gazette today, and it will take effect 60 days from its publication. While the previous 2008 law was already strict, the new version focuses heavily on eliminating loopholes in advertising and promotion and introduces a new, strict prohibition on sales during late-night/early morning hours. Penalties for violations have also been substantially increased.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Comparison: New 2025 Laws vs. Previous 2008 Law</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Aspect</strong></td><td><strong>Previous Law (2008)</strong></td><td><strong>New 2025 Amendment</strong></td><td><strong>Impact &amp; Analysis</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>1.Sales Times (The Most Direct Change)</strong></td><td><strong>No nationwide blanket ban on sales times.</strong>Restrictions were based on location (e.g., near schools, temples) and time of day for certain venues (e.g., entertainment places), but no universal "no sales" period.</td><td><strong>Expanded 24/7 Sales:</strong>Since 27 June 2025, following a new Prime Minister’s Office Notification on alcohol sales hours, Thailand has allowed extended sales in specific venues:International Airports – Lounges, bars, and duty-free shops may now serve alcohol beyond previous time restrictions.&nbsp;Licensed Hotels – In-room service is now allowed 24/7.Licensed Entertainment Venues – Extended hours until 4 am in designated provinces.General Retail Stores – No change; original sale hours remain in effect.&nbsp;</td><td>This is a major new change, allowing Hotels to serve customers at any time, even on days when alcohol sales are generally banned, and extends the opening hours of registered entertainment venues.&nbsp;Convenience stores, supermarkets, and other retail outlets are not allowed to sell alcohol between&nbsp;<strong>midnight and 11:00 AM</strong>. This aims to reduce late-night drinking and related social issues.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>2.Advertising &amp; Promotion (Massive Expansion)</strong></td><td>Prohibited direct advertising but had loopholes. "Marketing" was defined more narrowly.</td><td>Dramatically broadens the scope of prohibited activities:&nbsp;• New Definition: "Marketing communications" now explicitly includes public relations, news dissemination, creating brand image, and sponsoring events.&nbsp;• Sec 32/1: Bans all advertising except strictly defined "information."&nbsp;• Sec 32/2: Bans using celebrities/influencers to induce consumption.&nbsp;• Sec 32/3: Bans using alcoholic brand names/symbols on other products (e.g., soda, clothing). • Sec 32/4 &amp; 32/5: Bans Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities that promote the brand and bans publishing news about such activities.</td><td>This closes all major loopholes brands used for visibility.<br><strong>Sponsorships of sports events, music festivals, or university projects are now likely illegal.</strong> Using a beer logo on a free shirt or a brand sponsoring a charity run is prohibited. This is one of the strictest advertising regimes in the world.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>3.Penalties (Significantly Harsher)</strong></td><td>Fines were generally lower.</td><td>Penalties have been increased across the board:&nbsp;• Illegal Sales (Sec 40): Fine increased to up to 100,000 Baht and/or 1 year imprisonment.&nbsp;• New Advertising Violations (Sec 43/1): Up to 6 months imprisonment and/or a fine of up to 100,000 Baht.&nbsp;• For Businesses: Advertising/CSR violations can lead to fines of up to 500,000 Baht.&nbsp;• Daily Fines: Violators can also be fined up to 50,000 Baht per day until the violation is corrected.</td><td>The drastic increase in financial and criminal penalties is designed to ensure strict compliance. The daily fines make long-running violations extremely costly.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>4.Definition of "Alcoholic Beverage"</strong></td><td>Defined alcoholic beverages without any explicit exemption for very low alcohol content.</td><td><strong>Following the 2025 Amendment (No. 2), Section 3 now clarifies the exemption.</strong> Now explicitly excludes <strong>"beverages with an alcohol content of not more than 0.5 percent"</strong>(e.g., many kombuchas, alcohol-removed beers), alongside drugs and herbal products.</td><td>This provides clearer legal guidance on what is considered a controlled alcoholic beverage versus a non-alcoholic drink.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>5.Committee Structure</strong></td><td>Had a National Alcoholic Beverage Policy Committee.</td><td>Expands the committee to include more ministries, such as the Minister of Digital Economy and Society and the Minister of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation.</td><td>Reflects a more holistic, whole-of-government approach to alcohol control, recognizing its impact on digital media, youth, and research.</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Summary of Key Issues Addressed</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The new law aims to tackle several core issues that were presumably not fully resolved by the 2008 law:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Predatory Marketing:</strong> The previous law could not keep up with modern, indirect advertising techniques like influencer marketing, event sponsorship, and branded content. The new law attempts to ban all of it.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Late-Night Alcohol Availability:</strong> This has been expanded at the request of the Hotel and Tourism industry to better cater to the needs of tourists and entertainment venues in designated provinces, but other locations remain unchanged.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Insufficient Deterrence:</strong> The older penalties were perhaps not severe enough to deter large corporations from violating the rules. The new fines of 500,000 Baht and daily penalties are meant to change that.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Corporate "Greenwashing":</strong> The law specifically targets the use of CSR and public benefit activities as a form of brand promotion, arguing that it indirectly induces consumption.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Ancillary Marketing</strong>: The law specifically targets the marketing and advertising of other items, whether drinks or clothing, such as soda or mineral water, effectively banning the advertising of the brand as a whole. </li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Important Note</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">As per&nbsp;<strong>Section 43</strong>, the existing ministerial regulations from the 2008 law remain in effect&nbsp;<em>unless</em>&nbsp;they conflict with this new amendment. The relevant ministries have&nbsp;<strong>one year</strong>&nbsp;from the effective date (which is 60 days after its publication on Sept 9, 2025) to issue new detailed regulations that will specify the exact rules and procedures under this new law.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->

It also closes advertising loopholes such as clothing / soda. Hotels may sell 24/7, and low-alcohol drinks are exempt. ]]></excerpt:encoded>

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand's Updated Visa Policies (September 2025)]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 26 Sep 2025 08:48:09 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand has recently formalized several changes to its visa policies. The main goals are to simplify the system, prevent misuse (like "visa runs" and overstays), and better manage tourism. Rather than eliminating visas, the changes restructure them and add new limits on how often they can be used.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Streamlined Non-Immigrant Visas (Effective August 31, 2025)</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand has consolidated its 17 non-immigrant visa categories into 7 broader types. This simplifies the application process but may reduce options for very specific purposes. The eligibility requirements and rights for each visa remain largely unchanged.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The new categories are:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant B (Business and Work):</strong> For employment, business, and investment.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant ED (Education):</strong> For students, researchers, and interns.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant O (Family and Dependents):</strong> For family members of Thai nationals or residents.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant OA/OX (Retirement):</strong> For retirees aged 50 and older.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant M (Media and Journalism):</strong> For media professionals on assignment.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant F (Official Duties):</strong> For diplomats and government officials.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Non-Immigrant R (Religious Activities):</strong> For religious workers and volunteers.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This reform comes as Thailand sees a 5% drop in foreign visitors year-to-date in 2025.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>New Limits on Visa-Exempt Entries</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">To stop "visa runs," new limits are now officially in place:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>All Entries:</strong> Travelers from the 93 eligible countries can only enter Thailand without a visa twice per calendar year. A third attempt will likely be denied.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Land Borders:</strong> Entries by land from neighboring countries are limited to two per year, granting a 15-day stay each time. Local citizens have similar limits, although with longer stays, except for Malaysians, who have unlimited entries.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Potential Shortening of Visa-Free Stays</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand may soon reduce the standard visa-free stay from 60 days to 30 days for many nationalities. This could happen in late 2025. The option to extend for another 30 days at a local immigration office (for a fee) would remain, allowing a total 60-day stay. This would return the rules to their pre-COVID status.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The government believes this will prevent people from using tourist entries for illegal work, especially after complaints about "zero-dollar tours."</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Note:</strong>&nbsp;As of September 2025, the 60-day stay is still in effect. Always verify before you travel.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Other Key Changes Increasing Scrutiny</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Proof of Funds:</strong> Since May 1, 2025, all tourists must show proof of sufficient funds (like bank statements) upon entry.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Digital Arrival Card:</strong> The Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC) is now mandatory and must be completed online at least 72 hours before arrival.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Elite Visa Change:</strong> The affordable 5-year "Bronze Tier" Elite visa ended on June 30, 2025, reducing long-stay options.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Cambodian Nationals:</strong> Due to border issues, the visa-exempt stay for Cambodians was reduced from 60 days to 7 days in June 2025.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These changes are part of a larger effort to modernize Thai immigration. Despite these tighter rules, the country still aims to attract over 40 million visitors in 2025.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For the most current information, For the latest updates, check the official Thai Immigration website (immigration.go.th) or your nearest Thai embassy, as policies can change without notice. </p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""></p>

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Why 'Alleged' Statements Offer Little Protection Against Defamation or Libel in Thailand ]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 01 Oct 2025 07:13:07 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A dangerous misconception persists in business and media circles: that using the word "alleged" when reporting an accusation provides a safe harbour from defamation claims. In Thailand, this assumption is not only incorrect but can also lead to severe civil and criminal penalties.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thai law prioritises the <strong>overall impression</strong> a publication leaves on an ordinary reader. If the context, headlines, or tone suggest someone is guilty of misconduct, the mere presence of the word "alleged" will not shield the publisher from liability.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This is a critical point of divergence from some common law systems. In Thailand, defamation is not merely a civil tort; it is also a <strong>criminal offence</strong>, carrying the potential for imprisonment. This dual threat necessitates a significantly higher degree of caution.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Legal Framework in Thailand: Civil and Criminal Liability&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Two primary legal sources govern defamation and Libel in Thailand:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>The Thai Civil and Commercial Code (CCC):</strong> Sections 420 and 423 provide the basis for civil liability. A person who, contrary to the truth, asserts or circulates a statement which injures the reputation or credit of another is liable to compensate for the resulting injury (CCC Section 423).&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>The Thai Penal Code:</strong> Sections 326-328 address criminal defamation. Section 326 states that whoever, imputing anything to the other person before a third party in a manner likely to impair the person's reputation or place such person in contempt or hatred, shall be punished with imprisonment not exceeding one year and/or a fine not exceeding twenty thousand Baht.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The key takeaway is that an aggrieved party in Thailand can sue for financial damages <strong>and</strong> file a criminal complaint that could lead to the publisher's imprisonment.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Why "Alleged" is an Inadequate Shield in the Thai Context</strong>&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thai courts, like their common law counterparts, look at the substance of a publication, not just its form. The "sting" of the accusation is what matters. If the ordinary, reasonable reader is left with the impression that there is fire, merely pointing out that you are only describing "smoke" with the word "alleged" is often insufficient. Consider a news headline: <em>"CEO Allegedly Embezzles Company Funds."</em> While it includes "allegedly," the prominent accusation can still destroy the CEO's reputation. In a Thai court, the defence would bear the heavy burden of proving the truth of the underlying embezzlement claim to avoid liability, not merely that the accusation was made.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Furthermore, the defences available are strict. For example:&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Truth as a Defence:</strong> Under Section 330 of the Penal Code, proving the truth of a statement is a defence only if it is made for the public benefit. This is a higher bar than in many common law jurisdictions, where truth can be an absolute defence. The publisher must prove both the factual truth <strong>and</strong> the public benefit element.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Good Faith Report: </strong>Under Section 329, there are limited privileges for fair and accurate reports of official proceedings, but these are narrowly construed. Sensationalising or presenting such reports out of context can easily void this protection.&nbsp;</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>The Peril of Republishing Allegations</strong>&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A fundamental principle in Thai defamation law, consistent with international norms, is that <strong>repeating a defamatory statement is considered equivalent to making it oneself</strong>. Sharing a damaging post on social media or reporting a third-party's accusation without proper context is not a neutral act. The law views the republisher as adopting the statement and assuming full responsibility for its defamatory sting.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>A Practical Guide to Mitigating Defamation Risk in Thailand</strong>&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Given the severe consequences, businesses, journalists, and individuals must exercise extreme care. The following chart outlines a prudent approach to publication.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10668,"sizeSlug":"full","linkDestination":"none","align":"center"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/defamation-article-infographic.png" alt="" class="wp-image-10668"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion&nbsp;</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In Thailand's legal landscape, where defamation can lead to both financial ruin and imprisonment, relying on semantic tricks like the word "alleged" is a profound professional risk. The courts will look past the label to the damaging impression it creates.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The only safe path is to prioritise accuracy, context, and balance in all communications. Before publishing any potentially damaging statement, one must be prepared to prove its truth for the public benefit, not just its existence as an allegation. In Thailand, more than in many common law countries, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.&nbsp;</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[A New Era for Innovation: Understanding Thailand’s Draft Startup Promotion and Development Act]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 22 Oct 2025 04:17:20 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:image {"id":10723,"sizeSlug":"full","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Draft-Startup-Promotion-and-Development-Act-—-Summary.png" alt="" class="wp-image-10723"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand is positioning itself at the forefront of Southeast Asia's innovation economy with the introduction of the Draft Startup Promotion and Development Act. This proposed legislation represents a strategic governmental initiative designed to systematically address the legal and operational challenges that have historically constrained the growth and competitiveness of new businesses. Acknowledging the critical role startups play in driving economic progress, technological advancement, and job creation, the Draft seeks to establish a comprehensive and supportive legal framework. The ultimate objective is to enhance entrepreneurial capacity, improve access to funding, and foster essential business networks. The public consultation period for this pivotal Draft is currently open until 27 October 2025, inviting stakeholder input to refine the proposed measures.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Regulatory Framework and Oversight Authorities</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Draft legislation proposes the establishment of a dedicated Startup Promotion Committee. This committee will be vested with the authority to oversee and formulate policies aimed at promoting startup development nationwide. The National Innovation Agency (NIA) is designated to act as the primary coordinator and secretariat for this initiative. The NIA’s role, as highlighted in its public communications, is to bridge the public and private sectors, ensuring a cohesive approach to promoting startups. The agency will manage a one-stop service centre, disseminate critical information regarding rights and benefits, and facilitate connections to domestic and international funding opportunities for qualifying enterprises.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Eligibility Criteria for Startup Recognition</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">To qualify for the benefits outlined in the Draft, startups must satisfy a set of specific criteria and submit a formal self-declaration to the NIA. The eligibility requirements are structured to ensure support is directed toward genuine, early-stage companies. These requirements include a stipulation that the startup must be a limited company or public limited company incorporated for no more than ten years at the time of application. Furthermore, the startup must demonstrate an average annual revenue of not more than 300 million baht over the preceding three consecutive years. The entity must not have paid dividends to its shareholders, reinforcing its focus on reinvestment and growth. Regarding ownership, the startup must not be controlled by another company, except in specific circumstances where the controlling entity is itself a startup or a company established in partnership with a higher education institution for research and innovation purposes. Recognised startups are required to annually update their information through the NIA’s electronic system to maintain their status and benefits.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Comprehensive Review of Benefits for Newly Established Businesses</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Draft Startup Promotion and Development Act offer a suite of benefits that directly address the most significant pain points for newly established businesses in Thailand. These provisions are designed to create a more fertile ground for innovation and scaling.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">One of the most significant benefits is the exemption from certain shareholding restrictions. This provision permits startups to hold their own shares, a practice typically restricted under conventional corporate law. This flexibility is crucial for modern fundraising strategies, including employee stock option plans (ESOPs), which are instrumental in attracting and retaining top-tier talent. It also provides greater latitude for corporate restructuring, mergers, and acquisitions, as well as for offering shares to the public or issuing debentures in compliance with Securities and Exchange Commission regulations. This single change can dramatically alter a startup's ability to structure deals and incentivise key personnel.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Beyond shareholding, the Draft mandates that relevant government agencies provide support in other critical areas. This includes potential benefits related to taxation, such as incentives for investors or tax holidays for the startups themselves, which can preserve vital capital during the early, revenue-light stages. Immigration benefits could facilitate easier entry and stay for foreign experts, founders, and investors, addressing Thailand’s previous challenges in attracting global talent. Enhanced support for intellectual property protection is also implied, which is paramount for startups whose primary assets are often intangible. Furthermore, the centralised one-stop service centre operated by the NIA will streamline bureaucratic processes, saving new businesses considerable time and resources that would otherwise be spent navigating multiple government departments.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These benefits are available for a period of five years from the legislation’s enactment, with a potential extension of up to ten years for startups engaged in the agricultural sector, acknowledging the longer development cycles in agri-tech.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Status of the Proposed Legislation and Path Forward</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">As of the current timeline, the Draft Startup Promotion and Development Act is in the public consultation phase. This period, which remains open until October 27, 2025, allows feedback from entrepreneurs, investors, legal experts, and other stakeholders to be incorporated into the final version of the law. Following this consultation, the Draft will proceed through the legislative process, which includes review and approval by the Cabinet and the National Assembly before it can be enacted. The active role of the NIA in publicising the Draft indicates a strong governmental commitment to seeing this legislation realised.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Preparatory Steps for Prospective Startups</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In anticipation of the Draft’s eventual enactment, emerging and existing startups are advised to undertake several preparatory steps. They should meticulously verify their eligibility against the established criteria, including the incorporation date, revenue, dividend history, and ownership structure. It is also prudent to begin gathering and maintaining accurate documentation, including financial statements and corporate ownership details, to facilitate a smooth self-declaration process with the NIA. Proactively engaging with the NIA through its available channels will provide early insights and readiness. A thorough understanding of the full range of benefits, particularly the nuances of the shareholding exemption and sector-specific incentives, will enable businesses to plan strategically for growth. Finally, a commitment to ongoing compliance with the Draft’s regulations is essential to sustain eligibility and avoid penalties.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">What does it mean for new businesses in Thailand?</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Draft Startup Promotion and Development Act mark a significant milestone in the modernisation of Thailand’s economic policy framework. By establishing a transparent, flexible, and growth-oriented regulatory structure, the Draft provides a robust foundation for a thriving and dynamic startup ecosystem. Upon its enactment, it is anticipated to cultivate a more vibrant and investor-friendly environment that will accelerate the growth, innovation, and global success of emerging businesses throughout the Kingdom.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">References</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The Secretariat of the Cabinet, Thailand. Media releases concerning new economic promotion policies.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Bangkok Post. Reporting on Thailand's economic and innovation policies.</li>

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s Pending Labour Law Reforms: A Shift Towards Modern Work-Life Protections]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Thu, 30 Oct 2025 05:04:01 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">On 24 September 2025, the Thai House of Representatives unanimously approved in principle two draft Labour Protection Bills, signalling the most significant potential overhaul of the country’s employment landscape in decades.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This legislative initiative, now under review by an ad hoc committee, aims to align Thailand’s labour standards with modern societal needs and global benchmarks, focusing on work-life balance, inclusivity, and employee welfare.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The first draft bill proposes substantive changes to basic employment terms. A key amendment is the reduction of the standard working week from 48 hours to 40 hours, with a further limit of 35 hours for hazardous occupations. This shift acknowledges evolving productivity models and employee well-being.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Furthermore, the mandate for at least two weekly rest days, with no more than five consecutive working days, seeks to systematically combat employee burnout. Also, paid annual leave will increase to 10 days after 120 days of continuous service —a significant increase from the previous 6 days after 1 full year — giving employees greater flexibility and time off from their employment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The second draft bill introduces pioneering social provisions. It enshrines a broad non-discrimination clause that protects employees on the basis of disability, gender identity, religion, beliefs, or political views. Notably, it institutionalises menstrual leave, granting female employees up to three days per month, distinct from sick leave—a measure that, as reported by Bangkok Post, aims to destigmatise health issues and promote gender-sensitive workplaces.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The introduction of family care leave, allowing up to 15 days annually, and stringent requirements for private, equipped breastfeeding facilities with dedicated break times reflect an intent to support employees’ parental responsibilities and address one of the causes of Thailand’s declining birth rate.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Collectively, these drafts impose new obligations on employers to foster inclusive and supportive environments. While the final form of the legislation is pending review, its underlying principles mark a clear move towards a global standard for Thailand’s labour protection regulations. Businesses should anticipate these changes and begin evaluating their policies and hiring models to ensure future compliance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10747,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Thailands-Labour-Law-Reforms-Key-Changes-Comparison-Chart-Read-Only-1024x662.webp" alt="" class="wp-image-10747"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[The Evolution of Thailand’s Business Rehabilitation Framework]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 31 Oct 2025 04:29:23 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s business rehabilitation regime under the Bankruptcy Act B.E. 2483 (1940) continues to serve as a vital legal mechanism for companies facing financial distress. The cornerstone of this process is the court’s meticulous assessment of whether a debtor possesses a credible justification for rehabilitation, a determination that artfully blends strict legal criteria with a pragmatic evaluation of commercial feasibility. This judicial gatekeeping function is paramount in balancing the interests of debtors seeking a lifeline with the rights of creditors seeking repayment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Section 90/3 of the Bankruptcy Act, a petitioner must satisfy several conditions to enter rehabilitation. The judiciary pays particular attention to two intertwined elements: the root cause of the insolvency or inability to pay debts, and the substantive justification for rehabilitation, along with the feasibility of the proposed recovery plan. These are not procedural checkboxes; they form the substantive core of the court’s role in safeguarding economic value and preventing the misuse of the process.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The requirement for a credible justification demands that a debtor demonstrate a realistic and substantiated opportunity to recover. Courts look beyond a simple declaration of financial distress, scrutinising whether the debtor retains a viable operational core, whether the proposed restructuring is practicable, and whether the plan offers a reasonable probability of success. This principle was reinforced in the Supreme Court Decision No. 1088/2566, where a petition was dismissed because the debtor failed to provide a clear and convincing rehabilitation plan, presenting instead a vague proposal that lacked operational and financial specifics. The court found the justification for rehabilitation to be fundamentally unpersuasive.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The legal landscape is poised for a significant transformation. The draft amendments to the Bankruptcy Act, anticipated to take effect in late 2025, propose a series of changes to make rehabilitation more accessible, expedient, and cost-effective, particularly for individuals and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). As reported by the Bangkok Post, these reforms are part of a broader governmental effort to address economic fragility and encourage distressed businesses to seek protection earlier.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The proposed amendments introduce a multi-tiered system. For ordinary business rehabilitation, the debt threshold will rise substantially from THB 10 million to THB 50 million. A new, distinct track for SMEs expands eligibility to include public limited companies and, crucially, removes the contentious mandatory prepackaged plan requirement. This change acknowledges the resource constraints of smaller enterprises. Furthermore, the introduction of expedited rehabilitation procedures and clearer creditor classification and voting thresholds aims to streamline proceedings and reduce litigation costs.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">From a judicial perspective, these amendments will necessitate an evolution in the court’s evaluative role. The removal of the prepackaged plan for SMEs means courts will shift their focus to assessing feasibility through the dynamic processes of creditor meetings and formal inquiries. This places greater emphasis on judicial discretion and a fact-intensive review during the proceedings, rather than at the initial filing stage. The expedited procedures address the current multi-year timeline and compel the courts to conduct their substantive evaluations quickly, focusing on the core indicators of recovery potential without being bogged down by procedural formalities in smaller cases.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Judicial discretion remains at the heart of the process. The Act intentionally refrains from defining rigid time frames for insolvency or a fixed formula for feasibility. Instead, courts are empowered to consider the totality of circumstances, including prevailing economic headwinds, sector-specific challenges, and the debtor’s historical performance and management credibility.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Ultimately, the Thai judiciary’s approach to rehabilitation is a continuous balancing act between legal precision and economic pragmatism. The justification must be credible, the plan must be feasible, and the entire process must be conducted fairly with all stakeholders.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">As Thailand refines its insolvency architecture through these forthcoming amendments, businesses under economic pressure should remain informed and prepared to navigate this more complex rehabilitation regime.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Comparison of Rehabilitation Frameworks: Existing vs. Draft Amendments</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Feature</strong></td><td><strong>Existing Regime</strong></td><td><strong>Draft Amendment Proposals</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Debt Threshold for Ordinary Rehabilitation</strong></td><td>THB 10 million</td><td>THB 50 million</td></tr><tr><td><strong>SME Eligibility</strong></td><td>Limited to private limited companies and certain partnerships.</td><td>Expanded to include public limited companies and other juristic persons as defined by the SME Promotion Act.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Prepackaged Plan for SME Rehabilitation</strong></td><td>Mandatory submission with the petition.</td><td>Requirement removed, allowing for plan development post-filing.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Procedural Tracks</strong></td><td>Primarily a single, standard procedure.</td><td>Introduction of a distinct, expedited rehabilitation procedure for faster, simpler cases.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Creditor Classification &amp; Voting</strong></td><td>Complexities and disputes often arise over classification.</td><td>Clearer guidelines and simplified voting thresholds for plan approval to enhance predictability.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Primary Objective</strong></td><td>Debt restructuring and business continuation for qualifying entities.</td><td>Enhanced accessibility and cost-effectiveness, especially for SMEs and individuals, promote earlier intervention.</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s New Labour Protection Act (No. 9) B.E. 2568 (2025): Key Amendments]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 12 Nov 2025 00:47:04 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand has enacted the <strong>Labour Protection Act (No. 9) B.E. 2568 (2025)</strong>, introducing a series of amendments to modernize the country’s employment law framework. The Act was published in the <em>Royal Gazette</em> on <strong>7 November 2025</strong> and will take effect <strong>30 days after publication</strong>.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The changes expand worker protections, update family-related leave entitlements, and simplify compliance procedures for employers. Collectively, they reflect Thailand’s effort to strengthen employee welfare and align domestic labour standards with international norms.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Expanded Protections for Contracted Workers</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A key reform extends statutory protections to individuals previously outside the full scope of the Labour Protection Act.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Government agencies</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">State enterprises</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Public organizations</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These workers are now entitled to the same fundamental benefits as other employees, including:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Minimum wage protections</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Weekly and traditional holidays</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Annual and sick leave</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Maternity and other family-related leave</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Any disputes arising from these employment relationships will now fall under the <strong>jurisdiction of the Labour Court</strong>, ensuring a dedicated and consistent legal process.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Enhanced Leave and Family Support Provisions</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The amendments introduce several new and expanded forms of leave, addressing both family and health-related needs.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":4} -->
<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Maternity Leave</strong></h4>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Increased to <strong>120 days per pregnancy</strong>, with the first <strong>60 days fully paid</strong>.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">An additional <strong>15 days of paid leave at 50% of wages</strong> is available where the newborn suffers from <strong>medical complications, disorders, or disabilities</strong>.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":4} -->
<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Paternity Leave</strong></h4>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Fathers are now entitled to <strong>15 days of paid paternity leave</strong> to support their spouse following childbirth.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":4} -->
<h4 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Menstrual Leave</strong></h4>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Act introduces <strong>one day of menstrual leave per menstrual cycle</strong>, separate from sick leave. Wages for this leave are to be paid in accordance with the employer’s internal policy or collective labour agreement.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These changes reflect a policy emphasis on gender inclusivity, family welfare, and equitable workplace support.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Simplified Employer Reporting Obligations</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Employers with <strong>ten or more employees</strong> must now submit their <strong>annual employment and working conditions report</strong> directly to the <strong>Director-General of the Labour Department</strong> each January.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This replaces the previous multi-step submission process and aims to simplify compliance management.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Market and Industry Reactions</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Initial responses to the new law have been mixed.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Labour advocates</strong> have welcomed the reforms as a positive step toward improved welfare and closing protection gaps for contract-based workers.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Employers and business groups</strong>, including SMEs and public sector contractors, have expressed concern about the potential <strong>increase in operating costs</strong> linked to expanded paid leave entitlements and benefit coverage.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Observers note that the practical impact will depend on how efficiently organizations adapt their human resource policies and financial systems to comply with the updated obligations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Broader Policy Context</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This legislative reform reflects Thailand’s broader policy trend toward enhanced worker protection and social support. It also serves as part of a demographic response to the country’s <strong>declining birth rate</strong> and aims to promote better work-life balance for employees.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Review and update internal HR policies and employment contracts</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Revise payroll systems to reflect new entitlements</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Prepare for annual compliance reporting under the new rules</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These amendments mark an important evolution in Thailand’s labour landscape, balancing economic considerations with strengthened employee rights and social welfare objectives.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><em>This article is provided for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Readers should seek professional counsel before acting on any information contained herein.</em></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

		<title><![CDATA[Thailand's Bold Leap: Proposed Foreign Business Act Amendments to Boost Competitiveness]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 17 Nov 2025 03:56:03 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>

		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:image {"id":10826,"sizeSlug":"large","linkDestination":"none"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/fba-article-infographic-791x1024.png" alt="" class="wp-image-10826"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<h2>Thailand's Bold Leap: Proposed Foreign Business Act Amendments to Boost Competitiveness</h2>
<p>Thailand is taking a significant step towards a more dynamic and competitive economic future. Recent reports in the Bangkok Post and The Nation have highlighted the Cabinet's approval in principle to amend the Foreign Business Act (FBA) of 1999. This landmark initiative, driven by the Law Reform Commission, recognises that after 25 years, the current law requires modernisation to reflect today's global business landscape.</p>
<p>The proposed amendments signal a strategic pivot from a protectionist stance to a forward-looking policy focused on enhancing national competitiveness. The goal is clear: to attract high-value foreign investment, empower startups and future industries, and integrate Thai enterprises more deeply into the global value chain.</p>
<h3>Key Proposed Changes &amp; Rationale</h3>
<p>The driving force behind this reform is the understanding that the existing FBA can be a barrier to innovation and growth. By updating the restrictive lists and streamlining administrative processes, Thailand aims to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Attract “Future Businesses” through high-tech and startup development.</li>
<li>Accelerate technology transfer by easing entry for foreign expertise.</li>
<li>Strengthen Thai competitiveness and empower domestic private sector innovation.</li>
</ul>
<p>Below is a simplified summary of the major proposed changes:</p>
<table class="simple-table">
<tbody>
<tr>
<th>Aspect</th>
<th>Current FBA Framework</th>
<th>Proposed Amendments</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>List 3: “Other Services”</td>
<td>A broad category that restricts many service and tech sectors unintentionally.</td>
<td>Expected to be narrowed with clearer definitions; high-tech and R&amp;D services may be excluded from restrictions.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>New Business Exemptions</td>
<td>Limited flexibility; new business models often require case-by-case review.</td>
<td>New fast-track notification system for “future businesses” rather than full licensing.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Administrative Process</td>
<td>Little transparency and slow status tracking for license applications.</td>
<td>More digitalisation, a modern tracking system, and reduced bureaucracy.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3>A Positive Trajectory for Business in Thailand</h3>
<p>These changes are expected to create a more predictable, competitive environment for investment:</p>
<p><strong>For Startups &amp; Tech Firms:</strong> Clearer establishment pathways, improved access to talent, and a stronger innovation ecosystem.</p>
<p><strong>For Foreign Investors:</strong> Reduced regulatory uncertainty and a more open landscape in emerging sectors.</p>
<p><strong>For All Businesses:</strong> Streamlined processes that reduce administrative overhead and improve ease of doing business.</p>
<p>With the Ministry of Commerce finalising the reform framework, this signals a strong, forward-looking shift in Thailand’s economic policy direction. It is a highly positive development for stakeholders across the ASEAN region.</p>

<!-- wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s Intensified Visa-Free Screening: Not New Policy, But Newly Enforced]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 24 Nov 2025 04:30:35 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand is once again experiencing a “crackdown” on visa-exempt entries and the misuse of tourist visas. While the situation may seem like a new development, the underlying framework has not changed. As we previously explained in our analysis of repeated visa-exempt entries, Thailand has long treated multiple visa-free visits as a matter of immigration-officer discretion, with an informal understanding that two entries per year is the safest baseline.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">What has changed is awareness, coordination, and consistent enforcement.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Officer Discretion: The Core Principle Remains Unchanged</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand has previously indicated limits on the number of visa-exempt entries permitted per year. Immigration officers continue to assess each traveller’s intentions based on conduct, documentation, and travel behaviour.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This remains true today. The current enforcement simply reinforces what was always the rule:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">If an officer suspects that a traveller is not a genuine tourist, additional interview may be requested after which entry may be refused.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">If travellers cannot answer basic questions about itinerary, accommodation, or duration, refusal is likely.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">If travel patterns resemble long-term residence or undeclared employment, officers will intervene.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The legal framework is unchanged — but the scrutiny is now more consistent and coordinated.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">What Actually Changed? Enforcement, Not Law</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The major development is the visibility of the current campaign. Following the 12 November national directive, all ports of entry are actively screening for extended-stay patterns, particularly travellers who:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Enter visa-exempt (or a 60-day tourist visa),</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Extend for 30 days,</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Repeat,</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Accumulate approximately 150 days per year.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This does not align with typical tourism and is receiving closer attention.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Placeholder Bookings Now a Serious Risk</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Authorities have also identified widespread use of unpaid, non-ticketed flight reservations (“placeholder bookings”). These were historically tolerated by some officers and airlines, but immigration has now warned that presenting an unpaid itinerary may result in immediate deportation. This is a meaningful operational change and should be taken seriously.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Key Red Flags Identified by Phuket Airport Immigration</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Phuket Airport Immigration has highlighted the following indicators for enhanced screening:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Signs of illegal or undeclared work</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Inability to describe travel plans</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Lack of a coherent itinerary</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Insufficient funds</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">No valid, paid onward or return ticket</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Nervous or inconsistent behaviour</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Frequent border runs inconsistent with tourism</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Travellers with approximately 150 days of stay within a year should expect interviews, with outcomes entirely at officer discretion.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Genuine Circumstances Still Considered</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Despite tighter enforcement, immigration leadership has confirmed that legitimate cases will still be admitted. Officers may allow entry for:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Family visits</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Processing long-term visa documentation</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Administrative or transitional travel needs</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These decisions remain case-by-case, and travellers with clear, honest explanations continue to be admitted without issues.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Lawful Alternatives: Thailand’s Modernised Visa Pathways</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For travellers who frequently stay in Thailand or wish to avoid discretionary immigration decisions, several modern visa pathways now provide predictable, compliant options:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Destination Thailand Visa (DTV)</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A new programme suitable for medium-term stays, remote work, lifestyle travel, and extended tourism.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Fully online application through the official e-Visa portal</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Must be applied for from overseas</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A practical replacement for repeated visa-free entries</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Long-Term Resident (LTR) Visa</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Designed for remote professionals, high-income individuals, retirees, and specialists.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Applications can be made inside Thailand</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">BOI LTR officers are widely recognised for their supportive and efficient approach</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The process is straightforward enough that most applicants can apply themselves</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Other long-term options include the Non-OA retirement visa, Non-O spousal visa, and Non-O dependent visa.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s legal framework for visa-exempt entry has not changed — but the enforcement climate has. Travellers relying on repeated visa-free entries or multi-entry tourist visas should review their circumstances and consider transitioning to one of Thailand’s formal visa pathways to maintain stability and compliance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Legal Mechanisms to Expedite Land Administration Actions in Thailand]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 28 Nov 2025 10:54:43 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Department of Lands (DOL), operating under the Ministry of the Interior, constitutes the foundational institution for real property rights in the Kingdom of Thailand. Its mandate, encompassing the issuance of title deeds, the registration of encumbrances such as sales, mortgages, and leases, and the authorisation of land subdivision, is critical to the security and predictability of real estate transactions. Delays within this administrative apparatus can precipitate significant commercial detriment, including liquidity constraints, project stagnation, and the erosion of investor confidence. This analysis examines the juridical framework governing administrative timelines at the DOL and delineates the legal remedies available to parties adversely affected by procedural delays.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:image {"id":10886,"sizeSlug":"full","linkDestination":"none","align":"center"} -->
<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-full"><img src="https://i0.wp.com/silqlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/land-actions-fixed.png?fit=960%2C2222&amp;ssl=1" alt="" class="wp-image-10886"/></figure>
<!-- /wp:image -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1. Systemic Sources of Delay</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Operational inefficiencies within the DOL often stem from structural factors, including multi-layered approval protocols, resource constraints, and a continued reliance on manual documentation. A particularly impactful source of delay arises from annotations placed on title deeds. Pursuant to Section 60 of the Land Code B.E. 2497 (1954), a competent official may issue an order prohibiting any transaction concerning a land parcel pending an investigation into the legality of its issuance<sup>[1]</sup>. While a mere investigatory annotation under Section 60 does not, de jure, invalidate the title, its practical effect is to render the property commercially illiquid, as prospective purchasers and financiers are understandably reluctant to engage with an encumbered asset.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2. Statutory Timelines for Administrative Action</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Thai legislature has enacted specific laws to curtail bureaucratic inertia by imposing defined timeframes for governmental action.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Act on the Determination of Timeframes in the Justice Process B.E. 2565 (2022) represents a significant development. This statute obligates all government agencies under the Ministry of the Interior, including the DOL, to publicly prescribe and disseminate clear timelines for completing their services<sup>[2]</sup>. Should an official fail to act within the prescribed period, the Act mandates a written explanation for the delay, an estimated completion date, and notification to the relevant parties<sup>[3]</sup>.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Furthermore, the Land Code itself provides a specific regimen for title investigations. Section 61 stipulates that an investigation, once ordered, must be concluded within sixty days<sup>[4]</sup>. This period may be extended once for a further sixty days upon a resolution by an investigation committee<sup>[5]</sup>. Subsequently, a final order must be issued by the Director-General of the DOL or their delegate within fifteen days from the receipt of the investigation report<sup>[6]</sup>. However, the provision for a single permissible extension in the Land Code contrasts with potential operational practices where investigations may be repeatedly prolonged under a broad interpretation of necessity, thereby undermining the legislative intent for expedition.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3. Available Legal Remedies for Unwarranted Delay</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Parties facing undue delays possess a hierarchy of legal avenues to compel action or seek redress.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">a. Administrative Complaint</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Initial recourse typically involves internal administrative channels. A petition can be filed directly with the Chief of the relevant Provincial Land Office or the Director-General of the DOL. Alternatively, complaints may be submitted to the Damrongdhama Centre, the Ministry of the Interior's central grievances body, which operates as an intermediary to facilitate resolution within the bureaucracy.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">b. Judicial Review</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Where administrative complaints prove ineffective, judicial remedies remain available. Under the Administrative Procedure Act B.E. 2539 (1996), Section 37 establishes that written administrative orders must provide reasons, including key facts, legal grounds, and any discretionary considerations applied. This requirement promotes transparency and allows affected individuals to understand and challenge decisions effectively. Exceptions apply in urgent situations where verbal administrative orders may be issued. In such cases, the responsible official is still obligated to provide written reasons upon request by the affected party, within a reasonable time. Failure to provide such justification or to act on a formal request may constitute administrative inaction<sup>[7]</sup>. If this request is refused or ignored, the matter may be petitioned to the Administrative Court, which has jurisdiction to order an agency to perform its legal duty within a specified time.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">c. Liability for Damages</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Liability for Wrongful Acts of Officials Act B.E. 2539 (1996) enables a claimant to sue the state for compensation arising from an unlawful act or omission by a government officer<sup>[8]</sup>. This can be coupled with a civil claim under Section 420 of the Civil and Commercial Code for damages resulting from a wrongful act. The Supreme Administrative Court has affirmed that unjustified administrative delays can constitute a wrongful act for which the state is liable<sup>[9]</sup>.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">d. Criminal Sanctions for Misconduct</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In egregious cases involving malfeasance or dereliction of duty, criminal provisions under the Thai Penal Code, including Section 157, which criminalises official misconduct, may be invoked.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4. Summary of Rights to Expedite Land Actions</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In summary, the rights available to expedite land administration actions in Thailand are substantial:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Right to a Defined Timeline:</strong> Under the Act on the Determination of Timeframes B.E. 2565, a right exists to have services rendered within the DOL’s publicly announced timeframes, with a corresponding right to a written explanation for any default.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Right to a Time-Bound Investigation:</strong> Pursuant to Sections 61 bis of the Land Code, a right exists for any title investigation to be concluded within a maximum of 135 days (60-day investigation, plus a 60-day extension, plus a 15-day decision period).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Right to Administrative Petition:</strong> A right exists to petition the DOL internally and through the Damrongdhama Centre to address and resolve delays.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Right to Judicial Intervention:</strong> Under the Administrative Procedure Act B.E. 2539, a right exists to petition the Administrative Court to issue an order compelling the DOL to perform its legal duty within a judicially mandated timeframe.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Right to Compensation:</strong> A right exists to claim damages from the state under the Liability for Wrongful Acts of Officials Act B.E. 2539 and the Civil and Commercial Code for losses sustained due to unlawful delay.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While these legal mechanisms provide robust tools for addressing individual instances of delay, their efficacy is often contingent on sustained, strategically deployed legal action. Ultimately, the consistent application of these remedies by aggrieved parties serves not only to resolve discrete disputes but also to reinforce the principles of administrative accountability and legal certainty within the Thai real property regime.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">References</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Act on the Determination of Timeframes in the Justice Process B.E. 2565 (2022), Section 5.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Ibid., Section 7.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Land Code B.E. 2497 (1954), Section 61, Paragraph Four.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Ibid.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Ibid., Paragraph Five.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- /wp:list-item -->
