					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thai Labour Law: Time Off, Working Hours &amp; Equal Treatment]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Tue, 09 Dec 2025 06:59:45 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">When navigating employment in Thailand, companies must give careful attention to time-off entitlements, working hours and special regimes for hazardous duties. Under the Labour Protection Act B.E. 2541 (the "Labour Act") and related regulations, a Thai employer has clear obligations, and best practice matters. Below is a structured overview of key issues, what employers should know, and some practical tips.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Public holidays and selecting the days off</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Section 29 of the Labour Act, an employer must announce at least 13 holidays per year, including National Labour Day (1 May). In practice, the Ministry publishes a Ministerial Regulation or notification each year setting out the official holidays that qualify. The government will follow their own set of holidays that companies are not required to follow.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">As of 2019, there are 19 holidays to choose the mandated 13 from. What this means:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The minimum is 13 paid holidays. Many companies will announce more and include certain additional days such as Christmas Day, which is not publicly celebrated in Thailand.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A best-practice approach is to align the company holiday calendar with the lists published by the Bank of Thailand and the Stock Exchange of Thailand. These offer transparent, annually-published lists of bank and financial market holidays.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Companies should be aware that certain government agencies may recognize other holidays. For example, immigration closes for Royal Ploughing Ceremony Day (วันพืชมงคล). While traditionally a civil servant and state enterprise holiday, banks and most companies do not observe it.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The Thai government often announces extra ad-hoc holidays each year via cabinet resolutions, but private employers are not required to follow them; adopting these additional days is entirely at the company's discretion as long as the Section 29 minimum of 13 holidays is met.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thus, when drafting your time-off policy or holiday roster, adopt a core holiday list (for example following the Bank of Thailand) and make clear that extra days will be considered but will follow the Bank of Thailand holiday list.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Employers must announce and display the annual holiday list in the workplace, ensuring all employees are clearly informed of the official holidays in advance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Weekly day off, working hours and rest breaks</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Thai law, the following rules apply:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Weekly holiday:</strong> the employer must provide at least one day off per week; the interval between weekly rest days may not exceed six days.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Normal working hours (for regular or office work):</strong> up to 8 hours per day, and up to 48 hours per week.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Hazardous work:</strong> for work which may be harmful to the health or safety of the employee (as defined by Ministerial Regulations), normal working hours are up to 7 hours per day, and up to 42 hours per week.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Rest break during a working day:</strong> after five consecutive hours of work, the employer must provide a rest period of not less than one hour. The employer and employee may agree to shorter intervals of rest, but the total break time per day still cannot be less than one hour.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Overtime:</strong> work performed beyond normal working hours may qualify as payable overtime, but it is at the employee’s discretion, except in limited emergency situations. In practice, salaried employees may be expected to work beyond standard hours to complete their duties, though overtime compensation rules still apply.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Practical implications for employers:</strong></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">When setting the standard working week for your business, you can use the 8-hour/48-hour benchmark unless your operations fall into the hazardous-work category.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">For hazardous operations you must apply the stricter 7/42 rule.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Make sure your work rules specify what constitutes a weekly holiday or rest day, and ensure your scheduling avoids an interval longer than 6 consecutive working days without a rest day.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Workers who work more than five hours continuously must have at least one hour’s break (which should not be counted as working time).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Contracts, employment handbooks and internal policies should reflect these limits and ensure overtime, work on holidays, etc., are handled properly. Section 24 and 25 of the Labour Act set out the rules for overtime and work on holidays.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Dangerous and hazardous professions: reduced hours</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">One of the important distinctions under the Labour Act is that where work may be harmful to the health or safety of employees under Ministerial Regulations, the maximum working hours are reduced from 8 hours per day to 7. Section 23 of the Labour Act reads: “Where the work may be hazardous… the normal working hours shall not exceed seven hours per day and the total working time per week shall not exceed forty-two hours.”</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Although the exact list of hazardous work is prescribed by Ministerial Regulation, typical examples of such work include:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Mining or construction underground, underwater, in a cave or tunnel.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Work on platforms 10 metres or more above the ground.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Production or transport of explosive or inflammable material.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Metal smelting, casting or rolling; metal pressing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Work with heat, cold, vibration, noise or light of an abnormal level.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Work involving hazardous chemical substances or poisonous microorganisms.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Equal treatment of women and permitted professions</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Labour Act sets out clear protections for female employees and prescribes certain restrictions. At the same time, the broader Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 prohibits gender-based discrimination (including at work) and mandates equal pay for equal work.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Key points for female employees under the Labour Act include:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Section 15:</strong> “An employer shall treat male and female employees equally in their employment, unless the nature or conditions of the work does not allow the employer to do so.”</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Section 38:</strong> A female employee shall not be required by the employer to do certain kinds of work, including mining or underground/under-water work, working on scaffolding 10 metres or more above the ground, producing or transporting explosive or inflammable materials, or other work prescribed in ministerial regulations.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Section 39:</strong> A pregnant female employee shall not, in most cases, be required to work between 22.00 and 06.00, to work overtime or on a holiday, or to perform certain work (involving vibrating machinery or engines; driving or being in a vehicle; lifting or carrying loads exceeding 15 kg; working in a boat) except where specific exceptions under regulations apply.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Employers should review where roles are “male only” or “female only” as this may be discriminatory unless legitimately tied to job nature (for example, safety, health or pregnancy risk).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For roles falling into the prohibited list under Sections 38 and 39, female employees must not be placed into those roles and pregnant female employees must be accommodated as required.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Where pregnant employees are involved, consider redesigning duties, adjusting hours, granting alternative duties, or giving non-hazardous assignments in line with the law.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion: best-practice checklist for companies</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">To put this into a practical and easy-to-follow checklist:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Prepare and post a holiday calendar: adopt the Bank of Thailand lists and allow for additional holidays.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Publish the calendar in advance, and ensure employees know which days are company holidays.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Set standard working hours at 8 hours per day and 48 hours per week unless your work is in a hazardous category, in which case switch to 7/42.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Identify hazardous operations, classify them, and apply the stricter hours and safety regime.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Ensure at least one day off per week and do not exceed six consecutive working days.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Provide rest breaks of at least one hour after five hours of work.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Review job roles and ensure female employees are treated equally without discrimination; however, employers must comply with the restricted-work list for female and especially pregnant employees.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">With these steps in place, employers can ensure that they are compliant with Thai labour laws and also present to employees a clear, fair and transparent time-off and working-hours policy aligned with both legal minimums and modern employment best practice. For reference, the Bank of Thailand list of holidays is available here: <a href="https://www.bot.or.th/en/financial-institutions-holiday.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">https://www.bot.or.th/en/financial-institutions-holiday.html</a>.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:shortcode -->
[publishpress_authors_box layout="ppma_boxes_188"]
<!-- /wp:shortcode -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s LTR Visa &amp; Why Most Applicants Don’t Need a Consultant]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Wed, 10 Dec 2025 10:42:52 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s Long-Term Resident (LTR) Visa continues to be a key initiative aimed at attracting defined categories of foreign nationals. As interest in the programme grows, so too has the number of service providers marketing high-fee “assistance packages” for applicants. In our experience, these services are rarely necessary. The LTR application process is designed to be straightforward, objective, and fully accessible online.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The visa is available to four clearly defined groups: Wealthy Global Citizens, Wealthy Pensioners, Work-from-Thailand Professionals, and Highly Skilled Professionals. A significant benefit of the LTR scheme is that eligible dependants may be included under the primary applicant, with recent regulatory updates removing previous limits on family members.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For applicants in the Wealthy Global Citizen category, the requirements are purely numerical. Individuals must show a minimum of USD 1 million in net assets and an investment of at least USD 500,000 in approved Thai instruments. These amounts may overlap, and the supporting documentation—bank statements, bond certificates, share registers, or property titles—is entirely financial in nature.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Wealthy Pensioner route is similar. Applicants aged 50 or older must demonstrate stable passive income of USD 80,000 per year, or a lower income combined with a minimum USD 250,000 investment in Thailand. Again, the assessment is based solely on verifiable financial documentation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Work-from-Thailand Professional category introduces employment-based criteria, including employer revenue thresholds, income requirements, or alternative qualifications such as a master’s degree or ownership of intellectual property. Although the document set is broader—employment contracts, company financials, and proof of qualifications—these are standard records that most applicants already possess.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Across all categories, the underlying structure of the LTR programme is consistent: this is an administrative process, not a discretionary one. The online platform sets out the eligibility criteria, the documentation required, and the steps to follow. Applications are assessed against objective rules, and approval depends solely on whether the submitted evidence meets the published thresholds.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Some consultants and agencies market “guaranteed approvals” or “expedited processing” at significant cost. Applicants should be aware that no such fast-track exists. Processing timelines are fixed by the reviewing authorities, and there is no mechanism for negotiation or preferential treatment. Unlike visa categories involving work permits or corporate structuring, the LTR does not require legal interpretation or complex regulatory navigation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For anyone who meets the published criteria, the most efficient and cost-effective approach is simply to apply directly.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">If you believe you are eligible, save your money and submit the application yourself.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s 2025 Cannabis Regulatory Overhaul: A Hybrid Framework That Tightens Control but Stops Short of Comprehensive Reform]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 12 Dec 2025 04:20:24 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s new cannabis regulations, approved in December 2025, represent the most substantial shift in national cannabis policy since decriminalization in June 2022. However, these rules do not replace all earlier ministerial directives or create a unified cannabis law. Thailand now operates under a hybrid regulatory framework that combines a structured medical-use system with fragmented rules issued between 2022 and 2024. Understanding this dual structure is essential for operators preparing for the 2026 re-licensing cycle.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1. Background (2022–2024)</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">When cannabis was removed from the narcotics list in 2022, no Cannabis Act, licensing system, or central governing authority was introduced. The draft Act stalled in parliament, producing a regulatory vacuum filled by ministerial directives, controlled-herb notifications, temporary circulars, local zoning orders, and consumer-protection rules.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Issuing authorities</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>MOPH</strong> — Public health rules, public smoking, retail restrictions</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>DTAM</strong> — Controlled-herb notifications, seller registration, supply-chain documentation</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Ministry of Interior / Provincial Governors</strong> — Temporary circulars, operating hours, local bans</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Local Authorities</strong> — Zoning, distance-from-school rules</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Consumer Protection Board</strong> — Advertising and promotion restrictions</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This fragmented approach resulted in inconsistent enforcement, unclear sourcing rules, no national traceability, no consumption-room rules, and contradictory local interpretations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2. The 2025 Rules: Shift to a Medical-Use System</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The 2025 framework shifts cannabis into a formal medical-clinic system with:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Prescription-only sales</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">On-site medical personnel</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Mandatory traceability reporting to DTAM/MOPH</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Controlled, approved formulations only</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Clinic-grade facilities and records</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This ends the consumer-retail model that existed from 2022–2024.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3. The 2025 Rules Do <em>Not</em> Replace All Previous Regulations</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Several earlier directives continue to apply:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Controlled-herb notifications (DTAM)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Sourcing &amp; supply-chain documentation rules</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Advertising bans</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Public-smoking prohibitions</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">FDA packaging and product standards</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Local zoning &amp; operating-hour rules</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Operators must comply with both the 2025 medical framework and all unrepealed directives issued from 2022–2024.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4. Re-Licensing, Renewal &amp; Ownership Transfer</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Existing licences remain temporarily valid, but any renewal, ownership change, or relocation triggers a full reassessment under 2025 clinic rules.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Retail-style shops may not qualify as clinics</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">On-site medical staff required</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Full clinic infrastructure required</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">POS system must support medical traceability</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Sourcing must be fully GACP-compliant</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This creates a “soft grandfathering” regime: continue operating for now, but renewal becomes the compliance bottleneck.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">5. GACP Traceability &amp; Mandatory POS Integration</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Clinics must implement full-chain traceability, including:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">cultivation licence &amp; batch number</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">processing &amp; harvest records</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">transport records</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">prescription number &amp; prescriber ID</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">patient ID, dosage &amp; sale date</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Sales cannot be completed unless all required documentation is present.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">6. On-Site Consumption Rooms</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>2022–2024:</strong> On-site consumption was illegal because public-smoking rules covered commercial premises.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>2025 onwards:</strong> Consumption rooms are permitted only inside licensed medical clinics and must meet strict criteria:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">patients only (prescription required)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">consumption logged in treatment notes</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">supervision by medical staff</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">isolated, ventilated, non-visible rooms</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">no recreational or walk-in use</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">7. Remaining Gaps</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand still lacks a single cannabis law, unified licensing authority, enforcement framework, harmonised definitions, and a complete penalty structure. These gaps remain until the Cannabis &amp; Hemp Act passes parliament.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion for Clients</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Existing licences remain valid, but renewal requires meeting full medical-clinic standards.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">GACP/POS traceability is mandatory.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">On-site consumption now has a lawful pathway under clinical controls.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Operators must comply with both 2025 rules and remaining 2022–2024 directives.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A unified cannabis law will only exist once the Cannabis &amp; Hemp Act is enacted.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Navigating Thailand’s Regulatory Landscape for Short-Term Professional Assignments]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Thu, 18 Dec 2025 07:30:30 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand presents a more complex picture for professionals arriving for short-term work, even when the work is unpaid. Recent incidents, such as the detention of a Spanish actress for allegedly working without a permit, underscore the authorities’ rigorous interpretation of what constitutes “work.” For businesses and individuals planning brief professional engagements, understanding these rules is not just advisable, it is essential.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Contrary to the common assumption, Thailand’s definition of “work” under the Foreigners’ Working Management Emergency Decree is expansive. It encompasses any activity involving physical or intellectual effort, regardless of whether payment is received. This includes providing technical assistance, volunteering, conducting training workshops, supervising teams, installing equipment, consulting, public speaking at events, and even creating social media content for commercial purposes. The line between a business meeting and actionable work is finer than many realise.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For most short-term professional activities, the only gateway is the Non-Immigrant “B” Visa, typically valid for a 90-day stay. However, the visa alone does not authorise work. Separate work authorisation is almost always mandatory. Thailand offers a short-term work permit valid for 15 days, extendable once, on a discretionary basis, for specialist or urgent commercial tasks sponsored by a local entity. This provision is useful, yet its narrow application requires careful planning.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Specific activities may fall under a permissible “business visitor” category, such as attending conferences as a passive participant, general meetings, or non-operational market research. Yet the moment these activities shift to hands-on service delivery, training, or active consulting, a work permit becomes legally required. This distinction is pivotal, as visa professionals often note that border immigration officers exercise significant discretion, particularly in cases of very brief, non-recurring visits that don’t affect the local labour market.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The risks of non-compliance are draconian. Penalties for the individual can include substantial fines, imprisonment, deportation, visa cancellation, and entry bans. Employers or sponsoring entities also face legal and financial repercussions for facilitating unauthorised work. These regulations apply uniformly; even influencers or content creators earning revenue from material produced in Thailand are subject to work permit and, where applicable, filming license requirements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This stringent approach exists alongside Thailand’s ambition to become a regional hub for MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions) tourism. While the government actively promotes this sector, the legal framework for participation remains clear. Speaking at a conference, for example, is considered work. The authorities may, in practice, exercise forbearance for short-duration event participation, but this is an informal tolerance, not a legal exemption.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Ultimately, the cornerstone of any short-term professional assignment in Thailand is early, meticulous preparation. Reliance on visa exemptions or tourist entries for work purposes is an unacceptable gamble. The responsibility falls on both the visiting professional and the host organisation to secure the correct visa and work authorisation well in advance. Given the potential for interpretation and regulatory change, obtaining specialised legal advice before travel is the most prudent path to ensure a productive and compliant visit.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><em>This article is for informational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Regulations are subject to change, and professional counsel should be sought for specific situations.</em></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Right over Leased Asset (ROLA): A Legal Alternative to Nominee Property Structures in Thailand]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 05 Jan 2026 07:09:36 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Foreign investors interested in Thai real estate face strict restrictions on direct land ownership under the Land Code Act. While certain indirect arrangements have historically been considered, authorities have increased enforcement against non-compliant structures, emphasizing the importance of lawful options. One established legal mechanism is the Sap-Ing-Sith right (known in Thai as ทรัพย์อิงสิทธิ), commonly referred to in English as a "Right over Leased Asset" (ROLA) introduced under the Sap-Ing-Sith Act B.E. 2562 (2019). This registered real right provides foreigners with long-term control over immovable property while complying with ownership laws.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Overview of Sap-Ing-Sith</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Sap-Ing-Sith right is a registrable property interest issued by the Land Department. It allows the holder to possess, use, and manage the property as specified in the agreement, for a maximum initial term of 30 years (renewable subject to agreement with the landowner). It is governed by its own specific legislation, designed to facilitate investment without altering core land ownership rules.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The certificate is distinct from a standard title deed and serves as official evidence of the holder’s rights.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In practice, the Sap-Ing-Sith right is often described in English as a “Right over Leased Asset” (ROLA). This term is not a separate legal right, but a functional English description commonly used to help foreign investors understand the nature of the registered interest.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Eligible Property Types</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A Sap-Ing-Sith right may be established over:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Land holding a formal title deed (Chanote).</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Structures built on titled land.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Condominium units registered under strata title.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Advantages Over Standard Long-Term Leasehold</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Compared to a conventional 30-year lease (governed by the Civil and Commercial Code), the Sap-Ing-Sith right offers enhanced protections and functionality:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">It is a registered real right (in rem), providing stronger enforceability against third parties, rather than a personal contractual obligation.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The right is transferable (with landowner consent where required), inheritable, and may be used as collateral for financing.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Holders can independently apply for construction permits, utility connections, and other official authorizations without relying on the underlying owner.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Once registered, the underlying title is protected; no new encumbrances can be placed on the property without the holder’s consent.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These features make Sap-Ing-Sith a secure option for long-term property utilization, particularly for residential or investment purposes.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Foreign investors should consult qualified legal professionals to assess suitability and ensure proper registration. Other compliant alternatives include freehold condominium ownership (within the 49% foreign quota) and registered leases combined with superficies or usufruct rights.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[THAILAND’S CANNABIS CROSSROADS: A RETURN TO MEDICAL RIGOUR RESHAPES A BUDDING INDUSTRY]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Thu, 08 Jan 2026 04:53:48 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s experiment with cannabis liberalisation is undergoing a profound and contentious recalibration. The Ministry of Public Health (MOPH) is advancing a new draft ministerial regulation designed to impose stringent oversight on the sector, a decisive pivot away from the largely unregulated commercial free-for-all that emerged post-2022 and back towards a strictly medical framework. This shift, while framed as a necessary correction to safeguard public health, is causing significant industry consolidation, widespread business closures, and heated public debate.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Regulatory Reversal: From Open Market to Medical Gatekeeping</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The draft “Ministerial Regulation on Permits for Research, Export, Sale, or Processing of Controlled Herbs for Commercial Purposes” has received Cabinet approval and is under final review by the Office of the Council of State. It explicitly replaces the 2016 regulation, deemed wholly inadequate for the landscape that followed cannabis’s delisting as a narcotic in 2022. That delisting, while initially celebrated by entrepreneurs, created a regulatory vacuum, leading to the proliferation of over 20,000 dispensaries and hemp shops nationwide, many operating in a grey area with minimal controls.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The new regulation aims to dismantle this grey market. Its core principle is the restriction of commercial distribution to explicitly health-oriented venues: medical facilities where physicians prescribe and supervise dispensing, licensed pharmacies, authorised herbal product shops, and traditional Thai medicine clinics. This fundamentally excludes the general retail “cannabis cafe” or recreational dispensary model that flourished in tourist areas. As Public Health Minister Somsak Thepsutin stated to Bangkok Post, “The new law will clearly define that cannabis is for medical use only… The free use of cannabis will be over.”</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Operational Earthquake: Compliance Costs and Mandatory Upgrades</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For existing dispensaries and cultivators, the draft stipulates operational mandates that pose significant financial and logistical hurdles. Premises must have legally verified ownership or possession. They must install efficient systems to eliminate odour and smoke, a direct response to community complaints about public nuisance. Dedicated storage with controlled temperature and humidity, with products elevated from direct floor contact, is compulsory. Perhaps most critically, at least one employee certified by the Department of Thai Traditional and Alternative Medicine must be on duty at all times.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These requirements, particularly the need for a certified professional, redefine the business from a retail operation to a quasi-healthcare outlet. An anonymous owner of three dispensaries in Bangkok explained to Thai PBS World, “The cost of compliance is not just about renovations. Hiring a qualified traditional medicine practitioner full-time doubles my payroll for each shop. For small businesses, this is not a regulation, it’s an eviction notice.”</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This sentiment is reflected in recent licensing data: of the 8,636 licenses expiring in 2025, only 1,339, a mere 15.5%, were renewed, leading to over 7,297 closures. With thousands more licenses expiring in 2026 and 2027, a drastic industry downsizing is already underway.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Industry Contraction and Social Media Backlash</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Many operators are choosing closure over change, anticipating that the compliance costs and narrowed customer base—limited to those with prescriptions or seeking traditional medicine—will render their businesses unviable. The estimated number of remaining outlets has plummeted from a peak of nearly 20,000 to approximately 11,136.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This rapid contraction has ignited fierce discourse on social media, where the hashtag #SaveThaiCannabis has trended periodically. Entrepreneurs and consumers share stories of lost investments and anxiety over the return of a black market.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">“They invited us to plant the seeds, we invested our lives, and now they are burning the field,” posted one popular cannabis influencer on X (formerly Twitter), capturing the sense of betrayal felt by many early adopters.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Conversely, supportive voices online and in editorials, like one in The Nation, argue that the correction was inevitable, stating, “The unchecked commercialisation threatened to create a public health crisis, particularly among youth. The state’s primary duty is to protect its citizens, not commercial interests.”</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Patient Protections and the Medical Pathway Forward</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Amid the commercial turmoil, the MOPH has consistently emphasised protections for legitimate therapeutic users. The ministry guarantees “uninterrupted access for patients requiring cannabis therapeutically through hospital-based prescriptions,” asserting that there are sufficient qualified medical professionals nationwide to support the framework.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This ensures that patients relying on cannabis for conditions like chronic pain or chemotherapy-induced nausea will continue to have a regulated, quality-controlled supply, a system arguably more robust than the previous patchwork of dispensary recommendations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion: A Defined, Yet Diminished, Future</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s cannabis journey is entering a much more restrictive chapter. The impending regulation clearly prioritises medical and traditional applications within a tightly controlled supply chain. While this promises greater consumer safety and aligns with international drug control treaties, a factor often cited by government officials, it comes at the cost of a decimated commercial sector and significant financial losses for thousands of entrepreneurs.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The final implementation timeline hinges on the completion of the legislative review, but the policy direction is set. However, as with all Thai policy, a note of political uncertainty remains. As noted by health policy analyst Dr. Poonpat Leesakul in a Khaosod English interview, “This draft is a product of the current administration and its public health priorities. The broader legal framework, the much-debated Cannabis Act, remains stalled in parliament. The ultimate shape of Thailand’s cannabis industry may yet be influenced by future political shifts.”</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For now, the era of the wide-open cannabis shop is closing, making way for a system where the plant is treated not as a commodity, but as a controlled herb.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Contact us to assist your business through these changes.</strong><br>As a well-respected, established cannabis law firm staffed by legal professionals with deep industry knowledge, SILQ is a good choice to assist you in navigating these regulatory changes and continuing as a viable, legal business.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s Evolving Anti-Bribery Landscape]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Mon, 12 Jan 2026 07:09:48 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand is an economic powerhouse in Southeast Asia, a vital hub for trade, investment, and regional connectivity. However, Transparency International’s 2024 Corruption Perceptions Index ranks Thailand 108th out of 180 countries, underscoring that bribery remains a significant challenge for enterprises operating in the kingdom.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For companies operating in Thailand, recent changes require a clear understanding of the country’s evolving legal framework, which has been augmented by significant amendments designed to empower whistleblowers and stamp out government corruption.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Foundation of Anti-Bribery Law</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s primary anti-corruption legislation is the Organic Act on Anti-Corruption B.E. 2561 (2018). This law, supported by regulations issued by the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) and relevant provisions of the Penal Code, establishes a comprehensive regime. It criminalises both “active” bribery (the offering or giving of an improper advantage) and “passive” bribery (the solicitation or acceptance of an improper advantage by an official). The law applies broadly to Thai public officials, foreign officials, and officials of international organisations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Critically, there is no minimum monetary threshold for an act to constitute bribery. While NACC guidelines note that gifts of modest value (not exceeding 3,000 Thai Baht per occasion) may be acceptable on certain cultural or social occasions, this is not a safe harbor. Any benefit, regardless of size, that is linked to an intent to influence official action can give rise to liability. The courts have consistently upheld a strict interpretation. For instance, media reports frequently detail cases in which even relatively small sums offered to police or local officials have led to prosecution, underscoring that the law focuses on corrupt intent rather than the amount.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Shifting Climate of Enforcement and Tolerance</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">High-profile cases are regularly featured in Thai news outlets, signaling a lower tolerance for corruption. For example, in early 2023, widespread reports emerged of a major investigation into alleged bribery at a state-owned transportation agency, which led to multiple arrests. Similarly, reports in publications like Bangkok Post and The Nation have detailed crackdowns on corruption at local immigration offices, where officials were accused of soliciting payments for visa extensions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These reports highlight a crucial point: the perceived “normalisation” of small facilitation payments is becoming increasingly dangerous. What was once considered an unavoidable cost of doing business is now more likely to be identified and prosecuted. Companies can be held criminally and financially liable for the acts of their employees or associates if found to lack adequate internal preventive controls.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The New Whistleblower Dynamic</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The most significant recent development is the enactment of the Organic Act on Anti-Corruption (No. 2) B.E. 2568 (2025), which took effect in June 2025. This amendment introduces robust, explicit protections for whistleblowers who report corruption to the NACC in good faith.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The law now shields individuals from retaliatory lawsuits, disciplinary action, and harassment. It even allows the NACC to provide legal counsel and financial support to protected whistleblowers. As noted by Thai legal analysts quoted in Krungthep Turakij, this reform aims to “unclog the pipeline of information” by increasing the confidence of potential informants to come forward.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For companies, this creates a new operational reality. An internal compliance failure is now more likely to be reported directly to authorities.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Imperatives for a Proactive Corporate Response</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This evolving landscape demands a proactive and vigilant approach from businesses.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">First, companies must reinforce a zero-tolerance stance towards bribery, emphasising that requests from officials for inducements, no matter how casual or routine they may seem, should be met with extreme caution and reported internally. Training must be clear, practical, and regularly updated.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Second, implementing and demonstrably enforcing a robust internal compliance program is no longer just best practice; it is a primary legal defense. This program must include clear policies, risk assessments, due diligence on third parties, and meticulous financial controls aligned with the NACC’s guidelines.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Third, under the new whistleblower law, companies must ensure that their internal reporting mechanisms are credible, accessible, and secure. Employees must trust that internal reporting will be taken seriously and investigated confidentially, without fear of reprisal. A strong internal channel is the first line of defense against external reporting.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s rules of engagement are becoming stricter. The strengthening of the legal framework, coupled with active media scrutiny and enhanced whistleblower protections, signals a declining tolerance for corrupt practices. For the international business community, success now hinges on a commitment to rigorous compliance, a deep understanding of the local legal environment, and an unwavering policy of caution when faced with any request for an improper inducement. The cost of vigilance is far lower than the cost of exposure.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[A Practical Guide to Joint Ventures in Thailand: Key Legal Considerations for Foreign Investors]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 06 Feb 2026 09:34:16 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand’s strategic location and economic incentives make it an attractive destination for foreign investment. However, navigating its regulatory landscape requires careful planning, particularly when establishing a joint venture (JV), commonly referred to as a “Thai Majority Company”.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This guide synthesises key legal insights to help foreign investors understand the fundamental drivers, structures, and governance frameworks for JVs in Thailand.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1. The Primary Driver: Foreign Investment and Land Ownership Restrictions</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The structure of a JV in Thailand is predominantly shaped by foreign investment restrictions under the Foreign Business Act 1999 (FBA) and land ownership prohibitions under the Land Code. The FBA categorises business activities into three lists, restricting foreign involvement in sectors ranging from media and land trading (List One) to retail and services where Thai nationals are deemed not yet competitive (List Three).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">“A ‘foreigner’ is broadly defined under the FBA. This includes any juristic person registered in Thailand that has at least 50% of its share capital held by non-Thai nationals or foreign entities.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For land ownership purposes, a company may be treated as foreign if more than 49% of its registered capital is held by foreign entities or, in practice, if foreign shareholders constitute more than half of the total shareholder headcount.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Consequently, most foreign investments take the form of JVs with Thai partners to comply with these rules. A JV company wishing to own land must ensure that at least 51% of its shares are held by Thai investors and that foreign shareholders do not exceed half of the total number of shareholders.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Exemptions are available to companies granted investment promotion by the Board of Investment (BOI), to those holding a Foreign Business License, and to those operating in designated industrial estates under IEAT or the EEC, with appropriate concessions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2. Structuring and Governing the Joint Venture</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The most common JV vehicle is a private limited company governed by the Thai Civil and Commercial Code (CCC).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Control and Minority Protection:</strong> Default voting rules under the CCC grant effective control to shareholders holding &gt;50% of shares, and total control to those with ≥75%. Therefore, minority investors must negotiate protective provisions into the JV agreement and the company’s Articles of Association (AOA). These typically include veto rights over key matters, quorum requirements that require their presence at meetings, and board seat allocations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Constitutional Alignment:</strong> The AOA, filed with the Ministry of Commerce, is the supreme governing document for company management. Provisions from the JV or shareholders’ agreement must be meticulously reflected in the AOA. Any discrepancy generally leads to the AOA prevailing in company operations, potentially leaving a party in breach of the underlying JV agreement.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Director Duties and Conflicts:</strong> Directors owe fiduciary duties to the company under the CCC and are subject to statutory non-compete obligations, subject to shareholder approval and statutory exceptions. To manage conflicts of interest, JV agreements often codify arm’s-length principles for related-party transactions or designate such transactions as matters requiring a supermajority or minority veto.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3. Operational Considerations</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Asset Contributions:</strong> Contributions in kind (assets, labour) are permitted, but their valuation can be challenging and may require an independent appraiser to satisfy regulatory scrutiny.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Tax Implications:</strong> Contributing assets or businesses to a JV may trigger capital gains tax or value-added tax liabilities. Early consultation with a tax adviser is strongly recommended.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Intellectual Property (IP):</strong> IP ownership is a matter of negotiation. Parties commonly agree to joint ownership of IP developed during the JV’s operations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Competition Law:</strong> If the JV constitutes a merger, it may require approval or notification to the Trade Commission of Thailand under the Trade Competition Act.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4. Dispute Resolution: Planning for Contingencies</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While Thai law respects party autonomy in choosing governing law and dispute resolution methods, practical constraints exist.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Governing Law:</strong> For JVs operating in Thailand, choosing Thai law is advisable. Mandatory provisions of the CCC relating to company formation, dividends, and shareholder-company relationships are considered matters of Thai public order and cannot be contracted out of.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Arbitration:</strong> International arbitration is a common choice for cross-border JVs. Thailand is a party to the New York Convention, which facilitates the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards, provided they do not violate Thai public order or morals. Note that foreign court judgments are not directly enforceable but may be used as evidence in a Thai court.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">• <strong>Statutory Minority Protections:</strong> The CCC provides certain protections, such as the right for shareholders holding ≥20% of shares to call a meeting or request a registrar inspection, and the requirement for special resolutions (75% vote) for fundamental changes.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Conclusion</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Successfully establishing and operating a JV in Thailand requires a clear understanding of the foreign investment regime, proactive and precise legal drafting to align shareholder agreements with constitutional documents, and strategic planning for governance and potential disputes. Foreign investors are strongly advised to engage qualified local legal and tax counsel to navigate these complexities and structure a compliant, resilient, and profitable joint venture.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->
<hr class="wp-block-separator has-alpha-channel-opacity"/>
<!-- /wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Summary of New Ministerial Regulation on Wills: A must-read for expatriates in Thailand]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 20 Feb 2026 09:00:34 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">1.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Overview</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">On 22 January 2026, the Ministry of Interior published a new Ministerial Regulation replacing the 1960 rules governing Public Wills and related inheritance declarations. The regulation took effect on 24 March 2026 (60 days after publication).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This modernisation updates procedures, forms, and identity verification requirements for:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Public Wills (phinya-kam baep ekkasan fang muang)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Secret Wills (phinya-kam baep ekkasan lap)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Oral Wills (phinya-kam duay waja)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Declarations disinheriting statutory heirs</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Revocation of disinheritance</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Renunciation of inheritance</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">2.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Requirements for a Valid Public Will</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Section 1658 of the Thai Civil and Commercial Code, a Public Will must meet the following requirements:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Requirement</strong></td><td><strong>Description</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Made at District Office</strong></td><td>Must be made at any district office (<em>amphur</em>) or district office branch (<em>king amphur</em>), or in Bangkok at the district office (<em>khet</em>)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Presiding Officer</strong></td><td>Made in the presence of the District Chief (<em>nai amphur</em>) or Zone Director (<em>phu amnuaykan khet</em>)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Witnesses</strong></td><td>At least two witnesses must be present throughout</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Declaration</strong></td><td>The testator declares their intentions to the District Officer</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Recording</strong></td><td>The District Officer records the testator's wishes in writing</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Reading</strong></td><td>The document is read aloud to the testator and witnesses</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Acknowledgment</strong></td><td>Testator and witnesses acknowledge the content is correct</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Signatures</strong></td><td>Testator, both witnesses, and the District Officer sign the document</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Registration</strong></td><td>The will is registered in the official will register at the district office</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Storage</strong></td><td>The original is kept at the district office unless the testator requests to take possession</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">3.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Step-by-Step Guide for Expats</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Step 1: Prepare Required Documents</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Document</strong></td><td><strong>Notes</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Passport</strong></td><td><strong>Valid passport with current Thai visa (if applicable)</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>House registration (<em>Tabien Baan</em>)</strong></td><td><strong>If registered in Thailand</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Work permit</strong></td><td><strong>If applicable</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Thai marriage certificate</strong></td><td>If married to a Thai national (with official translation if originally foreign)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Divorce certificate</strong></td><td>If applicable (with official translation and Ministry of Foreign Affairs certification)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Children's birth certificates</strong></td><td>If naming children as beneficiaries (with official translation if foreign)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>List of assets in Thailand</strong></td><td>Including details of property, bank accounts, vehicles, etc.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Names and details of beneficiaries</strong></td><td>Full names, relationships, and identification details</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Name of proposed executor</strong></td><td>Full name and contact details</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Thai translator</strong></td><td>If you do not speak fluent Thai (recommended)</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Step 2: Draft Your Will Content</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Prepare the following information to present to the District Officer:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Personal details</strong>: Full name, age, current address</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Asset distribution</strong>: Clear specification of which assets go to which beneficiaries</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Executor appointment</strong>: Name of person who will manage your estate</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Alternative provisions</strong>: Contingency plans if beneficiaries predecease you</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Step 3: Visit the District Office</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Action</strong></td><td><strong>Details</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Location</strong></td><td>Any district office (<em>amphur</em>) in Thailand—you are not restricted to your home province</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Appointment</strong></td><td>Not typically required, but arriving early is advisable</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Who should attend</strong></td><td>You, two witnesses, and ideally a Thai speaker/translator</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Step 4: Complete the Process at the District Office</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Step</strong></td><td><strong>Description</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>1. Submit application</strong></td><td>File a request using the prescribed form (available at the district office)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>2. Present identification</strong></td><td>Show your passport and any other requested documents</td></tr><tr><td><strong>3. Declare your intentions</strong></td><td>Verbally state your will provisions to the District Officer</td></tr><tr><td><strong>4. Document preparation</strong></td><td>The District Officer will draft the will based on your declaration</td></tr><tr><td><strong>5. Verification</strong></td><td>The officer may request additional proof if there are concerns about age or mental capacity</td></tr><tr><td><strong>6. Reading</strong></td><td>The completed will is read aloud to you and your witnesses</td></tr><tr><td><strong>7. Confirmation</strong></td><td>You and your witnesses confirm the content is correct</td></tr><tr><td><strong>8. Signing</strong></td><td>All parties sign the will</td></tr><tr><td><strong>9. Registration</strong></td><td>The will is entered into the official register</td></tr><tr><td><strong>10. Receipt</strong></td><td>You receive an official receipt (<em>bai rap</em>) confirming registration</td></tr><tr><td>11. Storage decision</td><td>Decide whether the district office keeps the original or you take possession</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Step 5: Post-Completion</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Action</strong></td><td><strong>Details</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Keep the receipt</strong></td><td>Store the receipt safely—it is needed to request the will later</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Inform executor</strong></td><td>Tell your executor where the will is located and how to access it</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Review periodically</strong></td><td>Update your will after major life changes (marriage, divorce, children, asset changes)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Request copies</strong></td><td>You may request certified copies at any time</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">4.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Important Notes for Expats</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Language</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The entire process is conducted in Thai</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">It is strongly recommended to bring a qualified Thai translator or legal advisor</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The will itself will be written in Thai</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Witnesses</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Must be at least 20 years old</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Should not be beneficiaries under the will</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Should have valid identification (Thai ID card or passport)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Must understand Thai (as the will is read in Thai)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Costs</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Government fees apply (updated under the new regulation)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Additional costs for translation/legal assistance</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Taking Possession of Your Will</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Section 11 of the new regulation:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">You may request to take your will at any time</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">You must present the official receipt</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">You must sign acknowledging receipt in the will register</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The district office keeps a certified copy before releasing the original</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">If You Pass Away Before Collecting Your Will</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">The district office will contact the person named to receive the will (as specified in your application)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">That person must provide proof of identity and the testator's death certificate</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">If the death certificate cannot be verified from the central registry database, additional proof may be required</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">5.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Comparison: Public Will vs. Standard Written Will</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Aspect</strong></td><td><strong>Public Will (at Amphur)</strong></td><td><strong>Standard Written Will (with Lawyer)</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Preparation</strong></td><td>Done by district officer</td><td>Drafted by lawyer</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Cost</strong></td><td>Low (government fees only)</td><td>Higher (legal fees)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Language</strong></td><td>Thai only</td><td>Can be bilingual (Thai/English)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Storage</strong></td><td>Kept at district office (option to take possession)</td><td>You retain possession</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Legal review</strong></td><td>Basic verification</td><td>Comprehensive legal advice</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Complexity</strong></td><td>Best for straightforward estates</td><td>Suitable for complex situations</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Privacy</strong></td><td>Registered with the government</td><td>Private document</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Update process</strong></td><td>Must revoke and make a new will</td><td>Can execute a codicil or a new will</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">6.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Additional Declarations Available Under the New Regulation</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The regulation also covers:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Disinheritance</strong> (tat thayath doitham mai hai rap moradok)<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Formally exclude a statutory heir from inheriting</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Revocation of disinheritance</strong> (<em>thon kan tat thayath</em>)<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Restore an heir's right to inherit</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Renunciation of inheritance</strong> (<em>sala moradok</em>)<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Decline to accept an inheritance (must be unconditional)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list --></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Each requires a separate application and follows similar procedures to the Public Will.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">7.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Practical Tips for Expats</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Consider both options</strong>: A Public Will may suffice for simple estates, but complex situations (international assets, business structures) typically require a lawyer-drafted will</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Update regularly</strong>: Thai law does not automatically revoke a will upon marriage or divorce—you must actively update it</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Coordinate with foreign wills</strong>: If you have assets in multiple countries, ensure your Thai will works with your overall estate plan</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Seek professional advice</strong>: While the Public Will process is straightforward, understanding how it interacts with Thai inheritance law (particularly forced heirship rules for statutory heirs) warrants legal guidance</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This summary is based on Ministerial Regulation on Making Wills and Declarations of Intent Regarding Inheritance B.E. 2569 (2026), published in the Royal Gazette on 22 January 2026, effective 24 March 2026.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><a href="https://ratchakitcha.soc.go.th/documents/102677.pdf">https://ratchakitcha.soc.go.th/documents/102677.pdf</a></p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->
