					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand Proposes Landmark Reforms to Foreign Business Act to Attract Investment]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 06 Mar 2026 03:14:07 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Thai Ministry of Commerce has circulated draft ministerial regulations that propose excluding specific service activities from the scope of the Foreign Business Act B.E. 2542 (1999) (FBA). If enacted, foreign investors would be permitted to engage in these activities without obtaining a Foreign Business License (FBL). This reform initiative, approved in principle by the Thai Cabinet in April 2025, signals a strategic shift from a historically protectionist regime toward a framework designed to enhance national competitiveness and align with modern economic realities.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Current Regulatory Framework</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The FBA remains the principal legislation governing foreign participation in Thai businesses. The statute defines a "foreigner" broadly to include not only non-Thai nationals but also Thai-registered companies where at least 50 percent of the capital is held by non-Thai persons.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Restricted activities are categorised into three lists:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>List One</strong>: Businesses completely prohibited to foreigners due to special national considerations (e.g., media, land trading)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>List Two</strong>: Businesses requiring Cabinet approval due to impacts on national security, culture, or natural resources</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>List Three</strong>: Service businesses where Thai enterprises are considered "not yet ready to compete" with foreign operators</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In practice, List Three generates the most significant regulatory friction for foreign investors. Its broad scope encompasses many routine multinational operations—including management services, software development, and inter-company financial structuring—technically falling within restricted definitions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Where businesses fall within restricted categories, investors may currently structure operations through Board of Investment (BOI) promotion, treaty exemptions (such as the US-Thailand Treaty of Amity), or alternative corporate structures. The FBA also requires minimum capital of at least THB 2 million (approximately USD 54,000) for foreign businesses not requiring a license, rising to THB 3 million for restricted activities requiring permission.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Proposed Exemptions from Restricted Categories</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Department of Business Development (DBD) presented these reform initiatives at the "Shaping the Future of Foreign Business Facilitation in Thailand" seminar on 29th January 2026. The draft Ministerial Regulation proposes excluding the following ten business categories from List Three restrictions:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Telecommunication services for Type 1 telecommunications operators</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Treasury center businesses under exchange control laws</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Software development businesses</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Management services for affiliated or group companies</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Domestic credit guarantee services for affiliated or group companies</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Leasing space for installation of electronic payment devices, ATMs, or vending machines</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Petroleum drilling service businesses</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Lending businesses secured by collateral in connection with securities or derivatives transactions</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Businesses providing services as agent, dealer, consultant, or fund manager for derivatives contracts whose underlying commodities or variables are not subject to the Derivatives Act B.E. 2546 (2003)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Domestic trade related to traditional agricultural products</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Importantly, these businesses are proposed for complete removal from the restricted framework rather than reclassification to another list. If approved by Cabinet, the exemptions would operate through ministerial regulation carving out specific activities from List Three restrictions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Strategic Importance of Key Exemptions</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Several proposed exemptions address structural inefficiencies in the current regulatory approach:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Software development and IT services</strong>: Many multinational businesses establish regional development teams in Southeast Asia. Treating software development as a restricted "service business" has historically created unnecessary regulatory friction for technology companies that are primarily building products rather than competing with domestic service providers. The reforms specifically aim to support innovation-driven enterprises and startups.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Treasury centre operations</strong>: International corporate groups widely use treasury centres to centralise financial management functions including intercompany lending, cash pooling, and foreign exchange management. These structures improve efficiency and risk management across multinational operations. Requiring FBLs for treasury activities has added administrative complexity to standard corporate finance functions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Intra-group management and financing services</strong>: Parent companies and regional headquarters commonly provide strategic management and financial support to subsidiaries within the same corporate group. Classifying these internal support functions as restricted service businesses has historically required licenses for activities that are effectively internal governance rather than commercial services offered to the Thai market .</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Structural Considerations Beyond Specific Exemptions</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While the removal of specific businesses from restricted lists represents positive incremental reform, legal practitioners observe that the broader policy discussion sometimes focuses heavily on which services should be reclassified rather than addressing underlying framework issues.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The "service business" category in the FBA remains extremely broad, capturing activities ranging from professional services to routine internal corporate support functions. As a result, debates about whether particular services should remain restricted can become somewhat artificial. A more durable reform would likely involve revisiting how service activities are defined within the FBA altogether, rather than continuing to manage the law through periodic reclassification exercises.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Law Reform Commission has noted that the FBA's underlying protectionist framework, inherited from earlier regulations including Revolutionary Council Announcement No. 281 (1972), is no longer aligned with modern economic realities. The Commission has recommended revising criteria for determining which businesses qualify as foreign, updating annexed lists to support startup expansion, and promoting development of new economic sectors including digital economy and advanced technology industries.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Continued Compliance Requirements and Enhanced Enforcement</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Even if these reforms are adopted, the core structure of the FBA will remain in place. Foreign investors entering Thailand will still need to consider foreign ownership limits, FBL requirements for other activities, BOI promotion opportunities, and treaty-based exemptions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Critically, authorities are simultaneously intensifying enforcement against unlawful nominee structures. The DBD and Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding on preventing and suppressing the use of corporate mule accounts and Thai nationals as nominee shareholders. Their corporate registration database is now linked with the CIB's big data system to enhance analysis of suspicious legal entities.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In 2025, authorities conducted raids at 46 locations nationwide, implicating 442 juristic persons with registered capital of THB 1.189 billion and damages exceeding THB 3.6 billion. Penalties for nominee arrangements can include imprisonment of up to three years, fines between THB 100,000 and THB 1,000,000, and court-ordered cessation of operations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Practical Implications for Investors</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">From a practical standpoint, if these exemptions are implemented, certain technology, financial, and intra-group service activities may become easier to operate in Thailand without complex licensing structures. This aligns Thailand more closely with other ASEAN jurisdictions competing for foreign investment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">However, businesses should note that licensing timelines remain significant considerations. Standard FBL approval currently takes approximately three months, though the DBD has announced initiatives to reduce this to approximately one month through new guidelines on approval considerations and application forms .</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Companies exploring the Thai market may still consider non-trading structures such as representative offices or Trade and Investment Support Offices (TISO) when coordinating regional operations or conducting market research. The FBA's minimum capital requirements also remain binding and differ by situation—foreign-owned companies not requiring a license must have at least THB 2 million in fully paid capital before commencing business, rising to THB 3 million for restricted activities requiring permission.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Looking Forward</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The reform discussions highlight that Thailand's foreign investment framework is evolving, but it remains a system where structuring and regulatory planning are critical. Foreign investors who engage with the legal framework early, before finalising ownership structures or operational models, are typically better positioned to navigate the regulatory landscape efficiently while maintaining compliance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The government's shift from "protection" to "enhancing competitiveness potential" as the guiding principle for foreign investment regulation reflects recognition that the old rules no longer serve Thailand's economic ambitions. However, until structural issues with the FBA's classification system are addressed, reforms may continue to arrive incrementally rather than through comprehensive modernisation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For a broader overview of the reform proposals and policy direction, see our earlier analysis: </p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand Intensifies Crackdown on Nominee Shareholders]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Tue, 10 Mar 2026 02:33:56 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Department of Business Development (DBD) at Thailand's Ministry of Commerce is preparing to implement enhanced measures aimed at preventing the registration of juristic persons using Thai nationals as nominee shareholders for foreign business operators. Director-General Poonpong Naiyanapakorn announced that the department convened a high-level meeting with representatives from 17 leading law firms on Monday, March 9, 2026, to gather insights and recommendations for strengthening the regulatory framework governing corporate registrations involving foreign participation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The brainstorming session was designed to collect professional opinions on proposed amendments that would close existing loopholes and address what authorities describe as a persistent threat to Thailand's economic structure. According to DBD statistics, out of 782,542 active companies currently operating in the kingdom, approximately 118,016 involve foreign investment at levels between 0.01 and 49.99 percent. Officials estimate that more than 80 percent of these entities may involve Thai nationals holding shares in a nominee capacity for foreign interests.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Background and Regulatory Context</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The current initiative builds upon previous enforcement efforts, including DBD Order No. 2/2568, which took effect on January 1, 2026. That regulation introduced requirements for Thai shareholders to submit bank statements demonstrating genuine financial capacity and traceable fund sources when participating in companies with foreign shareholders holding less than 50 percent of shares or where foreign nationals are authorized signatories despite all-Thai shareholding structures. The DBD reports that this measure alone reduced nominee registration attempts by approximately 65 percent, though officials acknowledge continued attempts at circumvention.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The proposed regulatory expansion comes amid active investigations into suspected nominee arrangements across multiple business sectors. In early March 2026, the DBD identified 15 fruit-packing companies suspected of using Thai nominee shareholders, with 11 located in Ratchaburi province and others in Samut Prakan, Pathum Thani, Samut Sakhon, and Bangkok . These cases have been referred to the Central Investigation Bureau, the Department of Special Investigation, and the Anti-Money Laundering Office for further action. Investigators identified approximately 10 Thai nationals believed to be acting as nominee shareholders or directors, with some companies operating for five to six years while others were recently established.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Proposed Regulatory Framework</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The forthcoming measure, formally titled the "Draft Order of the Central Partnership and Company Registration Office No. .../2569 on Criteria and Methods for Registration in Cases of Amendments Adding Foreigners as Partners in Partnerships or Adding Foreigners as Authorized Signatories in Limited Companies," represents an escalation in the government's enforcement approach. The regulation would subject amendment applications involving foreign participation to heightened scrutiny, requiring additional documentation and verification procedures beyond those already implemented for initial registrations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The DBD's consultation with legal professionals focused on gathering practical perspectives regarding implementation challenges, potential unintended consequences, and refinement of criteria to ensure the measure effectively targets nominee structures without impeding legitimate foreign investment. Participants examined the operational impact of existing requirements and suggested adjustments to the proposed framework before its expected issuance in mid-March 2026, with enforcement commencing 1 April, 2026.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Current Enforcement Landscape</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The new measures operate within a broader interagency enforcement framework that has intensified throughout late 2025 and early 2026. The DBD has established real-time data integration with the Anti-Money Laundering Office, enabling immediate screening of shareholders and directors against AMLO databases. Where individuals appear on AMLO lists, registrars may require personal appearances, additional financial documentation, and proof of premises authorization before processing registrations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Address verification has also emerged as a significant enforcement tool. Under existing regulations, when a proposed registered office already hosts five or more juristic persons, registrars may request consent letters from premises owners and documentation proving legal rights to use the address. This so-called "Rule of Five" directly affects virtual office arrangements and shared workspace registrations, requiring operators to demonstrate that locations can genuinely support business operations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Recent investigations show the range of industries under scrutiny. Beyond the fruit-packing sector, authorities on Koh Phangan have been investigating luxury villa developments involving Ukrainian investors, where two companies with combined registered capital exceeding 100 million baht allegedly employed Thai nominee shareholders to circumvent foreign business restrictions. Such cases illustrate the DBD's focus on tourism-related businesses, real estate, and service sectors historically vulnerable to nominee arrangements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Legal Framework and Penalties</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The enforcement actions derive their authority from the Foreign Business Act B.E. 2542 (1999), which provides the basis for clear liability for both parties in nominee arrangements. Section 36 targets Thai nationals or juristic persons acting as nominees, providing that any person assisting or supporting a foreigner in operating a restricted business, or holding shares on behalf of a foreigner, shall be subject to imprisonment not exceeding three years, a fine of 100,000 to one million baht, or both . Courts may additionally order cessation of such assistance or termination of shareholding arrangements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Section 37 addresses foreign principals who operate businesses using Thai nominees, whether through shareholding arrangements or other similar methods designed to circumvent the Act. Foreign violators face identical penalties of up to three years imprisonment and fines ranging from 100,000 to one million baht. Where violations involve continuing non-compliance with court orders, offenders face daily fines of 10,000 to 50,000 baht until the violation ceases.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thai Supreme Court decisions have reinforced these provisions. In Supreme Court Decision No. 17923/2557 (2014), involving land holdings on Koh Samui, the Court convicted a foreign defendant under Section 37 for using a Thai nominee and the Thai defendant under Section 36 for acting as nominee. Similarly, in Decision No. 5457/2560 (2017), the Court found that sham loan agreements designed to give foreigners control over Thai businesses constituted prohibited nominee arrangements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Implementation and Compliance Considerations</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The DBD emphasizes that enhanced measures aim to prevent illicit nominee structures while preserving Thailand's attractiveness for legitimate foreign investment. Director-General Poonpong stressed that the consultation process seeks to balance effective enforcement against unnecessary regulatory burden, ensuring that compliance requirements do not unduly impede genuine business operations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For foreign investors and their Thai partners, the evolving regulatory environment demands careful attention to documentation and structural transparency. Thai shareholders must be prepared to demonstrate genuine financial capacity, with bank statements showing three months of transaction history and clear evidence of fund transfers matching share subscription amounts. Where individuals lack apparent financial capacity compared to investment amounts, registrars may suspend applications pending more verification.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The practical implications extend beyond initial incorporation. Amendment applications, share transfers, and director appointments now face scrutiny comparable to new registrations. Companies operating with foreign participation should review existing structures for compliance and anticipate that regulatory attention will continue intensifying across all sectors.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Compliance and Legal Considerations for Foreign Investors</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's continued campaign against nominee shareholdings reflects the sustained commitment to protecting the integrity of its business registration system and ensuring fair competition for domestic enterprises. The combination of enhanced documentation requirements, interagency information sharing, and active investigation across multiple industries signals that authorities view nominee arrangements as a priority enforcement area.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">With the new amendment regulation expected by mid-March 2026 and enforcement commencing 1 April, 2026, businesses and legal practitioners must prepare for continued evolution of the regulatory landscape. As the DBD shifts from form-based registration toward substance-based verification, transparency regarding ownership structures, funding sources, and business premises will prove essential for successful registration and ongoing compliance.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand's 3 Million Baht Investment Visa: A Potential Long-Term Stay Pathway – awaiting regulations]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Apr 2026 22:34:00 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand has introduced a regulatory framework that, upon full implementation, may establish a new long-term stay pathway linked to property investment. Commonly referred to as the "3-million-baht investment visa," this initiative aims to encourage foreign investment and could provide eligible foreign nationals with an accessible option for extended residence in Thailand.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">It is critical to understand that this investment does not, on its own, automatically grant residence status. Rather, the qualifying investment serves as a supporting justification for annual immigration extensions. Unlike traditional residency-by-investment programs, which grant residence rights upon qualifying investment, this structure offers renewable permission to stay, contingent on maintaining the investment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Legal Framework: Orders 237/2568 and 238/2568</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Effective October 2025, Immigration Orders 237/2568 and 238/2568 modernised the framework for investment-based extensions of stay. These orders introduced a practical THB 3 million investment threshold for applicants seeking annual extensions based on qualifying property arrangements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The process operates in two distinct legal stages:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Order No. 237/2568</strong> governs initial visa alignment and change of category to prepare for the investment extension</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Order No. 238/2568</strong> governs the one-year renewable extension and defines qualifying criteria</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The "Ministry Bridge": Certification Requirement</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">A defining feature distinguishing this pathway from other investment options is the mandatory certification requirement. To qualify for the reduced THB 3 million threshold, applicants must obtain a Certification Letter from the Ministry of Tourism and Sports (administered through Thailand Longstay Service Co., Ltd., or TLS - amongst others).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This certification verifies the applicant as a "long-stay tourism supporter." Without this document, immigration officers are legally required to default to the standard THB 10 million investment requirement applicable to other investment visa categories.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Qualifying Investment Structures</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under the proposed framework, foreign nationals may qualify for long-term stay permissions through the following qualifying investments :</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>1. Condominium Purchase (Recommended Structure)</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Minimum THB 3,000,000</strong> purchase price</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Completed condominium unit</strong> within foreign freehold quota (49% maximum foreign ownership)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Ownership registered</strong> at the Department of Lands in the applicant's name</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Transfer/registration dated on or after 1 October 2020</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Full purchase price transferred from abroad</strong> with proper documentation</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Important:</strong> Off-plan or under-construction units <strong>do not qualify</strong> until construction is complete and the transfer at the Land Office is completed. Deposits or stage payments do not satisfy requirements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>2. Registered Long-Term Leasehold</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Minimum THB 3,060,000 total lease value</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Lease term exceeding three years</strong>, registered at the Land Office</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Applicant clearly stated as lessee</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Suitable for houses or condominiums where foreign freehold is not available</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>3. High-Value Residential Rental</strong></h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Minimum THB 85,000 per month rental</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Initial application: <strong>evidence of three months' advance rent payment</strong></li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Annual extension</strong>: evidence of twelve months' advance rent payment</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Strict landlord eligibility</strong> requirements apply</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Critical Seller/Landlord Eligibility Requirement</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For all qualifying routes, the counterparty must be either:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A Thai individual; or</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">A Thai juristic person with foreign shareholding not exceeding 49% (Thai majority-owned)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Transactions with foreign individuals or foreign-majority entities as seller/landlord are unlikely to qualify, even where financial thresholds are met.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Foreign Exchange Documentation</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Foreign buyers must bring funds into Thailand in foreign currency. The receiving Thai bank must issue a Foreign Exchange Transaction Form (FETF or "Tor Tor 3") or a Credit Advice confirming the international remittance. This documentation is mandatory for:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Land Office registration of a condominium in a foreign name</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Immigration approval for investment-based extensions</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Where Wise or similar transfer services are used, applicants must obtain appropriate documentation from their Thai receiving bank confirming that the funds are from offshore.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Initial Stay and Extension Process</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Based on the framework, the anticipated process would operate as follows:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list {"ordered":true} -->
<ol class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Applicant enters Thailand on an appropriate non-immigrant visa (typically category O or similar)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Applicant acquires qualifying property or enters qualifying lease arrangement (minimum THB 3 million)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Documentation submitted to TLS for Ministry certification (currently unavailable pending regulations)</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Upon certification, the applicant applies for initial 90-day permission at Immigration</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Prior to expiry, the applicant applies for a 12-month extension under Order 238/2568</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Extensions are renewable annually, subject to maintained investment and compliance</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ol>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Eligible Family Members (Dependents)</strong></h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The program may permit inclusion of qualifying family members as dependents, without additional investment requirements:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Spouse:</strong> Legally registered marriage, relationship subsisting</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Children:</strong> Under 20 years, unmarried, residing in applicant's household (children over 20 may qualify on certain conditions.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Parents:</strong> Biological parents aged 50 years or older</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Documentation Requirements:</strong> All documents must be translated into Thai and certified by a translation agency accredited by the Department of Foreign Affairs (MFA).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Comparison with Existing Investment Options</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Feature</strong></td><td><strong>3M Proposed Pathway</strong></td><td><strong>10M Investment Visa (Non-Im IB)</strong></td><td><strong>LTR Visa</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Minimum Investment</strong></td><td>THB 3M (property)</td><td>THB 10M (property/bonds/deposit)</td><td>USD 250,000-500,000</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Validity</strong></td><td>Annual renewable</td><td>Annual renewable</td><td>10 years (5+5)</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Work Rights</strong></td><td>Prohibited</td><td>Prohibited</td><td>Digital Work Permit available</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Tax Benefits</strong></td><td>None specified</td><td>None</td><td>Exemption on overseas income</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Ministry Certification</strong></td><td>Required (TLS)</td><td>Not required</td><td>Not required (BOI approval)</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Practical Considerations and Current Status</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Regulatory Uncertainty:</strong> As of March 2026, complete implementing procedures for the 3-million-baht pathway remain opaque. While developers such as Sansiri have announced partnerships with Thailand Long Stay, the program cannot operate until administrative mechanisms are functioning.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Regional Implementation Variance:</strong> When operational, implementation may vary between immigration offices. Bangkok and major tourist centres (Phuket, Pattaya, and Chiang Mai) are likely to be familiar with TLS procedures, whereas provincial offices may have limited experience.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Health Insurance Requirements:</strong> Applicants should anticipate mandatory health insurance coverage meeting minimum thresholds (typically 400,000 THB or USD 40,000 for inpatient treatment).</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class=""><strong>Tax Residency Considerations:</strong> Persons spending more than 180 days annually in Thailand are considered tax residents and must declare foreign income brought into Thailand. Unlike LTR visa holders, standard investment extension holders do not enjoy special tax treatment.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Current Status and Key Takeaways for Investors</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's 3-million-baht investment visa pathway represents a potentially accessible option for foreign nationals seeking a longer-term stay while investing in Thai property. However, the program remains inoperative pending issuance of complete implementing regulations and establishment of administrative procedures.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Until the Ministry of Tourism certification process is fully functional and immigration authorities accept applications under this reduced threshold, foreign investors should approach representations by agents and consultants with appropriate caution. The existing 10-million-baht investment visa and LTR visa remain the only currently operable investment-linked pathways to extended residence in Thailand.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For investors considering relocation to Thailand, the 3-million-baht pathway may eventually provide a practical route to extended residence when properly structured and combined with appropriate legal and immigration planning. Professional advice from qualified legal practitioners is essential before committing to any property transaction in reliance upon this framework.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[Thailand’s Updated Bankruptcy Law: Prepackaged Bankruptcy Options]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Fri, 20 Mar 2026 08:16:24 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand is updating its Bankruptcy Act to introduce a formal pre-packaged rehabilitation mechanism, a reform recently approved by the House of Representatives and currently awaiting Senate review.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This development represents a significant shift in the country's corporate insolvency framework, building on foundations established after the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis while adapting international practices to Thailand's legal context.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Historical Context: From Liquidation-Only to Rehabilitation-Focused Regime</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Thailand's modern insolvency framework emerged from the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, which exposed critical gaps in the country's bankruptcy laws. Prior to 1998, the Bankruptcy Act B.E. 2483 (1940) primarily provided for liquidation proceedings. Insolvent debtors faced asset realisation and distribution to creditors, often through protracted processes that could span years. There were no statutory mechanisms for business rehabilitation, limiting options to winding up and often resulting in significant loss of enterprise value.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The crisis triggered urgent legislative action. In April 1998, amendments to the Bankruptcy Act introduced corporate rehabilitation proceedings under Chapter 3/1, drawing inspiration from the U.S. Chapter 11 model. These amendments allowed potentially viable companies to restructure their debts under court supervision, with features such as automatic stays on creditor actions, plan formulation, and class-based voting. The International Monetary Fund noted that this represented "an important step in addressing" the deficiency of a liquidation-oriented framework.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Further refinements followed in 1999, including the establishment of the specialised Central Bankruptcy Court to handle cases more efficiently. The recent amendments introducing pre-packaged rehabilitation build directly on this foundation, continuing Thailand's efforts to align its insolvency regime with international best practices while preserving going-concern value.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Understanding Pre-Packaged Rehabilitation</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Pre-packaged rehabilitation allows a debtor company and its key creditors to negotiate and secure an agreement on a restructuring plan <strong>before</strong> formally petitioning the court. Once a consensus is reached, the debtor files the pre-negotiated plan together with the rehabilitation petition. This approach enables the court to review and potentially approve the plan more swiftly, bypassing many time-intensive steps in conventional proceedings.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under traditional rehabilitation, a company must first file a petition, followed by court acceptance, appointment of a planner, creditor voting, and eventual plan approval—a sequence that can take months or even years. According to leading practitioners, pre-packaged plans could cut rehabilitation timelines by months—if creditor consensus is achieved".</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Legal Framework and Qualification Requirements</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">To understand how these options work in practice, it helps to compare them directly. The table below outlines the three main pathways available under Thai law for companies facing financial distress.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Table: Comparison of Bankruptcy and Rehabilitation Options Under Thai Law</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:table -->
<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><tbody><tr><td><strong>Aspect</strong></td><td><strong>Full Bankruptcy (Liquidation)</strong></td><td><strong>Traditional Rehabilitation</strong></td><td><strong>Pre-Packaged Rehabilitation</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Legal Basis</strong></td><td>Bankruptcy Act B.E. 2483, Section 90/3 (liquidation provisions)</td><td>Bankruptcy Act B.E. 2483, Chapter 3/1 (introduced 1998)</td><td><strong>Proposed amendments to Chapter 3/1 (pending approval)</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Primary Objective</strong></td><td>Liquidation and distribution of assets to creditors</td><td>Restructure debts to keep the business operating</td><td><strong>Expedited restructuring with a pre-negotiated agreement</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Debt Threshold</strong></td><td>THB 2 million for juristic persons</td><td>Minimum THB 10 million (proposed increase to THB 50 million for SMEs)</td><td><strong>Same as traditional rehabilitation</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Process Timeline</strong></td><td>Protracted; can span years</td><td>Months to years</td><td><strong>Potentially months if creditor consensus is achieved</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Court Involvement</strong></td><td>Full supervision</td><td>Full supervision with a planner appointment</td><td><strong>Formal approval required, but expedited review</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Negotiation Timing</strong></td><td>Post-filing</td><td>Post-filing, after planner appointment</td><td><strong>Pre-filing, between the debtor and key creditors</strong></td></tr><tr><td><strong>Debtor Control</strong></td><td>Loss of control to the official receiver</td><td>Control transfers to the plan preparer</td><td><strong>Debtor retains more negotiating influence pre-filing</strong></td></tr></tbody></table></figure>
<!-- /wp:table -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Key Differences from the U.S. Chapter 11 Model</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">While Thailand's pre-packaged mechanism draws inspiration from U.S. Chapter 11, important distinctions remain tailored to Thailand's legal system:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Court Involvement</strong>: Thai courts retain significant oversight, requiring formal approval of the petition and plan even in pre-packaged cases, along with potential appointment of a planner or administrator. In the U.S., confirmation can occur relatively quickly if the disclosure and voting requirements are satisfied.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Voting Requirements</strong>: Thailand applies strict class-based voting thresholds, typically requiring supermajorities in secured and unsecured classes. According to legal experts, there is "limited flexibility for cram-down compared to the U.S., where dissenting classes can be crammed down under certain conditions".</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Disclosure Standards</strong>: Thailand's disclosure obligations are still developing and may not yet match the rigorous requirements in the U.S., though greater transparency will likely evolve with practice.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class=""><strong>Market Maturity</strong>: The U.S. benefits from decades of precedent and established case law. Thailand's framework is emerging, meaning that judges, practitioners, and creditors will need time to become familiar with it.</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Related Reforms for Small and Medium Enterprises</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The pre-packaged amendments coincide with broader reforms targeting small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The Thai cabinet has approved proposed amendments that would:</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:list -->
<ul class="wp-block-list"><!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Increase the debt threshold for SME rehabilitation from THB 10 million to THB 50 million, adjusting for current economic conditions</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Remove the requirement for SMEs to be registered with the Office of Small and Medium Enterprise Promotion to qualify for reorganisation</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Eliminate mandatory pre-packaged plan requirements for SME rehabilitation</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item -->

<!-- wp:list-item -->
<li class="">Introduce expedited rehabilitation procedures specifically for SMEs</li>
<!-- /wp:list-item --></ul>
<!-- /wp:list -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">These changes aim to make rehabilitation "more accessible, convenient, and affordable, particularly for individuals and small and medium-sized enterprises" .</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Judicial Considerations in Rehabilitation Approval</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Section 90/3 of the Bankruptcy Act, courts must assess whether a debtor has a credible justification for rehabilitation. According to legal analysis, courts pay particular attention to "the cause of insolvency or inability to pay debts" and "the justification for rehabilitation and the feasibility of the proposed recovery plan" .</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The justification must demonstrate that the debtor has a realistic opportunity to recover and continue operations. This requires more than a declaration of financial distress; it demands a substantiated plan outlining how the business can be restored to viability. Courts assess whether the debtor retains operational capacity, whether restructuring is feasible, and whether the proposed plan is likely to succeed.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Looking Forward</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The introduction of pre-packaged rehabilitation presents both challenges and opportunities. Coordinating diverse creditor groups in advance can prove complex, particularly in cases involving multiple secured lenders or cross-border elements. Concerns over transparency, potential abuse, and judicial capacity to handle expedited reviews warrant careful monitoring.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Nevertheless, the reform offers substantial opportunities. Insolvency practitioners and legal professionals can play more proactive roles in facilitating pre-filing negotiations. For foreign investors, a more efficient restructuring pathway enhances Thailand's appeal as a jurisdiction aligned with global best practices.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">If supported by clear implementing regulations and consistent judicial application, pre-packaged rehabilitation holds promise to make corporate restructurings faster, less costly, and more effective—ultimately benefiting debtors, creditors, and the broader economy.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:separator -->

					<item>
		<title><![CDATA[The Koh Samui Building Permit Fraud Scandal: Legal Implications and Remedial Pathways for Affected Property Owners]]></title>
		<link></link>
		<pubDate>Thu, 26 Mar 2026 01:20:55 +0000</pubDate>
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[silq]]></dc:creator>
		<guid isPermaLink="false"></guid>
		<description></description>
		<content:encoded><![CDATA[<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Introduction</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In March 2026, authorities in Surat Thani province uncovered a sophisticated criminal operation involving the forgery of construction permits issued by Koh Samui Municipality, sending shockwaves through Thailand’s luxury real estate market and raising profound legal questions for property owners and investors across Southern Thailand. The scandal, which came to public attention following a social media post by a municipal legal officer on March 21, 2026, involves fraudulent Or.1 construction permits bearing forged signatures, including that of the mayor, and has exposed critical vulnerabilities in the administration of Thailand’s building control system.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The investigation has revealed that a clerical officer in the public works division, who joined the civil service in June 2022, is suspected of producing fraudulent permits in exchange for payments reportedly amounting to 100,000 baht per permit. While initial investigations have identified at least 10 fake permits linked to luxury villa developments popular with foreign buyers, authorities have expanded their inquiry to determine whether senior officials in the engineering division were involved in or benefited from the scheme. The case has prompted Koh Samui Mayor Ramnet Jaikwang to order a retrospective audit of all construction permits and to file a formal police complaint against the implicated official for forgery and official misconduct.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">The Nature and Scope of the Fraudulent Permit Scheme</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The fraudulent permit scheme exploited procedural vulnerabilities in Thailand’s construction approval system, specifically Section 39 Bis of the Building Control Act B.E. 2522 (1979), which permits developers to commence construction upon submission of certified documentation without awaiting formal municipal approval. This fast-track mechanism, designed to streamline development processes, relies heavily on the integrity of submitted documents and the professional certifications of licensed architects and engineers.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">According to investigative reports, fraud was first detected in October 2025 during routine inspections of private construction projects and commercial building modifications. Permit holders presented what appeared to be official Or.1 construction permits to inspectors, but verification revealed that these documents were not registered in the municipal system and contained forged signatures, including that of the mayor. The investigation has since identified nearly ten construction permits issued without proper authorisation, though authorities have acknowledged that the full scope of the fraud may be broader.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The scheme reportedly involved a network of lower-level officials who issued fraudulent paperwork to developers, often in connection with luxury villa projects, with external intermediaries acting as brokers to connect developers seeking expedited approvals with insiders capable of producing counterfeit permits. The involvement of external facilitators and the sophistication of the forgery have led investigators to suspect that a junior officer could not have acted alone, raising the possibility of a wider network that may include senior municipal officials.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">It is worth noting that this is not the first instance of irregular permit issuance on Koh Samui. Inspections conducted between 2024 and 2025 under the Samui Model, a joint initiative involving the Internal Security Operations Command Region 4, the Office of the Ombudsman, and the National Anti-Corruption Commission, uncovered more than 100 questionable building permits, including approvals issued in restricted areas and permits that violated environmental laws. Many of those cases remain under investigation by anti-corruption authorities and the police, suggesting that the recent scandal may reflect systemic issues rather than an isolated incident.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Implications for Property Owners Who Have Built Using Fraudulent Permits</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For property owners who have constructed buildings based on fraudulent Or.1 permits, the legal and practical implications are severe and multifaceted. These implications extend beyond mere administrative inconvenience to encompass structural safety concerns, potential demolition orders, insurance complications, and criminal exposure.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Structural Safety and Regulatory Compliance</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The most immediate concern for affected property owners is structural safety. Construction permits serve as the gateway for municipal oversight of building works, ensuring that projects comply with the Building Control Act, zoning regulations, structural engineering standards, and environmental requirements. When a permit is fraudulent, it necessarily means that the construction was not subjected to the mandatory review processes designed to verify compliance with these critical standards.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In the context of luxury villas on Koh Samui, many of which are situated on hillsides or elevated terrain, the structural integrity concerns are particularly acute. Hillside construction requires specialised engineering considerations related to soil stability, drainage, and seismic resistance, all of which are evaluated during the permit review process. Construction undertaken without proper oversight may lack essential safety features, posing risks not only to occupants but also to neighbouring properties and the broader community.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Legal Status and Enforcement Exposure</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Thai law, construction undertaken without a valid building permit is unlawful and exposes the property owner to enforcement action under the Building Control Act. The Act vests local competent officers with broad authority to address building violations, including the power to issue stop-work orders, prohibit building use, and ultimately order demolition.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Specifically, Section 40 of the Building Control Act authorises local competent officers to halt illegal construction and prohibit the use of buildings in areas where violations exist. Section 41 provides an opportunity for correction, allowing the building owner to submit correction applications and make necessary adjustments within a specified timeframe. However, Section 42 addresses the more serious scenario where violations are deemed uncorrectable or where orders are ignored, empowering officers to command demolition within a specified period.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Most critically, Section 43 provides that failure to comply with a demolition order allows the officer to request court action for the arrest and detention of non-compliant individuals and to conduct demolition at the owner’s expense, with the authority to seize or sell materials from the demolition to recover costs. These enforcement mechanisms are not theoretical; Thai courts have consistently upheld enforcement actions against unlawful construction, including in high-profile cases such as the Aetas Bangkok hotel, where the Supreme Administrative Court ordered the relevant authorities to enforce the Building Control Act, including the demolition of unlawfully constructed portions of the building.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Financial Consequences and Insurance Implications</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Property owners who have built using fraudulent permits face substantial financial exposure. Beyond the potential demolition costs, which can amount to millions of baht, owners may be subject to fines and penalties under the Building Control Act. Moreover, properties constructed without valid permits are unlikely to be insurable for structural defects or damage, as insurance policies typically require compliance with all applicable laws and regulations as a condition of coverage.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For owners who financed construction through Thai financial institutions, the discovery that the property lacks a valid building permit may constitute a default under their loan agreements, potentially triggering debt obligations and foreclosure proceedings. Similarly, properties with invalid permits cannot be lawfully transferred or sold, as the Land Office requires verification of building permit status as part of the due diligence process for property transactions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Potential Criminal Liability</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Property owners who unknowingly acquired or constructed properties using fraudulent permits may have defences against criminal prosecution, particularly if they can demonstrate good faith reliance on what appeared to be official documentation. However, owners who were complicit in the fraud or who had reason to suspect that the permits were irregular but proceeded with construction anyway may face criminal exposure under Thai law.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The investigation has already resulted in the filing of a police complaint against the implicated municipal official for forgery and misconduct in office. As the investigation expands, authorities have indicated that further legal action may be taken against other individuals involved, potentially including developers, brokers, and property owners who participated in or benefited from the scheme.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Implications for Prospective Purchasers of Affected Properties</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For individuals considering purchasing properties on Koh Samui that may be affected by the fraudulent permit scandal, the risks are substantial and warrant careful consideration. The acquisition of a property constructed under a fraudulent building permit can result in the purchaser inheriting all legal liabilities and financial burdens associated with the unlawful construction.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Title and Ownership Issues</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under the Thai land registration system, the Chanote or Nor Sor 3 Kor are documentary evidence of ownership. However, such title does not guarantee the legality of the structures constructed on the land. Accordingly, a purchaser acquiring land with an unlawfully constructed building may be exposed to enforcement risks, including restrictions on use, potential demolition orders, and limitations affecting financing, insurance, and future transactions.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Land Office may require verification of building permit status as part of the due diligence process for property transfers, particularly for properties with substantial structures. If the building permit is found to be fraudulent, the Land Office may refuse to register the transfer or require that the property be brought into compliance before registration can proceed.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Resale and Future Transfer Restrictions</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Properties constructed with fraudulent permits cannot be lawfully resold until the permit issue is resolved. Even if a purchaser is willing to accept the risk, the practical reality is that most buyers will require clean documentation as a condition of purchase. Financial institutions will generally not provide mortgage financing for properties with permit irregularities, further limiting the pool of potential buyers.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The discovery of permit fraud may also affect the validity of leases, particularly for foreign purchasers who acquire properties through leasehold structures. Thai law requires leases exceeding three years to be registered to be enforceable, and registration requires verification that the leased property complies with applicable laws.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Potential Claims Against Sellers and Developers</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Purchasers who acquire properties later discovered to have fraudulent permits may have legal recourse against the sellers or developers from whom they purchased. Under the Civil and Commercial Code, a seller is liable for defects in the property sold, including those that render the property unfit for its intended purpose or substantially diminish its value.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">However, the practical effectiveness of such claims depends on the seller's or developer's financial viability and continued presence in Thailand. Developers involved in fraudulent schemes may have structured their affairs to shield assets from claims, and foreign purchasers may face significant practical obstacles in pursuing litigation against Thai parties.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Legal Consequences Under Thai Law</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The issuance of fraudulent construction permits implicates multiple areas of Thai law, including criminal law, administrative law, and civil liability. Understanding these legal frameworks is essential for affected property owners and prospective purchasers.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Criminal Law Implications</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The forgery of official documents constitutes a serious criminal offence under the Thai Criminal Code. Section 265 provides that anyone who makes a forged official document or who uses a forged official document is subject to imprisonment for a term of six months to five years and a fine of ten thousand to one hundred thousand baht. The penalty increases if the document is used to cause damage to another person or the public.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In the Koh Samui case, the implicated municipal official faces investigation for forgery and misconduct in office. Additionally, external brokers who facilitated the issuance of fraudulent permits may face criminal charges as accomplices. Developers and property owners who knowingly participated in the scheme may also face criminal exposure.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Administrative Law Consequences</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">From an administrative law perspective, fraudulent permits are void ab initio, meaning they have no legal effect from the outset. The Koh Samui Municipality, through its ongoing retrospective audit, has the authority to declare fraudulent permits invalid and to take enforcement action against the affected properties.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Property owners who believe their permits may be fraudulent should note that administrative decisions regarding permit validity may be subject to challenge in the Administrative Court. Under the Administrative Court Act B.E. 2542, parties aggrieved by administrative decisions have the right to petition for judicial review, particularly where decisions involve unlawful acts or omissions by government officials.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Civil Liability</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Civil liability may arise both between private parties and between the state and affected property owners. Property owners who have suffered losses due to fraudulent permits may have claims against the individuals who issued or facilitated the permits, as well as potentially against the municipality for negligence in supervising its employees.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">However, claims against the municipality face significant hurdles under Thai administrative law. Government entities enjoy certain immunities, and recovery may be limited or subject to procedural requirements that differ from ordinary civil litigation.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Correction Pathways Under Thai Law</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For property owners affected by the fraudulent permit scandal, several pathways exist to correct the legal status of their properties, though each presents unique challenges and requirements.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Verification and Documentation</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The first step for any property owner who suspects their permit may be fraudulent is to verify the permit directly with Koh Samui Municipality. Owners should contact the public works or engineering division in person to confirm that their permit is registered and valid. It is essential to understand that reliance on documents provided by sellers, agents, or developers alone is insufficient, as these may be part of the fraudulent scheme.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Upon verification that the permit is fraudulent, owners should gather all relevant documentation, including the Or.1 permit, land title deed, architectural and engineering certifications, construction contracts, payment receipts, and any correspondence with brokers or developers. These documents will be essential for determining the appropriate remedial pathway and for any potential claims against responsible parties.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Application for Retrospective Permit</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For properties where the construction itself is otherwise compliant with applicable laws and regulations, the most straightforward remedial pathway is to apply for a retrospective building permit. Under the Building Control Act, local authorities have the discretion to consider applications for permits after construction has been completed, provided that the building meets all applicable safety and regulatory standards.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The retrospective permit application process typically requires submission of architectural plans, structural calculations, and certifications from licensed architects and engineers attesting to the building’s compliance with the Building Control Act. The municipality may also require inspections to verify the accuracy of submitted documentation and to confirm that the construction meets safety standards.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Property owners should be aware that retrospective permits are not available in all cases. If the building violates zoning regulations, encroaches on protected areas, or fails to meet structural safety requirements, the municipality may refuse to issue a permit and may instead order demolition or modification.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Modification and Correction</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">In cases where the building is generally compliant but has specific violations that can be corrected, the property owner may be able to obtain a permit by undertaking remedial works. Under Section 41 of the Building Control Act, local competent officers may order the correction of violations and allow the building owner to submit correction applications within a set timeframe.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">This pathway requires engagement with licensed architects and engineers who can assess the building, identify violations, and design corrective measures. The scope of required corrections may range from relatively minor modifications to significant structural alterations, depending on the nature of the violations.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Demolition and Reconstruction</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">For properties that cannot be brought into compliance with the Building Control Act, demolition may be the only option available. While this outcome is the most severe, property owners facing demolition orders should understand their rights under Thai law, including the right to challenge orders that are arbitrary or procedurally defective.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Under Section 42 of the Building Control Act, demolition orders must be issued with specified timeframes and must follow regulatory guidelines. Property owners who believe a demolition order is unjustified may seek review through administrative channels or challenge the order in the Administrative Court.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Claims for Compensation</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Property owners who have suffered losses due to fraudulent permits may have claims for compensation against the individuals responsible for the fraud. In cases where the municipality’s negligence contributed to the issuance of fraudulent permits, affected owners may also have claims against the municipality, though such claims face significant procedural and substantive hurdles.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">It is important to note that the pursuit of compensation claims should be carefully coordinated with efforts to correct the property’s legal status. In some cases, settlement of claims against developers or brokers may include agreements to fund corrective works or to participate in the permit rectification process.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Due Diligence for Future Transactions</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Koh Samui fake building permit scandal underscores the critical importance of thorough due diligence for anyone acquiring or developing property in Southern Thailand. Prospective purchasers should adopt a systematic approach to verifying the legal status of properties and should engage qualified professionals to assist in the verification process.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Direct Verification with Municipal Authorities</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The most essential due diligence step is direct verification of building permits with the relevant municipal authority. Purchasers should request that sellers provide the original Or.1 permit and should then verify with the municipality that the permit is registered in the official system and that all associated approvals are authentic. This verification should be conducted in person or through a reputable local legal professional, and reliance on copies or certifications provided by the seller is insufficient.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Engagement of Independent Professionals</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Purchasers should engage a qualified Thai real estate lawyer with experience in construction law and property fraud, as well as an independent, licensed architect or engineer to assess the property’s compliance with the Building Control Act. These professionals can identify red flags that may not be apparent to lay purchasers, such as discrepancies in signatures, missing municipal stamps, or inconsistencies between approved plans and constructed buildings.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Review of Broader Compliance</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Beyond the building permit itself, purchasers should verify that the property complies with all applicable laws and regulations, including zoning requirements, environmental impact assessment requirements where applicable, and restrictions on foreign ownership. For properties in coastal or hillside areas, additional scrutiny is warranted given the heightened regulatory scrutiny of such developments.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading {"level":3} -->
<h3 class="wp-block-heading">Transaction Structure Considerations</h3>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Purchasers should consider structuring transactions to mitigate risks associated with permit irregularities. This may include holding portions of the purchase price in escrow pending verification of permits, obtaining seller warranties regarding permit validity, and securing the right to terminate the purchase agreement if permit issues are discovered during due diligence.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:heading -->
<h2 class="wp-block-heading">Key Takeaways and Next Steps for Property Owners</h2>
<!-- /wp:heading -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The Koh Samui fake building permit scandal represents a serious breach of regulatory integrity with profound implications for property owners and investors in Southern Thailand. For owners who have constructed properties using fraudulent permits, the consequences range from financial losses and insurance complications to potential demolition orders and criminal exposure. For prospective purchasers, the risks of acquiring affected properties are substantial and require rigorous due diligence.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">The scandal also highlights systemic vulnerabilities in Thailand’s construction approval system, particularly the fast-track mechanism under Section 39 Bis of the Building Control Act, which prioritises expedited development at the potential cost of adequate oversight. As authorities continue their investigation and the retrospective audit of permits proceeds, property owners must take proactive steps to verify their documentation and seek appropriate legal remedies.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->

<!-- wp:paragraph -->
<p class="">Correcting the legal status of properties affected by fraudulent permits is possible through several pathways, including retrospective permit applications, modification and correction works, and, in some cases, demolition and reconstruction. However, each pathway requires engagement with qualified legal and technical professionals and careful coordination with municipal authorities. Property owners and prospective purchasers are strongly advised to seek professional guidance promptly to protect their interests and navigate the complex legal landscape exposed by the scandal.</p>
<!-- /wp:paragraph -->
